extraction_notes.note: The proof-sketch rule asks for rigor semi_formal on sketch proofs, but rigor is not allowed on proofs and the finishing step warns; the five sketches carry no rigor field and are marked by alternative: true on their proves edges.

The unnumbered '{\bf Claim:}' in the proof of Lemma 9 is treated as an inline claim step (step rule 7) with the labelled items (1)-(10) as its children; a Level-1 claim spanning its argument would leave the outer proof with a single step and its author labels unplaced.

The '(1=>2)' headings use the one-argument macro \BF{...}, which is not expanded and not detected as an author label; steps still start at them, except '(3=>4) This is obvious.', merged into the (2=>3) step as an immediate sentence.

Hand-tagged displays (\tag{1}, \tag{5}, \tag{a}, \tag{b}) inside proofs are not reported as facts and stay inside their proofs; the informal introduction definitions are recorded as also_stated_at of the Section 2 definitions; the two omitted summary/dependency figures are not represented.
Beliefs stated as 'we think' / 'we feel' were typed conjecture rather than remark or open_problem.
Proposition 2 is presented as the property 'almost all results' use, with proof omitted; typed external standard (uncited) rather than a paper result with rigor semi_formal.
Theorem 3 has no proof environment: its proof is the two prose paragraphs deriving coNP-hardness of the two decision problems (stated in minipages) from Theorems 8 and 9.
The derivation of Theorem 10 includes the sentence defining 'fixes', which is used only in that paragraph.

nodes.name: Interaction digraph
nodes.statement: The ``network'' terminology comes from the fact that the \EM{interaction digraph} of $f$ is often considered as the main parameter of $f$: the vertex set is $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and there is an arc from $j$ to $i$ if $f_i$ depends on input $j$.
nodes.statement_short: The interaction digraph of $f$ has vertex set $[n]$ and an arc $j\to i$ when $f_i$ depends on input $j$.

nodes.name: Černý's conjecture
nodes.statement: The central open problem concerning synchronization is the famous \v{C}ern\'y's conjecture \cite{C64,CPR71}, which says that any synchronizing deterministic automaton with $q$ states has a synchronizing word of length at most $(q-1)^2$.
assumptions: any synchronizing deterministic automaton with $q$ states
conclusions: has a synchronizing word of length at most $(q-1)^2$
nodes.statement_short: Every synchronizing DFA with $q$ states has a synchronizing word of length at most $(q-1)^2$.

nodes.name: Main theorem: synchronization of and-or-nets on strong signed digraphs without positive cycles
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a strongly connected signed digraph on $[n]$ without positive cycles. Either \begin{itemize} \item $G$ is a cycle and no BN on $G$ is synchronizing, or \item every and-or-net on $G$ has a synchronizing word of length at most $10(\sqrt{5}+1)^n$. \end{itemize}
assumptions: $G$ be a strongly connected signed digraph on $[n]$ without positive cycles
conclusions: $G$ is a cycle and no BN on $G$ is synchronizing
every and-or-net on $G$ has a synchronizing word of length at most $10(\sqrt{5}+1)^n$
nodes.statement_short: If $G$ is strong without positive cycles, either $G$ is a non-synchronizable cycle or every and-or-net on $G$ synchronizes within $10(\sqrt5+1)^n$ steps.
nodes.label: thm:main

nodes.name: Proof outline of Theorem 1 (introduction)
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be as in Theorem~\ref{thm:main} and non-trivial. To obtain the bound $10(\sqrt{5}+1)^n$, we prove that if $f$ is an and-or-net on $G$, the word $w$ in the previous lemma is of length at most $F(n+2)$, the $(n+2)$th Fibonacci number. From that, we next prove that if $G$ is not a cycle, then for every states $x,y$ there is a word $w$ of length at most $3F(n+4)$ such that $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$. This immediately implies that $f$ has a synchronizing word of length at most $3F(n+4)(2^n-1)$ and an easy computation shows that this is less than $10(\sqrt{5}+1)^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Outline: bound the flipping word by $F(n+2)$, synchronize pairs within $3F(n+4)$, then apply Černý's pairwise argument over all $2^n$ states.

nodes.name: Flipping bound F(n+2)
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be as in Theorem~\ref{thm:main} and non-trivial. To obtain the bound $10(\sqrt{5}+1)^n$, we prove that if $f$ is an and-or-net on $G$, the word $w$ in the previous lemma is of length at most $F(n+2)$, the $(n+2)$th Fibonacci number.
nodes.statement_short: For and-or-nets the flipping word of the lemma has length at most $F(n+2)$.

nodes.name: Pairwise and global synchronization
nodes.statement: From that, we next prove that if $G$ is not a cycle, then for every states $x,y$ there is a word $w$ of length at most $3F(n+4)$ such that $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$. This immediately implies that $f$ has a synchronizing word of length at most $3F(n+4)(2^n-1)$ and an easy computation shows that this is less than $10(\sqrt{5}+1)^n$.
nodes.statement_short: If $G$ is not a cycle, any two states merge within $3F(n+4)$, giving a synchronizing word of length $3F(n+4)(2^n-1)<10(\sqrt5+1)^n$.

nodes.name: Flipping lemma
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a non-trivial strongly connected signed digraph on $[n]$ without positive~cycles, and let $f$ be a BN on $G$. For all $i\in [n]$ and $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, we have $f^w(x)_i\neq x_i$ for some word~$w$.
assumptions: $G$ be a non-trivial strongly connected signed digraph on $[n]$ without positive~cycles
$f$ be a BN on $G$
$i\in [n]$ and $x\in\{0,1\}^n$
conclusions: we have $f^w(x)_i\neq x_i$ for some word~$w$
nodes.statement_short: On a non-trivial strong signed digraph without positive cycles, every component of every state can be flipped by some asynchronous word.
nodes.label: lem:flipping_lemma

nodes.name: Fast synchronization of some and-or-net
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a strongly connected signed digraph on $[n]$ without positive cycles, which is not a cycle. At least one and-or-net on $G$ has a synchronizing word of length at most $5n(\sqrt{2})^n$.
also_stated_at: Let $G$ be a strongly connected signed digraph on $[n]$ without positive cycles, which is not a cycle. At least one and-or-net on $G$ has a synchronizing word of length at most $5n(\sqrt{2})^n$.
assumptions: $G$ be a strongly connected signed digraph on $[n]$ without positive cycles, which is not a cycle
conclusions: At least one and-or-net on $G$ has a synchronizing word of length at most $5n(\sqrt{2})^n$
nodes.statement_short: For strong $G$ without positive cycles that is not a cycle, some and-or-net on $G$ synchronizes within $5n(\sqrt2)^n$ steps.
nodes.label: thm:fast

nodes.name: coNP-hardness of deciding and-or-synchronization
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a signed digraph on $[n]$. If $G$ is not strongly connected or has a positive cycle, then it is coNP-hard to decide if every and-or-net on $G$ is synchronizing (even if $G$ has maximum in-degree at most $2$ and a vertex meeting every cycle).
assumptions: $G$ be a signed digraph on $[n]$
$G$ is not strongly connected or has a positive cycle
conclusions: it is coNP-hard to decide if every and-or-net on $G$ is synchronizing (even if $G$ has maximum in-degree at most $2$ and a vertex meeting every cycle)
nodes.statement_short: Without strong connectivity or without the no-positive-cycle hypothesis, deciding whether all and-or-nets on $G$ synchronize is coNP-hard.
nodes.label: thm:complexity

nodes.name: Non-synchronizing BN when no in-degree 0 or 2
nodes.statement: If $G$ is a simple signed digraph without vertices of in-degree $0$ or $2$, then at least one BN on $G$ is not synchronizing.
also_stated_at: Suppose that $G$ is a simple signed digraph without vertices of in-degree $0$ or $2$. Then at least one BN on $G$ is not synchronizing.
assumptions: $G$ is a simple signed digraph without vertices of in-degree $0$ or $2$
conclusions: at least one BN on $G$ is not synchronizing
nodes.label: pro:02

nodes.name: Digraph
nodes.statement: A \EM{digraph} is a couple $G=(V,E)$ where $V$ is a set of vertices and $E\subseteq V^2$ is a set of arcs.
differentia: $E\subseteq V^2$ is a set of arcs

nodes.name: Induced subgraph $G[I]$ and $G\setminus I$
nodes.statement: Given $I\subseteq V$, the subgraph of $G$ induced by $I$ is denoted $G[I]$, and $G\setminus I$ means $G[V\setminus I]$.

nodes.name: Strongly connected component
nodes.statement: A \EM{strongly connected component} (\EM{strong component} for short) of a digraph $G$ is an induced subgraph which is \EM{strongly connected} (\EM{strong} for short) and maximal for this property.

nodes.name: Initial and terminal strong components
nodes.statement: A strong component $G[I]$ is \EM{initial} if $G$ has no arc from $V\setminus I$ to $I$, and \EM{terminal} if $G$ has no arc from $I$ to $V\setminus I$.

nodes.name: Source
nodes.statement: A \EM{source} is a vertex of in-degree zero.

nodes.name: Trivial digraph
nodes.statement: A digraph is \EM{trivial} if it has a unique vertex and no arc.
differentia: it has a unique vertex and no arc

nodes.name: Signed digraph
nodes.statement: A \EM{signed digraph} $G$ is a couple $(V,E)$ where $E\subseteq V^2\times\{-1,1\}$.

nodes.name: Arc sign, in-neighbor and out-neighbor
nodes.statement: If $(j,i,s)\in E$ then $G$ has an arc from $j$ to $i$ of sign $s$; we also say that $j$ is an in-neighbor of $i$ of sign $s$ and that $i$ is an out-neighbor of $j$ of sign $s$.

nodes.name: Simple and full-positive signed digraphs
nodes.statement: We say that $G$ is \EM{simple} if it has not both a positive arc and a negative arc from one vertex to another, and \EM{full-positive} if all its arcs are positive.
also_stated_at: We say that $G$ is \EM{simple} if it does not contains both a positive and negative arc from one vertex to another (if $G$ is strongly connected and has no positive cycles then it is necessarily simple).

nodes.name: Subgraph of a signed digraph
nodes.statement: A subgraph of $G$ is a signed digraph $(V',E')$ with $V'\subseteq V$ and $E'\subseteq E$.

nodes.name: Cycles and paths
nodes.statement: Cycles and paths of $G$ are regarded as simple subgraphs (and thus have no repeated vertices).

nodes.name: Sign of a cycle or a path
nodes.statement: The \EM{sign of a cycle or a path} of $G$ is the product of the signs of its arcs.
nodes.definiendum: sign of a cycle or a path

nodes.name: Underlying digraph
nodes.statement: The underlying (unsigned) digraph of $G$ has vertex set $V$ and an arc from $j$ to $i$ if $G$ has a positive or a negative arc from $j$ to $i$.

nodes.name: Configuration
nodes.statement: A \EM{configuration} on a finite set $V$ is a map $x$ from $V$ to $\{0,1\}$, and for $i\in V$ we write $x_i$ instead of $x(i)$.

nodes.name: Set of configurations $\{0,1\}^V$
nodes.statement: The set of configurations on $V$ is denoted $\{0,1\}^V$.

nodes.name: Restriction $x_I$
nodes.statement: Given $I\subseteq V$, we denote by $x_I$ the restriction of $x$ to $I$.

nodes.name: Indicator configuration $e_I$
nodes.statement: We denote by $e_I$ the configuration on $V$ defined by $(e_I)_i=1$ for all $i\in I$ and $(e_I)_i=0$ for all $i\in V\setminus I$.

nodes.name: Notation $e_i$
nodes.statement: If $i\in V$, we write $e_i$ instead of $e_{\{i\}}$.

nodes.name: Sum of configurations modulo two
nodes.statement: If $x,y$ are configurations on $V$ then $x+y$ is the configuration $z$ on $V$ such that $z_i=x_i+y_i$ for all $i\in V$, where the sum is modulo two.

nodes.name: All-zero and all-one configurations
nodes.statement: We denote by ${\mathbf{0}}$ and $\mathbf{1}$ the all-zero and all-one configurations.

nodes.name: Word, length and letter set
nodes.statement: A word $w$ over $V$ is a finite sequence of elements in $V$; its length is denoted $|w|$ and the set of letters that appear in $w$ is denoted $\{w\}$.

nodes.name: Concatenation of words
nodes.statement: The concatenation of two words $u$ and $v$ is denoted $u,v$ or $uv$.

nodes.name: Empty word
nodes.statement: The empty word, of length $0$, is denoted $\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Boolean network (BN)
nodes.statement: A \EM{Boolean network} (BN) with component set $V$ is a function $f:\{0,1\}^V\to\{0,1\}^V$.
also_stated_at: A \EM{Boolean network} (BN) is a finite dynamical system usually defined by a function \[ f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n,\qquad x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\mapsto f(x)=(f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x)). \]

nodes.name: Component function $f_i$
nodes.statement: For $i\in V$, we denote by $f_i$ the map from $\{0,1\}^V$ to $\{0,1\}$ defined by $f_i(x)=f(x)_i$ for all configurations $x$ on $V$.

nodes.name: $a$-constant function
nodes.statement: For $a\in\{0,1\}$, we say that $f_i$ is the \EM{$a$-constant function} if $f_i(x)=a$ for all $x\in\{0,1\}^V$.

nodes.name: Signed interaction digraph
nodes.statement: The \EM{signed interaction digraph} of $f$ is the signed digraph $G$ with vertex set $V$ such that, for all $i,j\in V$, there is a positive (negative) arc from $j$ to $i$ is there exists a configuration $x$ on $V$ with $x_j=0$ such that $f_i(x+e_j)-f_i(x)$ is positive (negative).
also_stated_at: the vertex set is $[n]$ and there is a positive (negative) arc from $j$ to $i$ if there is $x,y\in \{0,1\}^n$ that only differ in $x_j<y_j$ such that $f_i(y)-f_i(x)$ is positive (negative)
nodes.statement_short: $G$ has a positive (negative) arc $j\to i$ when flipping $x_j$ from 0 to 1 can increase (decrease) $f_i$.

nodes.name: BN on a signed digraph
nodes.statement: Given a signed digraph $G$, a BN \EM{on} $G$ is a BN whose signed interaction digraph is~$G$.
also_stated_at: If $G$ is the signed interaction digraph $f$ then we say that $f$ is a BN \EM{on} $G$.

nodes.name: $i$-unstable configuration
nodes.statement: Given a vertex $i$ in $G$, an \EM{$i$-unstable} configuration in $G$ is a configuration $x\in\{0,1\}^V$ such that $x_j\neq x_i$ for every positive in-neighbor $j$ of $i$ in $G$ and $x_j= x_i$ for every negative in-neighbor $j$ of $i$ in $G$.
differentia: $x_j\neq x_i$ for every positive in-neighbor $j$ of $i$ in $G$
$x_j= x_i$ for every negative in-neighbor $j$ of $i$ in $G$

nodes.name: Flipping property of unstable configurations
nodes.statement: If $i$ is a vertex of $G$ of in-degree at least one, and $x$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$, then $f_i(x)\neq x_i$ for every BN $f$ on $G$.
assumptions: $i$ is a vertex of $G$ of in-degree at least one
$x$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$
conclusions: $f_i(x)\neq x_i$ for every BN $f$ on $G$
nodes.label: pro:flipping

nodes.name: Conjunction
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a BN with component set $V$ and $G$ its signed interaction digraph. For $i\in V$, we say that $f_i$ is a \EM{conjunction} if, for all configurations $x$ on $V$, we have $f_i(x)=1$ if and only if $x_j=1$ for all positive in-neighbors $j$ of $i$ in $G$ and $x_j=0$ for all the negative in-neighbors $j$ of $i$ in $G$.
nodes.statement_short: $f_i$ is a conjunction if $f_i(x)=1$ exactly when all positive in-neighbors are 1 and all negative in-neighbors are 0.

nodes.name: Disjunction
nodes.statement: Similarly, we say that $f_i$ is a \EM{disjunction} if, for all configurations $x$ on $V$, we have $f_i(x)=0$ if and only if $x_j=0$ for all positive in-neighbors $j$ of $i$ in $G$ and $x_j=1$ for all the negative in-neighbors $j$ of $i$ in $G$.
nodes.statement_short: $f_i$ is a disjunction if $f_i(x)=0$ exactly when all positive in-neighbors are 0 and all negative in-neighbors are 1.

nodes.name: And-or-net
nodes.statement: We say that $f$ is an \EM{and-or-net} if $f_i$ is a conjunction or a disjunction for all $i\in V$.
differentia: $f_i$ is a conjunction or a disjunction for all $i\in V$
also_stated_at: We say that $f$ is an \EM{and-or-net} if, for every $i\in [n]$, the component $f_i$ of $f$ is a conjunction or a disjunction of positive or negative literals, that is, there is $a\in \{0,1\}$ such that, for every state $x$, we have $f_i(x)=a$ if and only if $x_j=a$ for all positive arcs of $G$ from $j$ to $i$ and $x_j\neq a$ for all negative arcs of $G$ from $j$ to $i$ (so if $a=1$ then $f_i$ is a conjunction, and if $a=0$ then $f_i$ is a disjunction).

nodes.name: And-net and or-net
nodes.statement: We say that $f$ is an \EM{and-net} (\EM{or-net}) if $f_i$ is a conjunction (disjunction) for all $i\in V$.

nodes.name: BNs on simple digraphs of in-degree at most two are and-or-nets
nodes.statement: If $G$ is simple and has maximum in-degree at most $2$, then every BN $f$ on $G$ is an and-or-net.
also_stated_at: if $G$ is a simple signed digraph with maximum in-degree at most two, then every BN on $G$ is an and-or-net
assumptions: $G$ is simple and has maximum in-degree at most $2$
conclusions: every BN $f$ on $G$ is an and-or-net

nodes.name: Asynchronous update $f^i$
nodes.statement: For all $i\in V$, we denote by $f^i$ the BN with component set $V$ defined as follows: for all configurations $x$ on $V$, we have $f^i(x)_i=f(x)_i$ and $f^i(x)_j=x_j$ for all $j\in V\setminus\{i\}$.

nodes.name: Action of a word $f^w$
nodes.statement: Given a word $w=i_1,\dots,i_\ell$ over $V$, we set $f^w=f^{i_\ell}\circ f^{i_{\ell-1}}\circ\dots\circ f^{i_1}$.

nodes.name: Synchronizing word; synchronizing BN
nodes.statement: We say that $w$ is a \EM{synchronizing word} for $f$ if $f^w$ is a constant function, and $f$ is \EM{synchronizing} if it has at least one synchronizing word.
also_stated_at: A word $w$ over $[n]$ \EM{synchronizes} $f$ if it synchronizes its asynchronous automaton, that is, if $f^w$ is a constant function. If $w$ synchronizes $f$ then $w$ is a \EM{synchronizing word} for $f$, and if $f$ admits a synchronizing word then $f$ is \EM{synchronizing}.

nodes.name: Asynchronous automaton
nodes.statement: The functions $f^i$ define a deterministic finite automaton, called \EM{asynchronous automaton} of~$f$, in a natural way: the alphabet is $V$, the set of states is $\{0,1\}^V$ and the transition function $\delta:\{0,1\}^V\times [n]\to\{0,1\}^V$ is defined by $\delta(x,i)=f^i(x)$ for all $(x,i)\in\{0,1\}^V\times [n]$.
also_stated_at: This asynchronous dynamics can be described by the paths of a deterministic finite automaton called \EM{asynchronous automaton} of $f$: the set of states is $\{0,1\}^n$, the alphabet is $[n]$ and the action of letter $i$ on a state $x$, denoted $f^i(x)$, is the state obtained from $x$ by updating the component $i$ only, that is, $f^i(x)=(x_1,\dots,f_i(x),\dots,x_n)$. These actions are extended to any word $w=i_1,\dots,i_\ell$ over the alphabet $[n]$ in the natural way, by setting $f^w=f^{i_\ell}\circ f^{i_{\ell-1}}\circ\dots\circ f^{i_1}$.
nodes.statement_short: The automaton with states $\{0,1\}^V$, alphabet $V$ and transitions $\delta(x,i)=f^i(x)$.

nodes.name: State diagram $\Gamma(f)$
nodes.statement: The \EM{state diagram} of the asynchronous automaton of $f$ is then the labelled digraph $\Gamma(f)$ with vertex set $\{0,1\}^V$ and with an arc from $x$ to $f^i(x)$ labelled by $i$ for all $(x,i)\in\{0,1\}^V\times [n]$.

nodes.name: And-net and or-net on a 3-vertex digraph synchronized by 231123
nodes.statement_short: A 3-vertex signed digraph with two negative cycles whose two BNs (and-net, or-net) are both synchronized by $w=231123$.
nodes.label: ex1

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement:
Let $V$ be the vertex set of $G$. Given an arc of $G$ from $j$ to $i$, we set $a_{ji}=0$ if this arc is positive and $a_{ji}=1$ otherwise. For all $i\in V$, let $d_i$ be the in-degree of $i$ in $G$, and suppose that $d_i
eq 0,2$. Let $f$ be the BN with component set $V$ defined as follows. Given a configuration $x$ on $V$, let $h_i(x)$ be the number of in-neighbors $j$ of $i$ with $x_j+a_{ji}=1$. For each vertex $i$, we fix an in-neighbor $\phi(i)$ of $i$ and we define $f_i$ as follows: for all configurations $x$ on $V$, \[ f_i(x)= \left\{  egin{array}{ll} 1&	extrm{ if $h_i(x)>d_i/2$,}\[1mm] x_{\phi(i)}+a_{\phi(i)i}&	extrm{ if $h_i(x)=d_i/2$},\[1mm] 0&	extrm{ if $h_i(x)<d_i/2$.} \end{array} ight. \] \medskip Let $H$ be the signed interaction digraph of $f$, and let us prove that $H=G$. One easily checks that $H$ is a subgraph of $G$. To prove the converse, suppose that $G$ has an arc from $j$ to $i$. If $d_i$ is odd there is $x$ such that $x_j+a_{ji}=0$ and $h_i(x)=(d_i-1)/2$. Thus $f_i(x)<f_i(x+e_j)$ so $H$ has an arc from $j$ to $i$ which is positive if $a_{ji}=0$ and negative otherwise. If $d_i$ is even then, since $d_i\geq 4$, there is $x$ such that $x_j+a_{ji}=x_{\phi(i)}+a_{\phi(i)i}=0$ and $h_i(x)=d_i/2$. We deduce that $f_i(x)<f_i(x+e_j)$ so $H$ has an arc from $j$ to $i$ which is positive if $a_{ji}=0$ and negative otherwise. Consequently, $H=G$, that is, $f$ is a BN on $G$. \medskip We now prove that $f$ is not synchronizing. Let $x,y$ be opposite configurations, that is, $x_i
eq y_i$ for all $i\in V$. We have $h_i(y)=d_i-h_i(x)$, thus if $h_i(x)
eq d_i/2$ then $f_i(x)
eq f_i(y)$. Otherwise, $h_i(x)=h_i(y)=d_i/2$ thus $f_i(x)=x_{\phi(i)}+a_{\phi(i)i}
eq y_{\phi(i)}+a_{\phi(i)i}=f_i(y)$. So $f_i(x)
eq f_i(y)$ in every case. Consequently, $f^i(x)$ and $f^i(y)$ are opposite. We deduce that, for any word $w$, $f^w(x)$ and $f^w(y)$ are opposite, and thus $f$ is not synchronizing.
nodes.statement_short: Construct a majority-type BN on $G$ with tie-breaking by a fixed in-neighbor; it maps opposite configurations to opposite configurations, so it never synchronizes.

nodes.name: Construct majority BN f
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be the vertex set of $G$. Given an arc of $G$ from $j$ to $i$, we set $a_{ji}=0$ if this arc is positive and $a_{ji}=1$ otherwise. For all $i\in V$, let $d_i$ be the in-degree of $i$ in $G$, and suppose that $d_i\neq 0,2$. Let $f$ be the BN with component set $V$ defined as follows. Given a configuration $x$ on $V$, let $h_i(x)$ be the number of in-neighbors $j$ of $i$ with $x_j+a_{ji}=1$. For each vertex $i$, we fix an in-neighbor $\phi(i)$ of $i$ and we define $f_i$ as follows: for all configurations $x$ on $V$, \[ f_i(x)= \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1&\textrm{ if $h_i(x)>d_i/2$,}\\[1mm] x_{\phi(i)}+a_{\phi(i)i}&\textrm{ if $h_i(x)=d_i/2$},\\[1mm] 0&\textrm{ if $h_i(x)<d_i/2$.} \end{array} \right. \]
nodes.statement_short: Define $f_i$ by comparing $h_i(x)$ with $d_i/2$, ties broken by a fixed in-neighbor $\phi(i)$.

nodes.name: f is a BN on G
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be the signed interaction digraph of $f$, and let us prove that $H=G$. One easily checks that $H$ is a subgraph of $G$. To prove the converse, suppose that $G$ has an arc from $j$ to $i$. If $d_i$ is odd there is $x$ such that $x_j+a_{ji}=0$ and $h_i(x)=(d_i-1)/2$. Thus $f_i(x)<f_i(x+e_j)$ so $H$ has an arc from $j$ to $i$ which is positive if $a_{ji}=0$ and negative otherwise. If $d_i$ is even then, since $d_i\geq 4$, there is $x$ such that $x_j+a_{ji}=x_{\phi(i)}+a_{\phi(i)i}=0$ and $h_i(x)=d_i/2$. We deduce that $f_i(x)<f_i(x+e_j)$ so $H$ has an arc from $j$ to $i$ which is positive if $a_{ji}=0$ and negative otherwise. Consequently, $H=G$, that is, $f$ is a BN on $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Check that every arc of $G$ appears in the interaction digraph of $f$ with the right sign, so $f$ is a BN on $G$.

nodes.name: f is not synchronizing
nodes.statement:
We now prove that $f$ is not synchronizing. Let $x,y$ be opposite configurations, that is, $x_i
eq y_i$ for all $i\in V$. We have $h_i(y)=d_i-h_i(x)$, thus if $h_i(x)
eq d_i/2$ then $f_i(x)
eq f_i(y)$. Otherwise, $h_i(x)=h_i(y)=d_i/2$ thus $f_i(x)=x_{\phi(i)}+a_{\phi(i)i}
eq y_{\phi(i)}+a_{\phi(i)i}=f_i(y)$. So $f_i(x)
eq f_i(y)$ in every case. Consequently, $f^i(x)$ and $f^i(y)$ are opposite. We deduce that, for any word $w$, $f^w(x)$ and $f^w(y)$ are opposite, and thus $f$ is not synchronizing.
nodes.statement_short: Opposite configurations stay opposite under every $f^i$, so $f$ is not synchronizing.

nodes.name: f_i separates opposite configurations
nodes.statement:
Let $x,y$ be opposite configurations, that is, $x_i
eq y_i$ for all $i\in V$. We have $h_i(y)=d_i-h_i(x)$, thus if $h_i(x)
eq d_i/2$ then $f_i(x)
eq f_i(y)$. Otherwise, $h_i(x)=h_i(y)=d_i/2$ thus $f_i(x)=x_{\phi(i)}+a_{\phi(i)i}
eq y_{\phi(i)}+a_{\phi(i)i}=f_i(y)$. So $f_i(x)
eq f_i(y)$ in every case.
nodes.statement_short: For opposite $x,y$, $f_i(x)\neq f_i(y)$ whether or not $h_i(x)=d_i/2$.

nodes.name: Opposition is preserved
nodes.statement: Consequently, $f^i(x)$ and $f^i(y)$ are opposite. We deduce that, for any word $w$, $f^w(x)$ and $f^w(y)$ are opposite, and thus $f$ is not synchronizing.
nodes.statement_short: Hence every word keeps $x,y$ opposite and $f$ is not synchronizing.

nodes.name: $I$-switch of a signed digraph
nodes.statement: Let $I\subseteq V$ and, for all $i\in V$, let $\sigma_I(i)=1$ if $i\in I$ and $\sigma_I(i)=-1$ if otherwise. The \EM{$I$-switch} of $G$ is the signed digraph $G^I=(V,E^I)$ with $E^I=\{(j,i,\sigma_I(j)\cdot s\cdot\sigma_I(i))\mid (j,i,s)\in E\}$; note that $G^I=G^{V\setminus I}$ and $(G^I)^I=G$.
nodes.statement_short: The $I$-switch $G^I$ flips the sign of every arc with exactly one endpoint in $I$.

nodes.name: Switch equivalence
nodes.statement: We say that $G$ is \EM{switch equivalent} to $H$ if $H=G^I$ for some $I\subseteq V$.

nodes.name: Switch preserves cycles and their signs
nodes.statement: Note also that $C$ is a cycle in $G$ if and only if $C^I$ is a cycle in $G^I$, and $C$ and $C^I$ have the same sign. Thus if $G$ has no positive (negative) cycles then every switch of $G$ has no positive (negative) cycles: this property is invariant by switch.
assumptions: $G$ has no positive (negative) cycles
conclusions: $C$ is a cycle in $G$ if and only if $C^I$ is a cycle in $G^I$, and $C$ and $C^I$ have the same sign
every switch of $G$ has no positive (negative) cycles
nodes.statement_short: Switching preserves cycles and their signs, so having no positive (negative) cycles is switch-invariant.

nodes.name: Symmetric version $G^s$
nodes.statement: The \EM{symmetric version} of $G$ is the signed digraph $G^s=(V,E^s)$ where $E^s=E\cup \{(i,j,s)\mid (j,i,s)\in E\}$.

nodes.name: Harary's theorem (switch version)
nodes.statement: A signed digraph $G$ is switch equivalent to a full-positive signed digraph if and only if $G^s$ has no negative cycles.
conclusions: A signed digraph $G$ is switch equivalent to a full-positive signed digraph if and only if $G^s$ has no negative cycles
equivalent_conditions: $G$ is switch equivalent to a full-positive signed digraph
nodes.label: pro:harary

nodes.name: $I$-switch of a BN
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a BN with component set $V$ and $I\subseteq V$. The \EM{$I$-switch} of $f$ is the BN $h$ with component set $V$ defined by $h(x)=f(x+e_I)+e_I$ for all configurations $x$ on $V$; note that if $h$ is the $I$-switch of $f$ then $f$ is the $I$-switch of $h$.

nodes.name: Properties of BN switches
nodes.statement: If $h$ is the $I$-switch of $f$, then: \begin{itemize} \item the signed interaction digraph of $h$ is the $I$-switch of the signed interaction digraph of $f$; \item if $f$ is an and-or-net, then $h$ is an and-or-net; \item for any word $w$, $h^w$ is the $I$-switch of $f^w$. \end{itemize}
assumptions: $h$ is the $I$-switch of $f$
conclusions: the signed interaction digraph of $h$ is the $I$-switch of the signed interaction digraph of $f$
if $f$ is an and-or-net, then $h$ is an and-or-net
for any word $w$, $h^w$ is the $I$-switch of $f^w$
nodes.statement_short: Switching a BN switches its signed interaction digraph, preserves and-or-nets and commutes with the action of words.
nodes.label: pro:BN_switch

nodes.name: Synchronizing word transferred through a switch
nodes.statement_short: The all-negative 3-cycle with a negative loop is a switch of Example 1's digraph, so $231123$ synchronizes every BN on it.
nodes.label: ex2

nodes.name: Standing notation for Section 3
nodes.statement: In all this section, $G$ is a signed digraph with vertex set $V$, and $n=|V|$.

nodes.name: Initial cycle
nodes.statement: An initial strong component of $G$ which is isomorphic to a cycle is an \EM{initial cycle} of $G$.

nodes.name: Initial cycles prevent synchronization
nodes.statement: If $G$ has an initial cycle, then no BN on $G$ is synchronizing.
assumptions: $G$ has an initial cycle
conclusions: no BN on $G$ is synchronizing
nodes.label: lem:initial_cycle

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Suppose that $G$ has an initial cycle with vertex set $I$, and let $f$ be a BN on $G$. Each vertex $i\in I$ has a unique in-neighbor in $G$, say $\phi(i)$, and $\phi(i)\in I$. Then one can easily check that $f_i(x)=x_{\phi(i)}+a_i$ for all configurations $x$ on $V$, where $a_i=0$ if the arc from $\phi(i)$ to $i$ is positive, and $a_i=1$ otherwise. Let $x$ and $y$ be $I$-opposite configurations, that is, $x_i\neq y_i$ for all $i\in I$. Then, for all $i\in I$, we have $f_i(x)=x_{\phi(i)}+a_i\neq y_{\phi(i)}+a_i=f_i(y)$, thus $f^i(x)$ and $f^i(y)$ are $I$-opposite configurations. We deduce that $f^w(x)$ and $f^w(y)$ are $I$-opposite configurations for any word $w$, and thus $f$ is not synchronizing.
nodes.statement_short: On an initial cycle each $f_i$ copies (or negates) its predecessor, so configurations opposite on the cycle stay opposite forever.

nodes.name: Cycle components copy predecessors
nodes.statement: Suppose that $G$ has an initial cycle with vertex set $I$, and let $f$ be a BN on $G$. Each vertex $i\in I$ has a unique in-neighbor in $G$, say $\phi(i)$, and $\phi(i)\in I$. Then one can easily check that $f_i(x)=x_{\phi(i)}+a_i$ for all configurations $x$ on $V$, where $a_i=0$ if the arc from $\phi(i)$ to $i$ is positive, and $a_i=1$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: On the initial cycle each $f_i(x)=x_{\phi(i)}+a_i$.

nodes.name: Opposition preserved by one update
nodes.statement: Let $x$ and $y$ be $I$-opposite configurations, that is, $x_i\neq y_i$ for all $i\in I$. Then, for all $i\in I$, we have $f_i(x)=x_{\phi(i)}+a_i\neq y_{\phi(i)}+a_i=f_i(y)$, thus $f^i(x)$ and $f^i(y)$ are $I$-opposite configurations.
nodes.statement_short: Each $f^i$ maps $I$-opposite configurations to $I$-opposite ones.

nodes.name: Not synchronizing
nodes.statement: We deduce that $f^w(x)$ and $f^w(y)$ are $I$-opposite configurations for any word $w$, and thus $f$ is not synchronizing.
nodes.statement_short: Hence every word keeps them $I$-opposite and $f$ is not synchronizing.

nodes.name: And-or-synchronizing digraph
nodes.statement: Let us say that $G$ is \EM{and-or-synchronizing} if every and-or-net on $G$ is synchronizing.

nodes.name: Source fixing a negative loop: non-synchronizing and-net
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be the following signed digraph: \[ \begin{tikzpicture} \node (1) at (0,0){$1$}; \node (2) at (1,0){$2$}; \draw[thick,->,red] (1.150) .. controls (-1,+1) and (-1,-1) .. (1.210); \path[thick,->] (2) edge[red] (1) ; \end{tikzpicture} \] Let $f$ be the and-net on $G$: $f_1(x)=\overline{x_1}\land \overline{x_2}$ and $f_2(x)=1$ for all configurations $x$ on~$[2]$. For $X=\{01,11\}$ we have $f^1(X)=X$ and $f^2(X)=X$. Hence, for any word $w$ we have $f^w(X)=X$ thus $f$ is not synchronizing.
nodes.statement_short: A negative loop fed by a source: the and-net leaves $X=\{01,11\}$ invariant, so it is not synchronizing.

nodes.name: Two and-or-synchronizing strong components giving a non-and-or-synchronizing digraph
nodes.statement_short: Two copies of an and-or-synchronizing strong digraph joined by positive arcs give a digraph without positive cycles, sources or initial cycles that is not and-or-synchronizing.

nodes.name: Forward path
nodes.statement: We say that a path $P$ of $G$ of is \EM{forward} if $P$ has at least one arc and the two vertices of the last arc belong to distinct strong components.
differentia: the two vertices of the last arc belong to distinct strong components

nodes.name: $i$-homogenous signed digraph
nodes.statement: Given a vertex $i\in V$, we say that $G$ is \EM{$i$-homogenous} if each strong component of $G$ contains a vertex $j$ such that all the forward paths from $j$ to $i$ have the same sign (obviously, if there is no forward paths from $j$ to $i$, then all the forward paths from $j$ to $i$ have the same sign).
nodes.statement_short: Every strong component contains a vertex all of whose forward paths to $i$ have the same sign.

nodes.name: Homogenous signed digraph
nodes.statement: We say that $G$ is \EM{homogenous} if it is $i$-homogenous for every $i\in V$.

nodes.name: Strong digraphs are homogenous
nodes.statement: For instance, if $G$ is strong, then there are no forward paths, and $G$ is trivially homogenous, so homogeneity is indeed a relaxation of strong connectivity.
assumptions: $G$ is strong
conclusions: there are no forward paths, and $G$ is trivially homogenous

nodes.name: Synchronization of and-or-nets on homogenous digraphs
nodes.statement: Suppose that $G$ is homogenous and has no positive cycles, no sources and no initial cycles. Then every and-or-net on $G$ has a synchronizing word of length at most $10(\sqrt{5}+1)^n$.
also_stated_at: Suppose that $G$ is homogenous and has no positive cycles, no sources and no initial cycles. Then every and-or-net on $G$ has a synchronizing word of length at most $10(\sqrt{5}+1)^n$.
assumptions: $G$ is homogenous and has no positive cycles, no sources and no initial cycles
conclusions: every and-or-net on $G$ has a synchronizing word of length at most $10(\sqrt{5}+1)^n$
nodes.statement_short: Homogeneity replaces strong connectivity: without positive cycles, sources and initial cycles, every and-or-net synchronizes within $10(\sqrt5+1)^n$.
nodes.label: thm:main2

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1 from Lemma 2 and Theorem 4
nodes.statement: Thus Theorem~\ref{thm:main} is a consequence of Lemma \ref{lem:initial_cycle} (first case) and Theorem~\ref{thm:main2} (second case).
nodes.statement_short: First case by Lemma 2 (a strong cycle is an initial cycle); second case by Theorem 4.

nodes.name: Homogeneity is switch-invariant
nodes.statement: If $G$ is homogenous, then every switch of $G$ is homogenous.
assumptions: $G$ is homogenous
conclusions: every switch of $G$ is homogenous
nodes.label: lem:invariant_homogeneity

nodes.name: No fixed vertex lemma
nodes.statement: Suppose that $G$ is $i$-homogenous and has no positive cycles and no sources. Let $f$ be a BN on $G$. For every configuration $x$ on $V$, there is a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)_i\neq x_i$.
assumptions: $G$ is $i$-homogenous and has no positive cycles and no sources
$f$ be a BN on $G$
configuration $x$ on $V$
conclusions: there is a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)_i\neq x_i$
nodes.statement_short: Under $i$-homogeneity, no positive cycles and no sources, component $i$ of any configuration can be flipped by some word.
nodes.label: lem:no_fixed_vertex

nodes.name: Sub-linear flipping word length
nodes.statement: A shortest word $w$ with the above property is obviously of length $|w|\leq 2^{n-1}$ (the number of configurations $y$ with $y_i=x_i$), but we think that $|w|$ is sub-linear according to the number $2^n$ of configurations.
nodes.statement_short: The shortest flipping word of Lemma 4 is believed sub-linear in the number $2^n$ of configurations.

nodes.name: Fibonacci numbers $F(n)$
nodes.statement: We obtained such a sub-linear bound when $f$ is an and-or-net: $|w|< F(n+2)$ where $F(0),F(1),F(2)\dots$ is the Fibonacci sequence.

nodes.name: Canalizing word
nodes.statement: Given a BN $f$ on $G$, a vertex $i\in V$ and $a\in\{0,1\}$, a \EM{canalizing word from} $(i,a)$ is a word $w$ over $V\setminus i$ without repeated letters such that, for some configuration $b$ on $\{w\}$ we have: \[ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^V,\qquad x_i=a~\Rightarrow f^w(x)_{\{w\}}=b. \]
nodes.genus: word $w$ over $V\setminus i$ without repeated letters
nodes.statement_short: A repetition-free word avoiding $i$ that forces its letters to fixed values $b$ whenever $x_i=a$.

nodes.name: Image of a canalizing word; canalized vertex
nodes.statement: If $w$ is canalizing from $(i,a)$, the configuration $b$ with the above property is called the \EM{image} of $w$, and for each $j\in\{w\}$, we say that $j$ is \EM{canalized} to $b_j$ by $w$.

nodes.name: Canalizing words in and-nets
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be the and-net on $G$. Take $i\in V$ and let $I$ be the set of positive out-neighbors of $i$ distinct from $i$. For any configuration $x$ on $V$, if $x_i=0$ then $f_j(x)=0$ for all $j\in I$. We deduce that any permutation of $I$ is a canalizing word from $(i,0)$, which canalizes each member of $I$ to $0$. Similarly, if $J$ is the set of negative out-neighbors of $i$ distinct from $i$, then any permutation of $J$ is a canalizing word from $(i,1)$, which canalizes each member of $J$ to $0$. We deduce that if $i$ has at least one out-neighbor distinct from $i$, then there is a canalizing word from $(i,0)$ or $(i,1)$ which is of length at least one (this basic property is crucial for the bound of Lemma~\ref{lem:no_fixed_vertex_2} below). Suppose now that $G$ has a full-positive path $P$ of length $\ell\geq 1$ with vertices $i_0,i_1,\dots,i_\ell$ in order. Then $w=i_1i_2\dots i_\ell$ is a canalizing word from $(i_0,0)$ which canalizes $i_k$ to $0$ for $1\leq k\leq\ell$.
nodes.statement_short: In the and-net, permutations of positive (negative) out-neighbors of $i$ are canalizing from $(i,0)$ ($(i,1)$), and full-positive paths give canalizing words.

nodes.name: Fibonacci inequality $F(n+2-m)+m\leq F(n+2)$
nodes.statement: The following bound on the length of the word $w$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:no_fixed_vertex}, which works for and-or-nets, is suited for a proof by induction; it implies the bound $|w|< F(n+2)$ announced above since $F(n+2-m)+m\leq F(n+2)$ for all $0\leq m\leq n$; this property will be used many times.
assumptions: $0\leq m\leq n$
conclusions: $F(n+2-m)+m\leq F(n+2)$

nodes.name: Fibonacci bound on flipping words for and-or-nets
nodes.statement: Suppose that $G$ is $i$-homogenous and has no positive cycles and no sources. Let $f$ be an and-or-net on $G$. Let $x$ be a configuration on $V$ and let $v$ be a longest canalizing word from $(i,x_i)$. There is a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)_i\neq x_i$~and \[ |w|< F(n-|v|+2)+|v|. \]
assumptions: $G$ is $i$-homogenous and has no positive cycles and no sources
$f$ be an and-or-net on $G$
$x$ be a configuration on $V$ and let $v$ be a longest canalizing word from $(i,x_i)$
conclusions: There is a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)_i\neq x_i$~and \[ |w|< F(n-|v|+2)+|v|. \]
nodes.statement_short: For and-or-nets, the flipping word has length less than $F(n-|v|+2)+|v|$, $v$ a longest canalizing word from $(i,x_i)$.
nodes.label: lem:no_fixed_vertex_2

nodes.name: Diffusion lemma for canalizing words
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a BN on $G$, $i\in V$ and $a\in\{0,1\}$. Let $w$ be a canalizing word from $(i,a)$ with image $b$, and suppose that no sources of $G$ are in $\{w\}$. For every $j\in\{w\}$, $G$ has a path from $i$ to $j$, whose internal vertices are in $\{w\}$, which is positive if $a=b_j$ and negative otherwise.
assumptions: $f$ be a BN on $G$, $i\in V$ and $a\in\{0,1\}$
$w$ be a canalizing word from $(i,a)$ with image $b$
no sources of $G$ are in $\{w\}$
conclusions: For every $j\in\{w\}$, $G$ has a path from $i$ to $j$, whose internal vertices are in $\{w\}$, which is positive if $a=b_j$ and negative otherwise
nodes.statement_short: Canalization from $(i,a)$ propagates along paths from $i$ whose sign matches whether $a=b_j$.
nodes.label: lem:diffusion

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement: We proceed by induction on $|w|$. If $|w|=0$ there is nothing to prove. Suppose that $|w|\geq 1$. Let $j$ be the last letter of $w$, and let $v$ be obtained from $w$ by removing the last letter (thus $v$ is the empty word if $|w|=1$). For convenience we set $b_i=a$ and $I=\{i\}\cup \{v\}$. We also write $\sigma(0)=-1$ and $\sigma(1)=1$. Hence, we have to prove that $G$ has a path from $i$ to $j$ of sign $\sigma(b_i)\cdot\sigma(b_j)$ whose internal vertices are in $\{w\}$. \medskip Since $j$ is not a source, there is a configuration $x$ on $V$ such that $f_j(x)\neq b_j$. Let $z=x$ if $x_i=a$ and $z=x+e_i$ otherwise, so that $z_i=a$ in any case. Let $y=f^v(z)$. Since $z_i=a$ we have $f_j(y)=f^w(z)_j=b_j$ and $y_k=f^w(z)_k=b_k$ for $k\in I$. Thus $f_j(y)\neq f_j(x)$ and we deduce that $j$ has an in-neighbor $k$ in $G$ of sign $(y_k-x_k)\cdot (f_j(y)-f_j(x))=\sigma(y_k)\cdot \sigma(f_j(y))=\sigma(y_k)\cdot \sigma(b_j)$. Since $x$ and $y$ can only differ in components inside $I$, we have $k\in I$, and we deduce that the sign of the arc from $k$ to $j$ is $\sigma(b_k)\cdot \sigma(b_j)$. If $k=i$ we are done: the desired path is the arc from $i$ to~$j$. Otherwise, $k\in\{v\}$. Since $v$ is a canalizing word from $(i,a)$ with image $b_{\{v\}}$, by induction, $G$ has a path from $i$ to $k$ of sign $\sigma(b_i)\cdot \sigma(b_k)$ whose internal vertices are in $\{v\}$. By adding the arc from $k$ to $j$ to this path, we obtain a path of sign $\sigma(b_i)\cdot \sigma(b_k)\cdot \sigma(b_k)\cdot \sigma(b_j)=\sigma(b_i)\cdot \sigma(b_j)$ from $i$ to $j$ whose internal vertices are in $\{w\}$. This completes the induction step.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $|w|$: the last letter $j$ has an in-neighbor $k$ in $\{i\}\cup\{v\}$ of the right sign; extend the inductive path to $k$ by the arc $k\to j$.

nodes.name: Induction on |w|, base case
nodes.statement: We proceed by induction on $|w|$. If $|w|=0$ there is nothing to prove.
nodes.statement_short: Induct on $|w|$; the empty word is trivial.

nodes.name: Set up the inductive step
nodes.statement: Suppose that $|w|\geq 1$. Let $j$ be the last letter of $w$, and let $v$ be obtained from $w$ by removing the last letter (thus $v$ is the empty word if $|w|=1$). For convenience we set $b_i=a$ and $I=\{i\}\cup \{v\}$. We also write $\sigma(0)=-1$ and $\sigma(1)=1$. Hence, we have to prove that $G$ has a path from $i$ to $j$ of sign $\sigma(b_i)\cdot\sigma(b_j)$ whose internal vertices are in $\{w\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $j$ be the last letter and $v$ the rest; reduce to finding a path of sign $\sigma(b_i)\sigma(b_j)$.

nodes.name: Find in-neighbor k of the right sign
nodes.statement: Since $j$ is not a source, there is a configuration $x$ on $V$ such that $f_j(x)\neq b_j$. Let $z=x$ if $x_i=a$ and $z=x+e_i$ otherwise, so that $z_i=a$ in any case. Let $y=f^v(z)$. Since $z_i=a$ we have $f_j(y)=f^w(z)_j=b_j$ and $y_k=f^w(z)_k=b_k$ for $k\in I$. Thus $f_j(y)\neq f_j(x)$ and we deduce that $j$ has an in-neighbor $k$ in $G$ of sign $(y_k-x_k)\cdot (f_j(y)-f_j(x))=\sigma(y_k)\cdot \sigma(f_j(y))=\sigma(y_k)\cdot \sigma(b_j)$. Since $x$ and $y$ can only differ in components inside $I$, we have $k\in I$, and we deduce that the sign of the arc from $k$ to $j$ is $\sigma(b_k)\cdot \sigma(b_j)$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare $x$ with $y=f^v(z)$ to get an in-neighbor $k\in I$ of $j$ whose arc has sign $\sigma(b_k)\sigma(b_j)$.

nodes.name: Case k = i
nodes.statement: If $k=i$ we are done: the desired path is the arc from $i$ to~$j$.
nodes.statement_short: If $k=i$ the arc $i\to j$ is the path.

nodes.name: Case k in v
nodes.statement: Otherwise, $k\in\{v\}$. Since $v$ is a canalizing word from $(i,a)$ with image $b_{\{v\}}$, by induction, $G$ has a path from $i$ to $k$ of sign $\sigma(b_i)\cdot \sigma(b_k)$ whose internal vertices are in $\{v\}$. By adding the arc from $k$ to $j$ to this path, we obtain a path of sign $\sigma(b_i)\cdot \sigma(b_k)\cdot \sigma(b_k)\cdot \sigma(b_j)=\sigma(b_i)\cdot \sigma(b_j)$ from $i$ to $j$ whose internal vertices are in $\{w\}$. This completes the induction step.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise extend the inductive path from $i$ to $k$ by the arc $k\to j$.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemmas 4 and 5
nodes.statement: The sketch is the following. Suppose that the initial state of $i$ is $0$, that is, $x_i=0$. So we want a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)_i=1$, that is, a word increasing the state of $i$. \medskip We first suppose that $i$ is of out-degree zero. Since $G$ has no sources, it has is a non-trivial initial strong component $S$. Since $G$ is $i$-homogenous and $i$ is of out-degree zero, there is a vertex $j$ in $S$ such that all the paths from $j$ to $i$ have the same sign, say positive. Then $j$ can be seen as an activator of $i$, so in order to increase the state of $i$, it is preferable to put $j$ in state~$1$. This is possible by induction on $S$, since $S$ is $j$-homogenous. So we consider a word $u$ that puts $j$ in state~$1$. Then we consider a longest canalizing word $v$ from $(j,1)$. If $i$ is canalized by $v$, then it necessarily gets the state $1$, since all the paths from $j$ to $i$ are positive, and we are done: starting from $x$, the word $uv$ increases the state of $i$. Otherwise, we ``remove'' $j$ and the vertices canalized by $v$. We obtain a ``subnetwork'' whose interaction graph $H$ satisfies all the hypotheses. Using induction, we get, for the subnetwork, a word $w$ that increases the state of $i$ and we are done: starting from $x$, the word $uvw$ increases the state of $i$. We then prove that $|uvw|\leq F(n+2)$ when $f$ is an and-or-net (which is the bound of the statement since $i$ is of out-degree zero). The argument is roughly the following. The induction used to obtain $u$ is done on $S$, which has at most $n-1$ vertices, and thus $|u|< F(n+1)$. The induction used to obtained $w$ is made on $H$, which has $n-1-|v|$ vertices, and we easily obtain $|vw|<F(n+1)$. So if $|u|\leq 1$ then $|uvw|<F(n+2)$ as desired. If $|u|\geq 2$ then it means, and this is the key point, that there is a {\em non-empty} canalizing word from either $(j,0)$ or $(j,1)$ and, by carefully analyzing the inductive calls, we obtain $|u|\leq F(n)$ in the first case, and $|vw|\leq F(n)$ in the second. So $|uvw|<F(n)+F(n+1)=F(n+2)$ in any case. \medskip We then suppose that $i$ is of out-degree at least one. We consider a longest canalizing word $v$ from $(i,0)$. If the word $vi$ increases the state of $i$ then we are done since $|v|+1< F(n-|v|+2)+|v|$. Otherwise, we ``remove'' the vertices canalized by $v$ from the network, and we ``remove'' the out-going arcs of $i$, considering that each out-neighbor of $i$ behaves as if the state of $i$ was permanently $0$. We obtain a ``subnetwork'' whose interaction graph $H$ satisfies all the hypotheses, and in which $i$ is of out-degree zero. By the first case, we get, for the subnetwork, a word $w$ that increases the state of $i$ and we are done: starting from $x$, the word $vw$ increases the state of $i$. Suppose now that $f$ is an and-or-net. Since $H$ has $n-|v|$ vertices we have $|w|< F(n-|v|+2)$ by the first case, so $|vw|< F(n-|v|+2)+|v|$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: if $i$ has out-degree zero, activate a vertex of an initial component and canalize, then recurse on a subnetwork; otherwise canalize from $i$ and reduce to the first case.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: The sketch is the following. Suppose that the initial state of $i$ is $0$, that is, $x_i=0$. So we want a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)_i=1$, that is, a word increasing the state of $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $x_i=0$ and look for a word increasing the state of $i$.
