If $i$ is canalized by $v$, then it necessarily gets the state $1$, since all the paths from $j$ to $i$ are positive, and we are done: starting from $x$, the word $uv$ increases the state of $i$. Otherwise, we ``remove'' $j$ and the vertices canalized by $v$. We obtain a ``subnetwork'' whose interaction graph $H$ satisfies all the hypotheses. Using induction, we get, for the subnetwork, a word $w$ that increases the state of $i$ and we are done: starting from $x$, the word $uvw$ increases the state of $i$. We then prove that $|uvw|\leq F(n+2)$ when $f$ is an and-or-net (which is the bound of the statement since $i$ is of out-degree zero). The argument is roughly the following. The induction used to obtain $u$ is done on $S$, which has at most $n-1$ vertices, and thus $|u|< F(n+1)$. The induction used to obtained $w$ is made on $H$, which has $n-1-|v|$ vertices, and we easily obtain $|vw|<F(n+1)$. So if $|u|\leq 1$ then $|uvw|<F(n+2)$ as desired. If $|u|\geq 2$ then it means, and this is the key point, that there is a {\em non-empty} canalizing word from either $(j,0)$ or $(j,1)$ and, by carefully analyzing the inductive calls, we obtain $|u|\leq F(n)$ in the first case, and $|vw|\leq F(n)$ in the second. So $|uvw|<F(n)+F(n+1)=F(n+2)$ in any case.
nodes.statement_short: Fix an activator $j$ in an initial component, set it by induction, canalize from it and recurse; the Fibonacci bound follows from a non-empty canalizing word.

nodes.name: Out-degree at least one case
nodes.statement: We then suppose that $i$ is of out-degree at least one. We consider a longest canalizing word $v$ from $(i,0)$. If the word $vi$ increases the state of $i$ then we are done since $|v|+1< F(n-|v|+2)+|v|$. Otherwise, we ``remove'' the vertices canalized by $v$ from the network, and we ``remove'' the out-going arcs of $i$, considering that each out-neighbor of $i$ behaves as if the state of $i$ was permanently $0$. We obtain a ``subnetwork'' whose interaction graph $H$ satisfies all the hypotheses, and in which $i$ is of out-degree zero. By the first case, we get, for the subnetwork, a word $w$ that increases the state of $i$ and we are done: starting from $x$, the word $vw$ increases the state of $i$. Suppose now that $f$ is an and-or-net. Since $H$ has $n-|v|$ vertices we have $|w|< F(n-|v|+2)$ by the first case, so $|vw|< F(n-|v|+2)+|v|$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Canalize from $(i,0)$, remove the canalized vertices and the out-arcs of $i$, and apply the first case.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemmas 4 and 5
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $G$ is $i$-homogenous and has no positive cycles and no sources. Let $f$ be a BN on $G$. Let $x$ be a configuration on $V$. We proceed by induction on the number $n$ of vertices in $G$. If $n=1$ the result is obvious: $i$ is the unique vertex and has a negative loop, so $f(x)
eq x$; hence we can take $w=i$ and since $1<F(3)=2$ we are done. So suppose that $n\geq 2$. We consider two cases.  igskip \BF{Case 1: $i$ is of out-degree zero}. We have to prove that $w$ exists, and $|w|< F(n+2)$ if $f$ is an and-or-net (since $i$ is of out-degree zero, the longest canalizing word from $(i,x_i)$ is the empty word). Since $i$ is of in-degree at least one, $G$ contains an initial component $S$ from which $i$ is reachable. Since $i$ is of out-degree zero, all the paths from $S$ to $i$ are forward. Since $G$ is $i$-homogenous, there is a vertex $j$ in $S$ such that all the paths from $j$ to $i$ have the same sign. Let $a=x_i+1$ if all the paths from $j$ to $i$ are positive, and $a=x_i$ otherwise. Let $m$ be the maximal size of a canalizing word from $(j,x_j)$ with only letters in $S$. We first prove, using the induction hypothesis, the following.  igskip 
oindent (1) {\em There is a word $u$ such that $f^u(x)_j=a$, and if $f$ is an and-or-net then} \[ |u|< F(n-m+1)+m\leq F(n+1). \] \medskip 
oindent This is obvious if $x_j=a$ (we take $u$ the empty word) so suppose that $x_j
eq a$. Let $J$ be the vertex set of $S$ and $I=V\setminus J$. Let $h$ be the BN with component set $J$ defined by $h(y_J)=f(y)_J$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ such that $y_I=x_I$. Since $G$ has no arc from $I$ to $J$, one can easily check that $S$ is the signed interaction digraph of $h$. Since $S$ is strong, $S$ is $j$-homogenous. Since $S$ is a subgraph of $G$, it has no positive cycles, and since $G$ has no sources, $S$ has no sources (that is, $S$ is non-trivial). Because $S$ has at most $n-1$ vertices, by induction, there is a word $u$ over $J$ such that $h^u(x_J)_j=a$ and we can then easily check that $f^u(x)_j=a$. If $f$ is an and-or-net then $h$ is also an and-or-net, and since $m$ is the maximal length of a canalizing word from $(j,x_j)$ in $h$, by induction we obtain $|u|< F(|J|-m+2)+m$. Since $|J|\leq n-1$ this proves (1).  igskip Let $u$ be a shortest word as in (1). Let $v$ be a longest canalizing word from $(j,a)$ and $b$ its image.  igskip 
oindent (2) {\em If $i\in\{v\}$ then $f^{uv}(x)_i
eq x_i$ and, if $f$ is an and-or-net, then $|uv|< F(n+2)$.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose that $i\in\{v\}$. By Lemma~ef{lem:diffusion}, $G$ has a path $P$ from $j$ to $i$ which is positive if and only if $a=b_i$. By the definition of $a$, we have $a
eq x_i$ if and only if $P$ is positive. Thus $x_i
eq b_i$ and since $f^u(x)_j=a$, we have $f^{uv}(x)_i=b_i
eq x_i$. If $f$ is an and-or-net, then $|u|< F(n+1)$ by (1) and since $|v|\leq n-1\leq F(n)$ we obtain $|uv|< F(n+2)$. This proves~(2).  igskip By (2) we can suppose that $i
ot\in\{v\}$. Let $b'$ be the configuration on $I=\{j\}\cup\{v\}$ such that $b'_j=a$ and ${b'}_{\{v\}}=b$. Note that, for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_j=a$ we have $f^v(y)_I=b'$. In particular, since $f^u(x)_j=a$, we have $f^{uv}(x)_I=b'$. \medskip Let $h$ be the BN with component set $J=V\setminus I$ defined by $h(y_J)=f(y)_J$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ such that $y_I=b'$. Let $H$ be the signed interaction digraph of $h$.  igskip 
oindent (3) {\em $H$ has no positive cycles and no sources.} \medskip 
oindent One easily check that $H$ is a subgraph of $G$, and thus it has no positive cycles. Suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ has a source $\ell$. Then it means that, for some $c$, we have $h_\ell(y_J)=f_\ell(y)=c$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_I=b'$. But then, for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_j=a$, we have $f^{v,\ell}(y)_I=f^v(y)_I=b'$ since $\ell
ot\in I$ and thus $f^{v,\ell}(y)_\ell=f_\ell(f^v(y))=c$. Thus $v,\ell$ is a canalizing word from $(j,a)$ longer than $v$, a contradiction. This proves (3).  igskip 
oindent (4) {\em $H$ is $i$-homogenous.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ is not $i$-homogenous. Then it has a strong component $F$ such that, for every vertex $\ell$ in $F$, $H$ has both a positive path and a negative path from $\ell$ to~$i$. Since $G$ is $i$-homogenous, $F$ is not a strong component of $G$ and thus $G$ has an arc from some vertex $k$ not in $F$ to some vertex $\ell$ in $F$. Let $y,z$ be two configurations on $V$ that only differ in component $k$ such that $f(y)_\ell
eq f(z)_\ell$. If $G$ has no arc from $I$ to $\ell$, then we can choose $y,z$ in such a way that $y_I=z_I=b'$. But then $h(y_J)_\ell
eq h(z_J)_\ell$ thus $H$ has an arc from $k$ to $\ell$, a contradiction. Hence $G$ has an arc from some vertex $k'\in I$ to $\ell$. By Lemma~ef{lem:diffusion}, $G$ has a path from $j$ to $k'$ whose vertices are all in $I$, and thus it has a path $P$ from $j$ to $\ell$ whose vertices are in $I$ excepted $\ell$. Since $\ell$ is in $F$, $H$ has a positive path $P^+$ from $\ell$ to $i$ and a negative path $P^-$ from $\ell$ to $i$. Then $P\cup P^+$ and $P\cup P^-$ are paths of $G$ from $j$ to $i$ of opposite signs, and this contradicts our choice of $j$. This proves (4).  igskip From (3) and (4) there is, by induction, a word $w$ over $J$ with $h^w(f^{uv}(x)_J)_i
eq x_i$. Since $f^{uv}(x)_I=b'$, and $w$ is a word over $J$, we have \[ f^{uvw}(x)_J=f^w(f^{uv}(x))_J=h^w(f^{uv}(x)_J) \] thus $f^{uvw}(x)_i
eq x_i$. \medskip It remains to prove the upper bound on the length of $uvw$ when $f$ is an and-or-net. So suppose that $f$ is an and-or-net. Then $h$ is also an and-or-net, and since $H$ has $n-|v|-1$ vertices, we have $|w|<F(n-|v|+1)$ by induction, and thus \[	ag{5} |vw|< F(n-|v|+1)+|v|\leq F(n+1). \] If $|u|\leq 1$ then $|uvw|< F(n+1)+1\leq F(n+2)$ as desired. So suppose that $|u|\geq 2$. Since $u$ is as short as possible, we have $x_j
eq a$ and $S$ has at least two vertices, so $j$ has an out-neighbor in $S$ distinct from $j$, say $k$. Since $f_k$ is a conjunction or a disjunction, the single letter $k$ is a canalizing word from $(j,c)$ for some $c\in\{0,1\}$. If $c=x_j$ then we deduce that $m\geq 1$, so $|u|\leq F(n)$ by (1), and with (5) we obtain $|uvw|< F(n+2)$. If $c=a$ then we deduce that $|v|\geq 1$, so $|vw|\leq F(n)$ by (5) and with (1) we obtain $|uvw|< F(n+2)$. Hence the desired bound is always obtained. This proves the first case.  igskip \BF{Case 2: $i$ is of out-degree at least one.} Let $a=x_i$ and let $v$ be a longest canalizing word from $(i,a)$. If $f^{v,i}(x)_i
eq a$ then we are done since $|v,i|\leq n$ and $n< F(n-m+2)+m$ for all $0\leq m<n$. So we assume that $f^{v,i}(x)_i=a$. Let $b$ be the image of $v$ and $I=\{v\}$.  igskip 
oindent (1) {\em There is no $c$ such that $f_i(y)=c$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_i=a$ and $y_I=b$.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose, for a contradiction, that $f_i(y)=c$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_i=a$ and $y_I=b$. Let $y$ be a configuration on $V$ with $y_i=a$ such that, for all positive (negative) in-neighbors $j$ of $i$ with $j
ot\in I$ we have $y_j
eq a$ ($y_j=a)$; if $j=i$ then $j$ is a negative in-neighbor of $i$ since $G$ has only negative cycles, and we have already imposed $y_j=a$. Suppose that $i$ has a positive in-neighbor $j\in I$. Since $G$ has only negative cycles, all the paths from $i$ to $j$ are negative. Hence, by Lemma~ef{lem:diffusion}, we have $a
eq b_j$. Thus, for {\em every} positive in-neighbor $j$ of $i$ we have $f^v(y)_j
eq a$, because $f^v(y)_j=y_j
eq a$ if $j
ot\in I$ and $f^v(y)_j=b_j
eq a$ otherwise. We prove similarly that, for every negative in-neighbor $j$ of $i$, we have $f^v(y)_j=a$. Hence $f^v(y)$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$, and since $i$ is not a source, by Proposition~ef{pro:flipping} we have $f_i(f^v(y))
eq a$. Since $f^v(y)_i=y_i=a$ and $f^v(y)_I=b$, we deduce that $c
eq a$. Now, since $f^v(x)_i=x_i=a$ and $f^v(x)_I=b$, we have $f_i(f^v(x))=c
eq a$ and thus $f^{v,i}(x)_i
eq a$, which contradicts our hypothesis. This proves (1).  igskip Given a configuration $y$ on $V$ we denote by $	ilde y$ the configuration on $V$ such that $	ilde y_i=a$ and $	ilde y_j=y_j$ for all $j
eq i$. Let $h$ be the BN with component set $J=V\setminus I$ such that $h(y_J)=f(	ilde y)_J$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_I=b$. Let $H$ be the signed interaction digraph of $h$. Note that $H$ is a subgraph of $G$ in which $i$ is of out-degree zero.  igskip 
oindent (2) {\em $H$ has no positive cycles and no sources.} \medskip 
oindent Since $H$ is a subgraph of $G$, it has no positive cycles. Suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ has a source $k$. Then there is $c$ such that $h(y_J)_k=c$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$. So if $y_i=a$ and $y_I=b$ then $f(y)_J=h(y_J)$ and thus $f(y)_k=h(y_J)_k=c$. For all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_i=a$, we have $f^{v}(y)_i=a$ and $f^v(y)_I=b$ and we deduce that $f^{v,k}(y)_k=c$. By (1) we have $k
eq i$ and since $k
ot\in I$ we deduce that $v,k$ is a canalizing word from $(i,a)$ longer than $v$, a contradiction. This proves (2).  igskip 
oindent (3) {\em $H$ is $i$-homogenous.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ is not $i$-homogenous. Then it has a strong component $F$ such that, for any vertex $\ell$ in $F$, $H$ has both a positive path and a negative path from $\ell$ to $i$. Since $G$ is $i$-homogenous, $F$ is not a strong component of $G$ and thus $G$ has an arc from some vertex $k$ not in $F$ to some vertex $\ell$ in $F$. Let $y,z$ be two configurations on $V$ that only differ in component $k$ such that $f(y)_\ell
eq f(z)_\ell$. If $G$ has no arc from $I\cup\{i\}$ to $\ell$, then we can choose $y,z$ in such a way that $y_I=z_I=b$ and $y_i=z_i=a$. But then $h(y_J)_\ell=f(y)_\ell
eq f(z)_\ell= h(z_J)_\ell$ thus $H$ has an arc from $k$ to $\ell$, a contradiction. Hence $G$ has an arc from some vertex $k'\in I\cup\{i\}$ to $\ell$. By Lemma~ef{lem:diffusion}, $G$ has a path from $i$ to $k'$ whose internal vertices are in $I$ (of length zero if $k=i$), and thus it has a path $P$ from $i$ to $\ell$ whose internal vertices are in $I$. Since $\ell$ is in $F$, $H$ has a positive path $P^+$ from $\ell$ to $i$ and a negative path $P^-$ from $\ell$ to $i$. Then $P\cup P^+$ and $P\cup P^-$ are cycles of $G$ of opposite signs, so $G$ has a positive cycle, a contradiction. This proves~(3).  igskip Since $i$ is of out-degree zero in $H$, we deduce from (2), (3) and the first case that there is a shortest word $w$ over $J$ such that $h^w(z_J)_i
eq a$ where $z=f^{v}(x)$. Since $w$ is of minimal length for this property, $i$ appears only once in $w$, in last position: $w=w',i$ for some word $w'$ not containing $i$. Since $z_I=b$, $z_i=a$ and $w'$ does not contain any letter in $I\cup\{i\}$, we deduce, setting $y=f^{w'}(z)$, that $y_J=h^{w'}(z_J)$. Furthermore, $y_I=b$ and $y_i=a$ so $f(y)_J=h(y_J)$. Consequently, \[ f^{vw}(x)_i=f(y)_i=h(y_J)_i=h(h^{w'}(z_J))_i=h^w(z_J)_i
eq a. \] \medskip It remains to prove the upper bound on the length of $vw$ when $f$ is an and-or-net. So suppose that $f$ is an and-or-net. Then $h$ is also an and-or-net, and since $H$ has $n-|v|$ vertices, we have $|w|< F(n-|v|+2)$ by the first case, and thus $|vw|< F(n-|v|+2)+|v|$ as desired. This proves the second case.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$ with two cases on the out-degree of $i$. Out-degree zero: set an activator in an initial component by induction, canalize from it and recurse on the remaining subnetwork; out-degree positive: canalize from $i$ and reduce to the first case.

nodes.name: Induction on n; base case
nodes.statement: Suppose that $G$ is $i$-homogenous and has no positive cycles and no sources. Let $f$ be a BN on $G$. Let $x$ be a configuration on $V$. We proceed by induction on the number $n$ of vertices in $G$. If $n=1$ the result is obvious: $i$ is the unique vertex and has a negative loop, so $f(x)\neq x$; hence we can take $w=i$ and since $1<F(3)=2$ we are done. So suppose that $n\geq 2$. We consider two cases.
nodes.statement_short: Induct on the number of vertices; for $n=1$ the negative loop flips $i$ with $w=i$.

nodes.name: Case 1: i of out-degree zero
nodes.statement:
\BF{Case 1: $i$ is of out-degree zero}. We have to prove that $w$ exists, and $|w|< F(n+2)$ if $f$ is an and-or-net (since $i$ is of out-degree zero, the longest canalizing word from $(i,x_i)$ is the empty word). Since $i$ is of in-degree at least one, $G$ contains an initial component $S$ from which $i$ is reachable. Since $i$ is of out-degree zero, all the paths from $S$ to $i$ are forward. Since $G$ is $i$-homogenous, there is a vertex $j$ in $S$ such that all the paths from $j$ to $i$ have the same sign. Let $a=x_i+1$ if all the paths from $j$ to $i$ are positive, and $a=x_i$ otherwise. Let $m$ be the maximal size of a canalizing word from $(j,x_j)$ with only letters in $S$. We first prove, using the induction hypothesis, the following.  igskip 
oindent (1) {\em There is a word $u$ such that $f^u(x)_j=a$, and if $f$ is an and-or-net then} \[ |u|< F(n-m+1)+m\leq F(n+1). \] \medskip 
oindent This is obvious if $x_j=a$ (we take $u$ the empty word) so suppose that $x_j
eq a$. Let $J$ be the vertex set of $S$ and $I=V\setminus J$. Let $h$ be the BN with component set $J$ defined by $h(y_J)=f(y)_J$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ such that $y_I=x_I$. Since $G$ has no arc from $I$ to $J$, one can easily check that $S$ is the signed interaction digraph of $h$. Since $S$ is strong, $S$ is $j$-homogenous. Since $S$ is a subgraph of $G$, it has no positive cycles, and since $G$ has no sources, $S$ has no sources (that is, $S$ is non-trivial). Because $S$ has at most $n-1$ vertices, by induction, there is a word $u$ over $J$ such that $h^u(x_J)_j=a$ and we can then easily check that $f^u(x)_j=a$. If $f$ is an and-or-net then $h$ is also an and-or-net, and since $m$ is the maximal length of a canalizing word from $(j,x_j)$ in $h$, by induction we obtain $|u|< F(|J|-m+2)+m$. Since $|J|\leq n-1$ this proves (1).  igskip Let $u$ be a shortest word as in (1). Let $v$ be a longest canalizing word from $(j,a)$ and $b$ its image.  igskip 
oindent (2) {\em If $i\in\{v\}$ then $f^{uv}(x)_i
eq x_i$ and, if $f$ is an and-or-net, then $|uv|< F(n+2)$.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose that $i\in\{v\}$. By Lemma~ef{lem:diffusion}, $G$ has a path $P$ from $j$ to $i$ which is positive if and only if $a=b_i$. By the definition of $a$, we have $a
eq x_i$ if and only if $P$ is positive. Thus $x_i
eq b_i$ and since $f^u(x)_j=a$, we have $f^{uv}(x)_i=b_i
eq x_i$. If $f$ is an and-or-net, then $|u|< F(n+1)$ by (1) and since $|v|\leq n-1\leq F(n)$ we obtain $|uv|< F(n+2)$. This proves~(2).  igskip By (2) we can suppose that $i
ot\in\{v\}$. Let $b'$ be the configuration on $I=\{j\}\cup\{v\}$ such that $b'_j=a$ and ${b'}_{\{v\}}=b$. Note that, for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_j=a$ we have $f^v(y)_I=b'$. In particular, since $f^u(x)_j=a$, we have $f^{uv}(x)_I=b'$. \medskip Let $h$ be the BN with component set $J=V\setminus I$ defined by $h(y_J)=f(y)_J$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ such that $y_I=b'$. Let $H$ be the signed interaction digraph of $h$.  igskip 
oindent (3) {\em $H$ has no positive cycles and no sources.} \medskip 
oindent One easily check that $H$ is a subgraph of $G$, and thus it has no positive cycles. Suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ has a source $\ell$. Then it means that, for some $c$, we have $h_\ell(y_J)=f_\ell(y)=c$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_I=b'$. But then, for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_j=a$, we have $f^{v,\ell}(y)_I=f^v(y)_I=b'$ since $\ell
ot\in I$ and thus $f^{v,\ell}(y)_\ell=f_\ell(f^v(y))=c$. Thus $v,\ell$ is a canalizing word from $(j,a)$ longer than $v$, a contradiction. This proves (3).  igskip 
oindent (4) {\em $H$ is $i$-homogenous.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ is not $i$-homogenous. Then it has a strong component $F$ such that, for every vertex $\ell$ in $F$, $H$ has both a positive path and a negative path from $\ell$ to~$i$. Since $G$ is $i$-homogenous, $F$ is not a strong component of $G$ and thus $G$ has an arc from some vertex $k$ not in $F$ to some vertex $\ell$ in $F$. Let $y,z$ be two configurations on $V$ that only differ in component $k$ such that $f(y)_\ell
eq f(z)_\ell$. If $G$ has no arc from $I$ to $\ell$, then we can choose $y,z$ in such a way that $y_I=z_I=b'$. But then $h(y_J)_\ell
eq h(z_J)_\ell$ thus $H$ has an arc from $k$ to $\ell$, a contradiction. Hence $G$ has an arc from some vertex $k'\in I$ to $\ell$. By Lemma~ef{lem:diffusion}, $G$ has a path from $j$ to $k'$ whose vertices are all in $I$, and thus it has a path $P$ from $j$ to $\ell$ whose vertices are in $I$ excepted $\ell$. Since $\ell$ is in $F$, $H$ has a positive path $P^+$ from $\ell$ to $i$ and a negative path $P^-$ from $\ell$ to $i$. Then $P\cup P^+$ and $P\cup P^-$ are paths of $G$ from $j$ to $i$ of opposite signs, and this contradicts our choice of $j$. This proves (4).  igskip From (3) and (4) there is, by induction, a word $w$ over $J$ with $h^w(f^{uv}(x)_J)_i
eq x_i$. Since $f^{uv}(x)_I=b'$, and $w$ is a word over $J$, we have \[ f^{uvw}(x)_J=f^w(f^{uv}(x))_J=h^w(f^{uv}(x)_J) \] thus $f^{uvw}(x)_i
eq x_i$. \medskip It remains to prove the upper bound on the length of $uvw$ when $f$ is an and-or-net. So suppose that $f$ is an and-or-net. Then $h$ is also an and-or-net, and since $H$ has $n-|v|-1$ vertices, we have $|w|<F(n-|v|+1)$ by induction, and thus \[	ag{5} |vw|< F(n-|v|+1)+|v|\leq F(n+1). \] If $|u|\leq 1$ then $|uvw|< F(n+1)+1\leq F(n+2)$ as desired. So suppose that $|u|\geq 2$. Since $u$ is as short as possible, we have $x_j
eq a$ and $S$ has at least two vertices, so $j$ has an out-neighbor in $S$ distinct from $j$, say $k$. Since $f_k$ is a conjunction or a disjunction, the single letter $k$ is a canalizing word from $(j,c)$ for some $c\in\{0,1\}$. If $c=x_j$ then we deduce that $m\geq 1$, so $|u|\leq F(n)$ by (1), and with (5) we obtain $|uvw|< F(n+2)$. If $c=a$ then we deduce that $|v|\geq 1$, so $|vw|\leq F(n)$ by (5) and with (1) we obtain $|uvw|< F(n+2)$. Hence the desired bound is always obtained. This proves the first case.
nodes.statement_short: Out-degree zero: activate a suitable vertex $j$ of an initial component, canalize from it, and recurse on the remaining subnetwork.

nodes.name: Choose initial component S and vertex j
nodes.statement: \BF{Case 1: $i$ is of out-degree zero}. We have to prove that $w$ exists, and $|w|< F(n+2)$ if $f$ is an and-or-net (since $i$ is of out-degree zero, the longest canalizing word from $(i,x_i)$ is the empty word). Since $i$ is of in-degree at least one, $G$ contains an initial component $S$ from which $i$ is reachable. Since $i$ is of out-degree zero, all the paths from $S$ to $i$ are forward. Since $G$ is $i$-homogenous, there is a vertex $j$ in $S$ such that all the paths from $j$ to $i$ have the same sign. Let $a=x_i+1$ if all the paths from $j$ to $i$ are positive, and $a=x_i$ otherwise. Let $m$ be the maximal size of a canalizing word from $(j,x_j)$ with only letters in $S$. We first prove, using the induction hypothesis, the following.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $j$ in an initial component $S$ with all paths to $i$ of one sign and the target value $a$.

nodes.name: (1) Set j to a by induction on S
nodes.statement: (1) {\em There is a word $u$ such that $f^u(x)_j=a$, and if $f$ is an and-or-net then} \[ |u|< F(n-m+1)+m\leq F(n+1). \] \medskip \noindent This is obvious if $x_j=a$ (we take $u$ the empty word) so suppose that $x_j\neq a$. Let $J$ be the vertex set of $S$ and $I=V\setminus J$. Let $h$ be the BN with component set $J$ defined by $h(y_J)=f(y)_J$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ such that $y_I=x_I$. Since $G$ has no arc from $I$ to $J$, one can easily check that $S$ is the signed interaction digraph of $h$. Since $S$ is strong, $S$ is $j$-homogenous. Since $S$ is a subgraph of $G$, it has no positive cycles, and since $G$ has no sources, $S$ has no sources (that is, $S$ is non-trivial). Because $S$ has at most $n-1$ vertices, by induction, there is a word $u$ over $J$ such that $h^u(x_J)_j=a$ and we can then easily check that $f^u(x)_j=a$. If $f$ is an and-or-net then $h$ is also an and-or-net, and since $m$ is the maximal length of a canalizing word from $(j,x_j)$ in $h$, by induction we obtain $|u|< F(|J|-m+2)+m$. Since $|J|\leq n-1$ this proves (1).
nodes.statement_short: By induction on the strong component $S$, a word $u$ with $|u|<F(n-m+1)+m$ sets $j$ to $a$.

nodes.name: Fix u and a longest canalizing word v
nodes.statement: Let $u$ be a shortest word as in (1). Let $v$ be a longest canalizing word from $(j,a)$ and $b$ its image.
nodes.statement_short: Take $u$ shortest and $v$ a longest canalizing word from $(j,a)$ with image $b$.

nodes.name: (2) If i is canalized, done
nodes.statement:
(2) {\em If $i\in\{v\}$ then $f^{uv}(x)_i
eq x_i$ and, if $f$ is an and-or-net, then $|uv|< F(n+2)$.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose that $i\in\{v\}$. By Lemma~ef{lem:diffusion}, $G$ has a path $P$ from $j$ to $i$ which is positive if and only if $a=b_i$. By the definition of $a$, we have $a
eq x_i$ if and only if $P$ is positive. Thus $x_i
eq b_i$ and since $f^u(x)_j=a$, we have $f^{uv}(x)_i=b_i
eq x_i$. If $f$ is an and-or-net, then $|u|< F(n+1)$ by (1) and since $|v|\leq n-1\leq F(n)$ we obtain $|uv|< F(n+2)$. This proves~(2).
nodes.statement_short: If $i\in\{v\}$, Lemma 6 gives the right sign, so $uv$ flips $i$ within $F(n+2)$.

nodes.name: Define the subnetwork h
nodes.statement: By (2) we can suppose that $i\not\in\{v\}$. Let $b'$ be the configuration on $I=\{j\}\cup\{v\}$ such that $b'_j=a$ and ${b'}_{\{v\}}=b$. Note that, for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_j=a$ we have $f^v(y)_I=b'$. In particular, since $f^u(x)_j=a$, we have $f^{uv}(x)_I=b'$. \medskip Let $h$ be the BN with component set $J=V\setminus I$ defined by $h(y_J)=f(y)_J$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ such that $y_I=b'$. Let $H$ be the signed interaction digraph of $h$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $I=\{j\}\cup\{v\}$ to $b'$ and define the subnetwork $h$ on $J=V\setminus I$ with digraph $H$.

nodes.name: (3) H has no positive cycles and no sources
nodes.statement: (3) {\em $H$ has no positive cycles and no sources.} \medskip \noindent One easily check that $H$ is a subgraph of $G$, and thus it has no positive cycles. Suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ has a source $\ell$. Then it means that, for some $c$, we have $h_\ell(y_J)=f_\ell(y)=c$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_I=b'$. But then, for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_j=a$, we have $f^{v,\ell}(y)_I=f^v(y)_I=b'$ since $\ell\not\in I$ and thus $f^{v,\ell}(y)_\ell=f_\ell(f^v(y))=c$. Thus $v,\ell$ is a canalizing word from $(j,a)$ longer than $v$, a contradiction. This proves (3).
nodes.statement_short: A source of $H$ would extend the longest canalizing word $v$.

nodes.name: (4) H is i-homogenous
nodes.statement:
(4) {\em $H$ is $i$-homogenous.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ is not $i$-homogenous. Then it has a strong component $F$ such that, for every vertex $\ell$ in $F$, $H$ has both a positive path and a negative path from $\ell$ to~$i$. Since $G$ is $i$-homogenous, $F$ is not a strong component of $G$ and thus $G$ has an arc from some vertex $k$ not in $F$ to some vertex $\ell$ in $F$. Let $y,z$ be two configurations on $V$ that only differ in component $k$ such that $f(y)_\ell
eq f(z)_\ell$. If $G$ has no arc from $I$ to $\ell$, then we can choose $y,z$ in such a way that $y_I=z_I=b'$. But then $h(y_J)_\ell
eq h(z_J)_\ell$ thus $H$ has an arc from $k$ to $\ell$, a contradiction. Hence $G$ has an arc from some vertex $k'\in I$ to $\ell$. By Lemma~ef{lem:diffusion}, $G$ has a path from $j$ to $k'$ whose vertices are all in $I$, and thus it has a path $P$ from $j$ to $\ell$ whose vertices are in $I$ excepted $\ell$. Since $\ell$ is in $F$, $H$ has a positive path $P^+$ from $\ell$ to $i$ and a negative path $P^-$ from $\ell$ to $i$. Then $P\cup P^+$ and $P\cup P^-$ are paths of $G$ from $j$ to $i$ of opposite signs, and this contradicts our choice of $j$. This proves (4).
nodes.statement_short: A bad strong component of $H$ would give paths from $j$ to $i$ of opposite signs in $G$.

nodes.name: Apply induction to H
nodes.statement: From (3) and (4) there is, by induction, a word $w$ over $J$ with $h^w(f^{uv}(x)_J)_i\neq x_i$. Since $f^{uv}(x)_I=b'$, and $w$ is a word over $J$, we have \[ f^{uvw}(x)_J=f^w(f^{uv}(x))_J=h^w(f^{uv}(x)_J) \] thus $f^{uvw}(x)_i\neq x_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $H$ yields $w$ with $f^{uvw}(x)_i\neq x_i$.

nodes.name: Length bound in Case 1
nodes.statement: It remains to prove the upper bound on the length of $uvw$ when $f$ is an and-or-net. So suppose that $f$ is an and-or-net. Then $h$ is also an and-or-net, and since $H$ has $n-|v|-1$ vertices, we have $|w|<F(n-|v|+1)$ by induction, and thus \[\tag{5} |vw|< F(n-|v|+1)+|v|\leq F(n+1). \] If $|u|\leq 1$ then $|uvw|< F(n+1)+1\leq F(n+2)$ as desired. So suppose that $|u|\geq 2$. Since $u$ is as short as possible, we have $x_j\neq a$ and $S$ has at least two vertices, so $j$ has an out-neighbor in $S$ distinct from $j$, say $k$. Since $f_k$ is a conjunction or a disjunction, the single letter $k$ is a canalizing word from $(j,c)$ for some $c\in\{0,1\}$. If $c=x_j$ then we deduce that $m\geq 1$, so $|u|\leq F(n)$ by (1), and with (5) we obtain $|uvw|< F(n+2)$. If $c=a$ then we deduce that $|v|\geq 1$, so $|vw|\leq F(n)$ by (5) and with (1) we obtain $|uvw|< F(n+2)$. Hence the desired bound is always obtained. This proves the first case.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|uvw|<F(n+2)$ using a non-empty canalizing word from $(j,x_j)$ or $(j,a)$.

nodes.name: Case 2: i of out-degree at least one
nodes.statement:
\BF{Case 2: $i$ is of out-degree at least one.} Let $a=x_i$ and let $v$ be a longest canalizing word from $(i,a)$. If $f^{v,i}(x)_i
eq a$ then we are done since $|v,i|\leq n$ and $n< F(n-m+2)+m$ for all $0\leq m<n$. So we assume that $f^{v,i}(x)_i=a$. Let $b$ be the image of $v$ and $I=\{v\}$.  igskip 
oindent (1) {\em There is no $c$ such that $f_i(y)=c$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_i=a$ and $y_I=b$.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose, for a contradiction, that $f_i(y)=c$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_i=a$ and $y_I=b$. Let $y$ be a configuration on $V$ with $y_i=a$ such that, for all positive (negative) in-neighbors $j$ of $i$ with $j
ot\in I$ we have $y_j
eq a$ ($y_j=a)$; if $j=i$ then $j$ is a negative in-neighbor of $i$ since $G$ has only negative cycles, and we have already imposed $y_j=a$. Suppose that $i$ has a positive in-neighbor $j\in I$. Since $G$ has only negative cycles, all the paths from $i$ to $j$ are negative. Hence, by Lemma~ef{lem:diffusion}, we have $a
eq b_j$. Thus, for {\em every} positive in-neighbor $j$ of $i$ we have $f^v(y)_j
eq a$, because $f^v(y)_j=y_j
eq a$ if $j
ot\in I$ and $f^v(y)_j=b_j
eq a$ otherwise. We prove similarly that, for every negative in-neighbor $j$ of $i$, we have $f^v(y)_j=a$. Hence $f^v(y)$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$, and since $i$ is not a source, by Proposition~ef{pro:flipping} we have $f_i(f^v(y))
eq a$. Since $f^v(y)_i=y_i=a$ and $f^v(y)_I=b$, we deduce that $c
eq a$. Now, since $f^v(x)_i=x_i=a$ and $f^v(x)_I=b$, we have $f_i(f^v(x))=c
eq a$ and thus $f^{v,i}(x)_i
eq a$, which contradicts our hypothesis. This proves (1).  igskip Given a configuration $y$ on $V$ we denote by $	ilde y$ the configuration on $V$ such that $	ilde y_i=a$ and $	ilde y_j=y_j$ for all $j
eq i$. Let $h$ be the BN with component set $J=V\setminus I$ such that $h(y_J)=f(	ilde y)_J$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_I=b$. Let $H$ be the signed interaction digraph of $h$. Note that $H$ is a subgraph of $G$ in which $i$ is of out-degree zero.  igskip 
oindent (2) {\em $H$ has no positive cycles and no sources.} \medskip 
oindent Since $H$ is a subgraph of $G$, it has no positive cycles. Suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ has a source $k$. Then there is $c$ such that $h(y_J)_k=c$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$. So if $y_i=a$ and $y_I=b$ then $f(y)_J=h(y_J)$ and thus $f(y)_k=h(y_J)_k=c$. For all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_i=a$, we have $f^{v}(y)_i=a$ and $f^v(y)_I=b$ and we deduce that $f^{v,k}(y)_k=c$. By (1) we have $k
eq i$ and since $k
ot\in I$ we deduce that $v,k$ is a canalizing word from $(i,a)$ longer than $v$, a contradiction. This proves (2).  igskip 
oindent (3) {\em $H$ is $i$-homogenous.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ is not $i$-homogenous. Then it has a strong component $F$ such that, for any vertex $\ell$ in $F$, $H$ has both a positive path and a negative path from $\ell$ to $i$. Since $G$ is $i$-homogenous, $F$ is not a strong component of $G$ and thus $G$ has an arc from some vertex $k$ not in $F$ to some vertex $\ell$ in $F$. Let $y,z$ be two configurations on $V$ that only differ in component $k$ such that $f(y)_\ell
eq f(z)_\ell$. If $G$ has no arc from $I\cup\{i\}$ to $\ell$, then we can choose $y,z$ in such a way that $y_I=z_I=b$ and $y_i=z_i=a$. But then $h(y_J)_\ell=f(y)_\ell
eq f(z)_\ell= h(z_J)_\ell$ thus $H$ has an arc from $k$ to $\ell$, a contradiction. Hence $G$ has an arc from some vertex $k'\in I\cup\{i\}$ to $\ell$. By Lemma~ef{lem:diffusion}, $G$ has a path from $i$ to $k'$ whose internal vertices are in $I$ (of length zero if $k=i$), and thus it has a path $P$ from $i$ to $\ell$ whose internal vertices are in $I$. Since $\ell$ is in $F$, $H$ has a positive path $P^+$ from $\ell$ to $i$ and a negative path $P^-$ from $\ell$ to $i$. Then $P\cup P^+$ and $P\cup P^-$ are cycles of $G$ of opposite signs, so $G$ has a positive cycle, a contradiction. This proves~(3).  igskip Since $i$ is of out-degree zero in $H$, we deduce from (2), (3) and the first case that there is a shortest word $w$ over $J$ such that $h^w(z_J)_i
eq a$ where $z=f^{v}(x)$. Since $w$ is of minimal length for this property, $i$ appears only once in $w$, in last position: $w=w',i$ for some word $w'$ not containing $i$. Since $z_I=b$, $z_i=a$ and $w'$ does not contain any letter in $I\cup\{i\}$, we deduce, setting $y=f^{w'}(z)$, that $y_J=h^{w'}(z_J)$. Furthermore, $y_I=b$ and $y_i=a$ so $f(y)_J=h(y_J)$. Consequently, \[ f^{vw}(x)_i=f(y)_i=h(y_J)_i=h(h^{w'}(z_J))_i=h^w(z_J)_i
eq a. \] \medskip It remains to prove the upper bound on the length of $vw$ when $f$ is an and-or-net. So suppose that $f$ is an and-or-net. Then $h$ is also an and-or-net, and since $H$ has $n-|v|$ vertices, we have $|w|< F(n-|v|+2)$ by the first case, and thus $|vw|< F(n-|v|+2)+|v|$ as desired. This proves the second case.
nodes.statement_short: Out-degree positive: canalize from $(i,x_i)$, freeze $i$ and the canalized vertices, and apply Case 1 to the subnetwork.

nodes.name: Longest canalizing word from (i,a)
nodes.statement: \BF{Case 2: $i$ is of out-degree at least one.} Let $a=x_i$ and let $v$ be a longest canalizing word from $(i,a)$. If $f^{v,i}(x)_i\neq a$ then we are done since $|v,i|\leq n$ and $n< F(n-m+2)+m$ for all $0\leq m<n$. So we assume that $f^{v,i}(x)_i=a$. Let $b$ be the image of $v$ and $I=\{v\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a longest canalizing word $v$ from $(i,x_i)$; if $v,i$ flips $i$ we are done.

nodes.name: (1) f_i not constant on the canalized cube
nodes.statement:
(1) {\em There is no $c$ such that $f_i(y)=c$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_i=a$ and $y_I=b$.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose, for a contradiction, that $f_i(y)=c$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_i=a$ and $y_I=b$. Let $y$ be a configuration on $V$ with $y_i=a$ such that, for all positive (negative) in-neighbors $j$ of $i$ with $j
ot\in I$ we have $y_j
eq a$ ($y_j=a)$; if $j=i$ then $j$ is a negative in-neighbor of $i$ since $G$ has only negative cycles, and we have already imposed $y_j=a$. Suppose that $i$ has a positive in-neighbor $j\in I$. Since $G$ has only negative cycles, all the paths from $i$ to $j$ are negative. Hence, by Lemma~ef{lem:diffusion}, we have $a
eq b_j$. Thus, for {\em every} positive in-neighbor $j$ of $i$ we have $f^v(y)_j
eq a$, because $f^v(y)_j=y_j
eq a$ if $j
ot\in I$ and $f^v(y)_j=b_j
eq a$ otherwise. We prove similarly that, for every negative in-neighbor $j$ of $i$, we have $f^v(y)_j=a$. Hence $f^v(y)$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$, and since $i$ is not a source, by Proposition~ef{pro:flipping} we have $f_i(f^v(y))
eq a$. Since $f^v(y)_i=y_i=a$ and $f^v(y)_I=b$, we deduce that $c
eq a$. Now, since $f^v(x)_i=x_i=a$ and $f^v(x)_I=b$, we have $f_i(f^v(x))=c
eq a$ and thus $f^{v,i}(x)_i
eq a$, which contradicts our hypothesis. This proves (1).
nodes.statement_short: Using an $i$-unstable configuration and Proposition 2, $f_i$ is not constant when $y_i=a$, $y_I=b$.

nodes.name: Define subnetwork with i frozen
nodes.statement: Given a configuration $y$ on $V$ we denote by $\tilde y$ the configuration on $V$ such that $\tilde y_i=a$ and $\tilde y_j=y_j$ for all $j\neq i$. Let $h$ be the BN with component set $J=V\setminus I$ such that $h(y_J)=f(\tilde y)_J$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_I=b$. Let $H$ be the signed interaction digraph of $h$. Note that $H$ is a subgraph of $G$ in which $i$ is of out-degree zero.
nodes.statement_short: Define $h$ on $J=V\setminus I$ with $i$'s influence frozen at $a$; in $H$, $i$ has out-degree zero.

nodes.name: (2) H has no positive cycles and no sources
nodes.statement:
(2) {\em $H$ has no positive cycles and no sources.} \medskip 
oindent Since $H$ is a subgraph of $G$, it has no positive cycles. Suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ has a source $k$. Then there is $c$ such that $h(y_J)_k=c$ for all configurations $y$ on $V$. So if $y_i=a$ and $y_I=b$ then $f(y)_J=h(y_J)$ and thus $f(y)_k=h(y_J)_k=c$. For all configurations $y$ on $V$ with $y_i=a$, we have $f^{v}(y)_i=a$ and $f^v(y)_I=b$ and we deduce that $f^{v,k}(y)_k=c$. By (1) we have $k
eq i$ and since $k
ot\in I$ we deduce that $v,k$ is a canalizing word from $(i,a)$ longer than $v$, a contradiction. This proves (2).
nodes.statement_short: A source of $H$ would extend $v$.

nodes.name: (3) H is i-homogenous
nodes.statement:
(3) {\em $H$ is $i$-homogenous.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ is not $i$-homogenous. Then it has a strong component $F$ such that, for any vertex $\ell$ in $F$, $H$ has both a positive path and a negative path from $\ell$ to $i$. Since $G$ is $i$-homogenous, $F$ is not a strong component of $G$ and thus $G$ has an arc from some vertex $k$ not in $F$ to some vertex $\ell$ in $F$. Let $y,z$ be two configurations on $V$ that only differ in component $k$ such that $f(y)_\ell
eq f(z)_\ell$. If $G$ has no arc from $I\cup\{i\}$ to $\ell$, then we can choose $y,z$ in such a way that $y_I=z_I=b$ and $y_i=z_i=a$. But then $h(y_J)_\ell=f(y)_\ell
eq f(z)_\ell= h(z_J)_\ell$ thus $H$ has an arc from $k$ to $\ell$, a contradiction. Hence $G$ has an arc from some vertex $k'\in I\cup\{i\}$ to $\ell$. By Lemma~ef{lem:diffusion}, $G$ has a path from $i$ to $k'$ whose internal vertices are in $I$ (of length zero if $k=i$), and thus it has a path $P$ from $i$ to $\ell$ whose internal vertices are in $I$. Since $\ell$ is in $F$, $H$ has a positive path $P^+$ from $\ell$ to $i$ and a negative path $P^-$ from $\ell$ to $i$. Then $P\cup P^+$ and $P\cup P^-$ are cycles of $G$ of opposite signs, so $G$ has a positive cycle, a contradiction. This proves~(3).
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise $G$ would contain cycles of opposite signs through $i$.

nodes.name: Apply Case 1 to H
nodes.statement: Since $i$ is of out-degree zero in $H$, we deduce from (2), (3) and the first case that there is a shortest word $w$ over $J$ such that $h^w(z_J)_i\neq a$ where $z=f^{v}(x)$. Since $w$ is of minimal length for this property, $i$ appears only once in $w$, in last position: $w=w',i$ for some word $w'$ not containing $i$. Since $z_I=b$, $z_i=a$ and $w'$ does not contain any letter in $I\cup\{i\}$, we deduce, setting $y=f^{w'}(z)$, that $y_J=h^{w'}(z_J)$. Furthermore, $y_I=b$ and $y_i=a$ so $f(y)_J=h(y_J)$. Consequently, \[ f^{vw}(x)_i=f(y)_i=h(y_J)_i=h(h^{w'}(z_J))_i=h^w(z_J)_i\neq a. \]
nodes.statement_short: Case 1 on $H$ gives $w=w',i$ and then $f^{vw}(x)_i\neq a$.

nodes.name: Length bound in Case 2
nodes.statement: It remains to prove the upper bound on the length of $vw$ when $f$ is an and-or-net. So suppose that $f$ is an and-or-net. Then $h$ is also an and-or-net, and since $H$ has $n-|v|$ vertices, we have $|w|< F(n-|v|+2)$ by the first case, and thus $|vw|< F(n-|v|+2)+|v|$ as desired. This proves the second case.
nodes.statement_short: $|vw|<F(n-|v|+2)+|v|$ by the first case.

nodes.name: Size of the terminal component of the asynchronous state diagram
nodes.statement: Suppose that $G$ is strong, non-trivial, and has no positive cycles. Let $f$ be any BN on $G$. It is proved in \cite{RC07} that the state diagram $\Gamma(f)$ of the asynchronous automaton of $f$ has a unique terminal strong component $A$. Furthermore, it is proved in \cite{A08} that $f$ has no fixed points, and thus $A$ contains at least $2$ configurations. But Lemma~\ref{lem:no_fixed_vertex} says something stronger: $A$ contains at least $n+1$ configurations. Indeed, for every configuration $x$ in $A$ and $i\in V$ we have $f^w(x)_i\neq x_i$ for some word $w$, and since $A$ is a terminal strong component of $\Gamma(f)$, we have $f^w(x)\in A$. Taking $w$ as short as possible, $i$ is the last letter of $w$, so $w=v,i$ for some word $v$, and $f^v(x)_i\neq f^w(x)_i$. Since $A$ is a terminal strong component of $\Gamma(f)$, the configurations $f^v(x)$ and $f^w(x)$ are both contained in $A$, and thay only differ in component $i$. This shows that, for every $i\in V$, there are two configurations in $A$ which differ only in component $i$ and this implies that $A$ contains at least $n+1$ configurations (see Appendix \ref{app:att_size} for details). We conjecture that the right lower bound is $2n$.
nodes.statement_short: For strong $G$ without positive cycles, the unique attractor of $\Gamma(f)$ has at least $n+1$ configurations by Lemma 4; conjecturally at least $2n$.
nodes.label: rem:att_size

nodes.name: Unique attractor of the asynchronous dynamics
nodes.statement: It is proved in \cite{RC07} that the state diagram $\Gamma(f)$ of the asynchronous automaton of $f$ has a unique terminal strong component $A$.
assumptions: $G$ is strong, non-trivial, and has no positive cycles
$f$ be any BN on $G$
conclusions: the state diagram $\Gamma(f)$ of the asynchronous automaton of $f$ has a unique terminal strong component $A$

nodes.name: Attractor size at least 2n
nodes.statement: We conjecture that the right lower bound is $2n$.
conclusions: the right lower bound is $2n$

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemma 7
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: bring $x$ to an $i$-unstable configuration, update $i$, then use a shortest flipping word for $y$ to break one in-neighbor and update $i$ again; length $<2F(n+2)$.

nodes.name: Reduce to x_i=1 and two positive in-neighbors
nodes.statement: The argument is roughly the following. If $x_i=y_i=0$ there is nothing to prove: we can take $w=\epsilon$. So suppose, without loss of generality, that $x_i=1$. The key points can be explained by assuming that $i$ has exactly two in-neighbors, say $j$ and $\ell$, both positive and distinct from~$i$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $x_i=1$ and $i$ has two positive in-neighbors $j,\ell$.

nodes.name: Make x i-unstable
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5 gives $u$ sending $x$ to an $i$-unstable configuration.

nodes.name: Case f_i(y')=1
nodes.statement_short: If $f_i(y')=1$ then both in-neighbors of $i$ are 1 in $y'$.

nodes.name: Update i
nodes.statement_short: Updating $i$ gives $x''_i=0$ and $y''_i=1$.

nodes.name: Break an in-neighbor of y
nodes.statement_short: A shortest prefix of a flipping word for $y''$ changes one in-neighbor of $i$.

nodes.name: Conclude with length bound
nodes.statement: Since $x'''_j=y'''_\ell=0$ we have $f_i(x''')=f_i(y''')=0$, thus $w=u,i,\tilde v,i$ has the desired properties. Furthermore, from the bound given in Lemma~\ref{lem:no_fixed_vertex_2}, we obtain $|u|,|v|<F(n+2)-1$ so that $|w|<2F(n+2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Updating $i$ again sets both to 0 with $|w|<2F(n+2)$.

nodes.name: Other cases
nodes.statement: The case where $i$ has more than two in-neighbors, with possibly some negative, is very similar. To treat the case where $i$ has a loop or is of in-degree one, some additional easy arguments have to be given.
nodes.statement_short: More in-neighbors, loops or in-degree one need only easy extra arguments.

nodes.name: Synchronizing a vertex at state 0
nodes.statement: Suppose that $G$ is $i$-homogenous and has no positive cycles and no sources. Suppose also that $G$ has a positive path $P$ from a vertex $j$ to $i$ such that $j$ is of in-degree at least two, and all the vertices of $P$ distinct from $j$ are of in-degree one (if $i$ is of in-degree at least two, this path always exists and is the trivial graph whose unique vertex is $i$). Let $f$ be the and-net on $G$ and let $x,y$ be configurations on $V$. There is a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)_i=f^w(y)_i=0$ and \[ |w|< 2F(n+2). \]
assumptions: $G$ is $i$-homogenous and has no positive cycles and no sources
$G$ has a positive path $P$ from a vertex $j$ to $i$ such that $j$ is of in-degree at least two, and all the vertices of $P$ distinct from $j$ are of in-degree one
$f$ be the and-net on $G$
$x,y$ be configurations on $V$
conclusions: There is a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)_i=f^w(y)_i=0$ and \[ |w|< 2F(n+2). \]
nodes.statement_short: For the and-net, any two configurations can be driven to agree at $i$ (state 0) by a word of length $<2F(n+2)$.
nodes.label: lem:fixing_a_vertex

nodes.name: Reaching an i-unstable configuration
nodes.statement: Suppose that $G$ is $i$-homogenous and has no positive cycles and no sources. Let $f$ be an and-or-net on $G$, let $x$ be a configuration on $V$, and let $r$ be the maximum length of a canalizing word from $(i,x_i)$. There is a word $w$, which does not contain $i$, such that $f^w(x)$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$ and \[ |w|< F(n-r+1)+r-1. \]
assumptions: $G$ is $i$-homogenous and has no positive cycles and no sources
$f$ be an and-or-net on $G$
$x$ be a configuration on $V$
$r$ be the maximum length of a canalizing word from $(i,x_i)$
conclusions: There is a word $w$, which does not contain $i$, such that $f^w(x)$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$ and \[ |w|< F(n-r+1)+r-1. \]
nodes.label: lem:coherent_local_configuration

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $x_i=0$. Let $h$ be the and-or-net on $G$ such that $h_j=f_j$ for all $j
eq i$ and $h_i$ is a conjunction. By Lemma ef{lem:no_fixed_vertex_2}, there is a shortest word $v$ such that $h^v(x)_i=1$ and $|v|<F(n-r+1)+r$ (because $r$ does not depend on $f_i$). Since $v$ is a shortest word, $i$ appears once in $w$, in last position. Let $w$ obtained from $v$ by removing the last letter~$i$. Then $h_i(h^w(x))=1$, and since $h_i$ is a conjunction, we deduce that $h^w(x)$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$. Since $i
ot\in\{w\}$ and $h_j=f_j$ for $j
eq i$, we have $h^w(x)=f^w(x)$. Thus $w$ has the desired properties. If $x_i=1$ the proof is similar, excepted that $h_i$ is a disjunction.
nodes.statement_short: Replace $f_i$ by a conjunction, apply Lemma 5 and drop the final letter $i$ of the shortest flipping word.

nodes.name: Modify f_i into a conjunction
nodes.statement: Suppose that $x_i=0$. Let $h$ be the and-or-net on $G$ such that $h_j=f_j$ for all $j\neq i$ and $h_i$ is a conjunction.
nodes.statement_short: For $x_i=0$, let $h$ agree with $f$ except $h_i$ is a conjunction.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 5
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:no_fixed_vertex_2}, there is a shortest word $v$ such that $h^v(x)_i=1$ and $|v|<F(n-r+1)+r$ (because $r$ does not depend on $f_i$).
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5 gives a shortest $v$ with $h^v(x)_i=1$.

nodes.name: Drop the last letter
nodes.statement: Since $v$ is a shortest word, $i$ appears once in $w$, in last position. Let $w$ obtained from $v$ by removing the last letter~$i$. Then $h_i(h^w(x))=1$, and since $h_i$ is a conjunction, we deduce that $h^w(x)$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Removing the final $i$ gives $w$ with $h^w(x)$ $i$-unstable.

nodes.name: Transfer to f
nodes.statement: Since $i\not\in\{w\}$ and $h_j=f_j$ for $j\neq i$, we have $h^w(x)=f^w(x)$. Thus $w$ has the desired properties. If $x_i=1$ the proof is similar, excepted that $h_i$ is a disjunction.
nodes.statement_short: Since $w$ avoids $i$, $f^w(x)=h^w(x)$; the case $x_i=1$ uses a disjunction.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7
nodes.statement:
If $x_i=y_i=0$ there is nothing to prove, so suppose, without loss of generality, that $x_i=1$. Let $r$ be the maximal length of a canalizing word from $(i,1)$. We prove that there is a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)_i=f^w(y)_i=0$ with  egin{enumerate} \item $|w|\leq 2F(n-r+2)+2r-2$ if $i$ is of in-degree at least two, \item $|w|\leq 2F(n+2)-1$ if $i$ is of in-degree one. \end{enumerate} \medskip Suppose first that $i$ is of in-degree at least two. By Lemma ef{lem:coherent_local_configuration} there is a word $u$, which does not contain $i$, such that $f^u(x)$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$ and \[ |u|\leq F(n-r+2)+r-2. \] Let $x'=f^u(x)$ and $y'=f^u(y)$. Since $x'$ is $i$-unstable, we have $f(x')_i=0$. Hence if $f(y')_i=0$ we are done by taking $w=u,i$. So suppose that $f(y')_i=1$. Let $x''=f^i(x')$ and $y''=f^i(y')$. Hence we have $x''_i=0$ and $y''_i=1$. We consider two cases. Suppose first that $i$ has a loop. Then it is negative thus $f(y'')_i=0$. Let $j$ be an in-neighbor of $i$ distinct from $i$. Then $x''_j=x'_j$ and since $x'$ is $i$-unstable, we have $x'_j=0$ if $j$ is a positive in-neighbor of $i$, and $x'_j=1$ otherwise, and we deduce that $f(x'')_i=0$ (because $f_i$ is a conjunction). So we are done with $w=u,i,i$. For the second case, suppose that $i$ has no loop. By Lemma~ef{lem:no_fixed_vertex_2}, there is a shortest word $v$ such that $f^v(y'')_i=0$ and \[ |v|\leq F(n-r+2)+r-1. \] Since $y''_i=1$ and $v$ is as short as possible, $i$ is the last letter of $v$ and at least one in-neighbor of $i$ appears in $v$. Let $\ell$ be the first in-neighbor of $i$ that appears $v$, and let $	ilde v$ the shortest prefix of $v$ containing $\ell$. Let $x'''=f^{	ilde v}(x'')$ and $y'''=f^{	ilde v}(y'')$. We have $y'''_\ell
eq y''_\ell$ since $v$ is as short as possible and $\ell$ appears once in $	ilde v$. Furthermore, $y''_\ell=y'_\ell$ since $\ell
eq i$ (because $i$ has no loop). So $y'''_\ell
eq y'_\ell$, and since $f(y')_i=1$, we deduce that $f(y''')_i=0$ (because $f_i$ is a conjunction). Let $j$ be an in-neighbor of $i$ distinct from $\ell$. Since $j$ does not appear in $	ilde v$ and $j
eq i$ (because $i$ has no loop), we have $x'''_j=x''_j=x'_j$. Since $x'$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$, we have $x'_i=0$ if $j$ is a positive in-neighbor of $i$, and $x'_i=1$ otherwise. Consequently, $f(x''')_i=0$ (because $f_i$ is a conjunction). So we are done with $w=u,i,	ilde v,i$, observing that $|	ilde v|\leq |v|-1$. \medskip Suppose now that $i$ is of in-degree one, and let $P$ be as in the statement. Let $s$ be the maximal length of a canalizing word from $(j,1)$. Since $G$ is $i$-homogenous, it is also $j$-homogenous and, by the first case, there is word $u$ such that $f^u(x)_j=f^u(y)_j=0$ and $|u|\leq 2F(n-s+2)+2s-2$. Let $v$ be an enumeration of the vertices of $P\setminus j$ in order. Since all the vertices of $P\setminus j$ are of in-degree one, $v$ is a canalizing word from $(j,1)$ and $(j,0)$. Thus $|v|\leq s$ and, since $P$ is positive and $f^u(x)_j=f^u(y)_j=0$, we obtain $f^{uv}(x)_i=f^{uv}(y)_i=0$ (by Lemma ef{lem:diffusion}). Furthermore, \[ |uv|\leq 2F(n-s+2)+3s-2. \] So it is sufficient to prove that, for all $n\geq 1$ and $0\leq s<n$, \[ 2F(n-s+2)+3s-2\leq 2F(n+2)-1. \] We proceed by induction on $n$. The case $n=1$ is obvious, so suppose that $n\geq 2$. If $s=n-1$ then the inequality to prove becomes $3n\leq 2F(n+2)$ which is easy to check. So suppose that $0\leq s\leq n-2$. Then, using the induction for the first inequality, we obtain \[  egin{array}{lll} 2F(n-s+2)+3s-2 &=&2F((n-1)-s+3)+3s-2\ &=&2F((n-1)-s+1)+2F((n-1)-s+2)+3s-2\ &\leq & 2F((n-1)-s+1)+2F((n-1)+2)-1\ &\leq & 2F(n)+2F(n+1)-1\ &= & 2F(n+2)-1, \end{array} \] completing the induction.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on the in-degree of $i$. In-degree $\geq2$: reach an $i$-unstable configuration (Lemma 8), update $i$, and use a shortest flipping word (Lemma 5); in-degree one: synchronize the head $j$ of the path and propagate along it.

nodes.name: WLOG x_i = 1
nodes.statement: If $x_i=y_i=0$ there is nothing to prove, so suppose, without loss of generality, that $x_i=1$. Let $r$ be the maximal length of a canalizing word from $(i,1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $x_i=1$ and let $r$ be the maximal canalizing length from $(i,1)$.

nodes.name: Refined bound by in-degree
nodes.statement:
We prove that there is a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)_i=f^w(y)_i=0$ with  egin{enumerate} \item $|w|\leq 2F(n-r+2)+2r-2$ if $i$ is of in-degree at least two, \item $|w|\leq 2F(n+2)-1$ if $i$ is of in-degree one. \end{enumerate} \medskip Suppose first that $i$ is of in-degree at least two. By Lemma ef{lem:coherent_local_configuration} there is a word $u$, which does not contain $i$, such that $f^u(x)$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$ and \[ |u|\leq F(n-r+2)+r-2. \] Let $x'=f^u(x)$ and $y'=f^u(y)$. So we are done with $w=u,i,i$. For the second case, suppose that $i$ has no loop. By Lemma~ef{lem:no_fixed_vertex_2}, there is a shortest word $v$ such that $f^v(y'')_i=0$ and \[ |v|\leq F(n-r+2)+r-1. \] Since $y''_i=1$ and $v$ is as short as possible, $i$ is the last letter of $v$ and at least one in-neighbor of $i$ appears in $v$. Let $\ell$ be the first in-neighbor of $i$ that appears $v$, and let $	ilde v$ the shortest prefix of $v$ containing $\ell$. Let $x'''=f^{	ilde v}(x'')$ and $y'''=f^{	ilde v}(y'')$. We have $y'''_\ell
eq y''_\ell$ since $v$ is as short as possible and $\ell$ appears once in $	ilde v$. Furthermore, $y''_\ell=y'_\ell$ since $\ell
eq i$ (because $i$ has no loop). So $y'''_\ell
eq y'_\ell$, and since $f(y')_i=1$, we deduce that $f(y''')_i=0$ (because $f_i$ is a conjunction). Let $j$ be an in-neighbor of $i$ distinct from $\ell$. Since $j$ does not appear in $	ilde v$ and $j
eq i$ (because $i$ has no loop), we have $x'''_j=x''_j=x'_j$. Since $x'$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$, we have $x'_i=0$ if $j$ is a positive in-neighbor of $i$, and $x'_i=1$ otherwise. Consequently, $f(x''')_i=0$ (because $f_i$ is a conjunction). So we are done with $w=u,i,	ilde v,i$, observing that $|	ilde v|\leq |v|-1$. \medskip Suppose now that $i$ is of in-degree one, and let $P$ be as in the statement. Let $s$ be the maximal length of a canalizing word from $(j,1)$. Since $G$ is $i$-homogenous, it is also $j$-homogenous and, by the first case, there is word $u$ such that $f^u(x)_j=f^u(y)_j=0$ and $|u|\leq 2F(n-s+2)+2s-2$. Let $v$ be an enumeration of the vertices of $P\setminus j$ in order. Since all the vertices of $P\setminus j$ are of in-degree one, $v$ is a canalizing word from $(j,1)$ and $(j,0)$. Thus $|v|\leq s$ and, since $P$ is positive and $f^u(x)_j=f^u(y)_j=0$, we obtain $f^{uv}(x)_i=f^{uv}(y)_i=0$ (by Lemma ef{lem:diffusion}). Furthermore, \[ |uv|\leq 2F(n-s+2)+3s-2. \] So it is sufficient to prove that, for all $n\geq 1$ and $0\leq s<n$, \[ 2F(n-s+2)+3s-2\leq 2F(n+2)-1. \] We proceed by induction on $n$. The case $n=1$ is obvious, so suppose that $n\geq 2$. If $s=n-1$ then the inequality to prove becomes $3n\leq 2F(n+2)$ which is easy to check. So suppose that $0\leq s\leq n-2$. Then, using the induction for the first inequality, we obtain \[  egin{array}{lll} 2F(n-s+2)+3s-2 &=&2F((n-1)-s+3)+3s-2\ &=&2F((n-1)-s+1)+2F((n-1)-s+2)+3s-2\ &\leq & 2F((n-1)-s+1)+2F((n-1)+2)-1\ &\leq & 2F(n)+2F(n+1)-1\ &= & 2F(n+2)-1, \end{array} \] completing the induction.
nodes.statement_short: Prove refined bounds depending on whether $i$ has in-degree at least two or one.

nodes.name: Bound for in-degree at least two
nodes.statement: \item $|w|\leq 2F(n-r+2)+2r-2$ if $i$ is of in-degree at least two,
nodes.statement_short: $|w|\leq 2F(n-r+2)+2r-2$ when $i$ has in-degree $\geq 2$.

nodes.name: Bound for in-degree one
nodes.statement: \item $|w|\leq 2F(n+2)-1$ if $i$ is of in-degree one. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $|w|\leq 2F(n+2)-1$ when $i$ has in-degree one.

nodes.name: In-degree at least two
nodes.statement:
Suppose first that $i$ is of in-degree at least two. By Lemma ef{lem:coherent_local_configuration} there is a word $u$, which does not contain $i$, such that $f^u(x)$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$ and \[ |u|\leq F(n-r+2)+r-2. \] Let $x'=f^u(x)$ and $y'=f^u(y)$. Since $x'$ is $i$-unstable, we have $f(x')_i=0$. Hence if $f(y')_i=0$ we are done by taking $w=u,i$. So suppose that $f(y')_i=1$. Let $x''=f^i(x')$ and $y''=f^i(y')$. Hence we have $x''_i=0$ and $y''_i=1$. We consider two cases. Suppose first that $i$ has a loop. Then it is negative thus $f(y'')_i=0$. Let $j$ be an in-neighbor of $i$ distinct from $i$. Then $x''_j=x'_j$ and since $x'$ is $i$-unstable, we have $x'_j=0$ if $j$ is a positive in-neighbor of $i$, and $x'_j=1$ otherwise, and we deduce that $f(x'')_i=0$ (because $f_i$ is a conjunction). So we are done with $w=u,i,i$. For the second case, suppose that $i$ has no loop. By Lemma~ef{lem:no_fixed_vertex_2}, there is a shortest word $v$ such that $f^v(y'')_i=0$ and \[ |v|\leq F(n-r+2)+r-1. \] Since $y''_i=1$ and $v$ is as short as possible, $i$ is the last letter of $v$ and at least one in-neighbor of $i$ appears in $v$. Let $\ell$ be the first in-neighbor of $i$ that appears $v$, and let $	ilde v$ the shortest prefix of $v$ containing $\ell$. Let $x'''=f^{	ilde v}(x'')$ and $y'''=f^{	ilde v}(y'')$. We have $y'''_\ell
eq y''_\ell$ since $v$ is as short as possible and $\ell$ appears once in $	ilde v$. Furthermore, $y''_\ell=y'_\ell$ since $\ell
eq i$ (because $i$ has no loop). So $y'''_\ell
eq y'_\ell$, and since $f(y')_i=1$, we deduce that $f(y''')_i=0$ (because $f_i$ is a conjunction). Let $j$ be an in-neighbor of $i$ distinct from $\ell$. Since $j$ does not appear in $	ilde v$ and $j
eq i$ (because $i$ has no loop), we have $x'''_j=x''_j=x'_j$. Since $x'$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$, we have $x'_i=0$ if $j$ is a positive in-neighbor of $i$, and $x'_i=1$ otherwise. Consequently, $f(x''')_i=0$ (because $f_i$ is a conjunction). So we are done with $w=u,i,	ilde v,i$, observing that $|	ilde v|\leq |v|-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Reach an $i$-unstable configuration, update $i$, then handle loop / no loop.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 8
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $i$ is of in-degree at least two. By Lemma \ref{lem:coherent_local_configuration} there is a word $u$, which does not contain $i$, such that $f^u(x)$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$ and \[ |u|\leq F(n-r+2)+r-2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 8 gives $u$ making $x$ $i$-unstable.

nodes.name: Update i once
nodes.statement: Let $x'=f^u(x)$ and $y'=f^u(y)$. Since $x'$ is $i$-unstable, we have $f(x')_i=0$. Hence if $f(y')_i=0$ we are done by taking $w=u,i$. So suppose that $f(y')_i=1$. Let $x''=f^i(x')$ and $y''=f^i(y')$. Hence we have $x''_i=0$ and $y''_i=1$.
nodes.statement_short: If $f(y')_i=0$ take $w=u,i$; else update $i$ to get $x''_i=0$, $y''_i=1$.

nodes.name: i has a loop
nodes.statement: We consider two cases. Suppose first that $i$ has a loop. Then it is negative thus $f(y'')_i=0$. Let $j$ be an in-neighbor of $i$ distinct from $i$. Then $x''_j=x'_j$ and since $x'$ is $i$-unstable, we have $x'_j=0$ if $j$ is a positive in-neighbor of $i$, and $x'_j=1$ otherwise, and we deduce that $f(x'')_i=0$ (because $f_i$ is a conjunction). So we are done with $w=u,i,i$.
nodes.statement_short: The negative loop resets $y''_i$ while $x''$ stays; $w=u,i,i$.

nodes.name: i has no loop
nodes.statement:
For the second case, suppose that $i$ has no loop. By Lemma~ef{lem:no_fixed_vertex_2}, there is a shortest word $v$ such that $f^v(y'')_i=0$ and \[ |v|\leq F(n-r+2)+r-1. \] Since $y''_i=1$ and $v$ is as short as possible, $i$ is the last letter of $v$ and at least one in-neighbor of $i$ appears in $v$. Let $\ell$ be the first in-neighbor of $i$ that appears $v$, and let $	ilde v$ the shortest prefix of $v$ containing $\ell$. Let $x'''=f^{	ilde v}(x'')$ and $y'''=f^{	ilde v}(y'')$. We have $y'''_\ell
eq y''_\ell$ since $v$ is as short as possible and $\ell$ appears once in $	ilde v$. Furthermore, $y''_\ell=y'_\ell$ since $\ell
eq i$ (because $i$ has no loop). So $y'''_\ell
eq y'_\ell$, and since $f(y')_i=1$, we deduce that $f(y''')_i=0$ (because $f_i$ is a conjunction). Let $j$ be an in-neighbor of $i$ distinct from $\ell$. Since $j$ does not appear in $	ilde v$ and $j
eq i$ (because $i$ has no loop), we have $x'''_j=x''_j=x'_j$. Since $x'$ is an $i$-unstable configuration in $G$, we have $x'_i=0$ if $j$ is a positive in-neighbor of $i$, and $x'_i=1$ otherwise. Consequently, $f(x''')_i=0$ (because $f_i$ is a conjunction). So we are done with $w=u,i,	ilde v,i$, observing that $|	ilde v|\leq |v|-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the prefix $\tilde v$ of a shortest flipping word for $y''$ up to the first in-neighbor $\ell$ of $i$; then $w=u,i,\tilde v,i$.

nodes.name: In-degree one
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $i$ is of in-degree one, and let $P$ be as in the statement. Let $s$ be the maximal length of a canalizing word from $(j,1)$. Since $G$ is $i$-homogenous, it is also $j$-homogenous and, by the first case, there is word $u$ such that $f^u(x)_j=f^u(y)_j=0$ and $|u|\leq 2F(n-s+2)+2s-2$. Let $v$ be an enumeration of the vertices of $P\setminus j$ in order. Since all the vertices of $P\setminus j$ are of in-degree one, $v$ is a canalizing word from $(j,1)$ and $(j,0)$. Thus $|v|\leq s$ and, since $P$ is positive and $f^u(x)_j=f^u(y)_j=0$, we obtain $f^{uv}(x)_i=f^{uv}(y)_i=0$ (by Lemma \ref{lem:diffusion}). Furthermore, \[ |uv|\leq 2F(n-s+2)+3s-2. \] So it is sufficient to prove that, for all $n\geq 1$ and $0\leq s<n$, \[ 2F(n-s+2)+3s-2\leq 2F(n+2)-1. \] We proceed by induction on $n$. The case $n=1$ is obvious, so suppose that $n\geq 2$. If $s=n-1$ then the inequality to prove becomes $3n\leq 2F(n+2)$ which is easy to check. So suppose that $0\leq s\leq n-2$. Then, using the induction for the first inequality, we obtain \[ \begin{array}{lll} 2F(n-s+2)+3s-2 &=&2F((n-1)-s+3)+3s-2\\ &=&2F((n-1)-s+1)+2F((n-1)-s+2)+3s-2\\ &\leq & 2F((n-1)-s+1)+2F((n-1)+2)-1\\ &\leq & 2F(n)+2F(n+1)-1\\ &= & 2F(n+2)-1, \end{array} \] completing the induction.
nodes.statement_short: Synchronize $j$ by the first case and propagate along the positive path $P$, then check the Fibonacci inequality by induction.

nodes.name: Synchronize j and propagate
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $i$ is of in-degree one, and let $P$ be as in the statement. Let $s$ be the maximal length of a canalizing word from $(j,1)$. Since $G$ is $i$-homogenous, it is also $j$-homogenous and, by the first case, there is word $u$ such that $f^u(x)_j=f^u(y)_j=0$ and $|u|\leq 2F(n-s+2)+2s-2$. Let $v$ be an enumeration of the vertices of $P\setminus j$ in order. Since all the vertices of $P\setminus j$ are of in-degree one, $v$ is a canalizing word from $(j,1)$ and $(j,0)$. Thus $|v|\leq s$ and, since $P$ is positive and $f^u(x)_j=f^u(y)_j=0$, we obtain $f^{uv}(x)_i=f^{uv}(y)_i=0$ (by Lemma \ref{lem:diffusion}). Furthermore, \[ |uv|\leq 2F(n-s+2)+3s-2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Synchronize $j$ at 0 and canalize along $P$ (Lemma 6) to get $|uv|\leq 2F(n-s+2)+3s-2$.

nodes.name: Reduce to an inequality
nodes.statement: So it is sufficient to prove that, for all $n\geq 1$ and $0\leq s<n$, \[ 2F(n-s+2)+3s-2\leq 2F(n+2)-1. \]
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to show $2F(n-s+2)+3s-2\leq 2F(n+2)-1$.

nodes.name: Prove the inequality
nodes.statement: We proceed by induction on $n$. The case $n=1$ is obvious, so suppose that $n\geq 2$. If $s=n-1$ then the inequality to prove becomes $3n\leq 2F(n+2)$ which is easy to check. So suppose that $0\leq s\leq n-2$. Then, using the induction for the first inequality, we obtain \[ \begin{array}{lll} 2F(n-s+2)+3s-2 &=&2F((n-1)-s+3)+3s-2\\ &=&2F((n-1)-s+1)+2F((n-1)-s+2)+3s-2\\ &\leq & 2F((n-1)-s+1)+2F((n-1)+2)-1\\ &\leq & 2F(n)+2F(n+1)-1\\ &= & 2F(n+2)-1, \end{array} \] completing the induction.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$ using the Fibonacci recurrence.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemma 9
nodes.statement: The argument is roughly the following. Since $G$ has no positive cycles, it has a vertex $i_1$ with only negative out-neighbors. By Lemma \ref{lem:fixing_a_vertex}, there is a word $v^1$ of length at most $2F(n+2)$ synchronizing $i_1$ at state $0$. We then consider the ``subnetwork'' $f'$ obtained by fixing $i_1$ at state $0$ and removing $i_1$. Since $i_1$ has only negative out-neighbors, the signed interaction digraph of $f'$ is $G\setminus i_1$. If $G\setminus i_1$ still satisfies all the conditions, then we can synchronize a new vertex $i_2$, with only negative out-neighbors, with a word $v^2$ of length at most $2F(n+1)$. Repeating this argument, we possible synchronize all components, obtaining a word $w=v^1v^2\dots $ with $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$ and $|w|\leq 2F(n+2)+2F(n+1)+\cdots +2F(3)$. Note that $|w|\leq 2F(n+4)-2$ since the sum of the $n$ first Fibonacci numbers is $F(n+2)-1$. However, this synchronizing process cannot be always completed, since $G\setminus i_1$ does not necessarily satisfy the appropriate conditions: it can have initial cycles. But these initial cycles are ``controlled'' by $i_1$ and, with fastidious arguments involving Lemmas~\ref{lem:no_fixed_vertex_2}, we can construct a word $\tilde v^1$ of length $|\tilde v^1|\leq 3F(n+2)$ synchronizing both $i_1$ and the vertices that belongs to the initial cycles of $G\setminus i_1$. From this point, we can ``remove'' $i_1$ and continue the synchronizing process without trouble. We eventually get a word $w=\tilde v^1\tilde v^2\dots$ such that $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$ and $|w|\leq 3F(n+4)-3$.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: repeatedly synchronize a vertex with only negative out-neighbors (Lemma 7) and remove it, controlling newly created initial cycles; total length $\leq 3F(n+4)-3$.

nodes.name: Synchronize a first vertex
nodes.statement: The argument is roughly the following. Since $G$ has no positive cycles, it has a vertex $i_1$ with only negative out-neighbors. By Lemma \ref{lem:fixing_a_vertex}, there is a word $v^1$ of length at most $2F(n+2)$ synchronizing $i_1$ at state $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $i_1$ with only negative out-neighbors and synchronize it at 0 by Lemma 7.

nodes.name: Iterate on subnetworks
nodes.statement: We then consider the ``subnetwork'' $f'$ obtained by fixing $i_1$ at state $0$ and removing $i_1$. Since $i_1$ has only negative out-neighbors, the signed interaction digraph of $f'$ is $G\setminus i_1$. If $G\setminus i_1$ still satisfies all the conditions, then we can synchronize a new vertex $i_2$, with only negative out-neighbors, with a word $v^2$ of length at most $2F(n+1)$. Repeating this argument, we possible synchronize all components, obtaining a word $w=v^1v^2\dots $ with $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$ and $|w|\leq 2F(n+2)+2F(n+1)+\cdots +2F(3)$. Note that $|w|\leq 2F(n+4)-2$ since the sum of the $n$ first Fibonacci numbers is $F(n+2)-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $i_1$ at 0, remove it and repeat, giving length at most $2F(n+4)-2$.

nodes.name: Initial cycles obstacle
nodes.statement: However, this synchronizing process cannot be always completed, since $G\setminus i_1$ does not necessarily satisfy the appropriate conditions: it can have initial cycles. But these initial cycles are ``controlled'' by $i_1$ and, with fastidious arguments involving Lemmas~\ref{lem:no_fixed_vertex_2}, we can construct a word $\tilde v^1$ of length $|\tilde v^1|\leq 3F(n+2)$ synchronizing both $i_1$ and the vertices that belongs to the initial cycles of $G\setminus i_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Removing $i_1$ can create initial cycles; these are controlled by $i_1$ with a word of length $\leq 3F(n+2)$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: From this point, we can ``remove'' $i_1$ and continue the synchronizing process without trouble. We eventually get a word $w=\tilde v^1\tilde v^2\dots$ such that $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$ and $|w|\leq 3F(n+4)-3$.
nodes.statement_short: Continuing gives $|w|\leq 3F(n+4)-3$.

nodes.name: Synchronizing two configurations of the and-net
nodes.statement: Suppose that $G$ is homogenous and has no positive cycles, no sources and no initial cycles. Let $f$ be the and-net on $G$. For every configurations $x,y$ on $V$, there is a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$ and \[ |w|\leq 3F(n+4)-3. \]
assumptions: $G$ is homogenous and has no positive cycles, no sources and no initial cycles
$f$ be the and-net on $G$
configurations $x,y$ on $V$
conclusions: there is a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$ and \[ |w|\leq 3F(n+4)-3. \]
nodes.statement_short: For the and-net on such $G$, any two configurations can be merged by a word of length at most $3F(n+4)-3$.
nodes.label: lem:2-synchronization

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 9
nodes.statement:
For inductive purpose, we prove the following claim. For $0\leq m<n$, let \[ g(n,m)=\sum_{t=m+1}^n 3F(t+2). \]  igskip 
oindent { f Claim:} {\em Suppose that $G$ is homogenous and has no positive cycles and no sources. Let $I$ be the set of vertices of $G$ that belong to an initial cycle of $G$. Let $f$ be the and-net on $G$. For every configurations $x,y$ on $V$ with $x_I=y_I$, there is a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$ and} \[ |w|\leq g(n,|I|). \]  igskip This implies the statement since if $G$ has no initial cycles then $I$ is empty, thus $x_I=y_I$ is always true, and we obtain \[ |w|\leq g(n,0)=\sum_{t=1}^{n} 3F(t+2)\leq 3\sum_{t=1}^{n+2} F(t)=3F(n+4)-3, \] where we use, for the last equality, the fact that $\sum_{t=1}^n F(t)=F(n+2)-1$ for all $n\geq 1$, which is easy to prove by induction on $n$. \medskip The claim is proved by induction on $n-|I|$, that is, the number of vertices that do not belong to an initial cycle. If $n-|I|=0$ then $I=V$ so $x_I=y_I$ means $x=y$ and there is nothing to prove (we can take $w=\epsilon$). So suppose that $n-|I|\geq 1$. We first prove that, up to a switch, some some practical assumptions on the signs of $G$ can be made.  igskip 
oindent (1) {\em We can suppose that every $i\in V\setminus I$ with in-degree one in $G$ has a positive in-neighbor.} \medskip 
oindent Let $U$ be the set of vertices of $G$ of in-degree one that do not belong to $I$. Then $G[U]$ is a disjoint union of out-trees, say $T_1,\dots,T_k$. For $\ell\in [k]$, let $U_\ell$ be the vertex set of $T_\ell$. By Proposition~ef{pro:harary}, there is $J^1_\ell\subseteq U_\ell$ such that the $J^1_\ell$-switch of $T_\ell$ is full-positive. Let $J^2_\ell=U_\ell\setminus J^1_\ell$. The $J^2_\ell$-switch of $T_\ell$ is also full-positive. Let $i_\ell$ be the source of $T_\ell$ and suppose, without loss, that $i_\ell\in J^1_\ell$. We set $J_\ell=J^1_\ell$ if the in-neighbor of $i_\ell$ in $G$ is negative, and $J_\ell=J^2_\ell$ otherwise. Hence, in the $J_\ell$-switch of $G$, the in-neighbor of each $i\in U_\ell$ is positive. Let $J=J_1\cup\dots\cup J_k$ and let $G'$ be the $J$-switch of $G$. Then, in $G'$, the in-neighbor of each $i\in U$ is positive. Let $f'$ be the $J$-switch of $f$. Since $J\subseteq U$, each vertex $i$ of in degree at least two in $G$ (or $G'$) is not in $J$, and thus $f'_i$ is a conjunction. So $f'$ is the and-net of $G'$. By Lemma~ef{lem:invariant_homogeneity}, $G'$ satisfies the condition of the claim. From Proposition ef{pro:BN_switch}, for any word $w$ we have $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$ if and only if $f'^w(x+e_J)=f'^w(y+e_J)$. Hence, without loss of generality, we can suppose that $G=G'$ and $f'=f$. This proves (1).  igskip So in the following, we suppose every $i\in V\setminus I$ of in-degree one in $G$ has a positive in-neighbor. Since $n-|I|\geq 1$, $G$ has a terminal strong component $S$ which is not an initial cycle. Let $i$ be a vertex in $S$ with only negative out-neighbors; such a vertex exists since otherwise $G$ has a (full-)positive cycle. Let $H=G\setminus i$.  igskip 
oindent (2) {\em $H$ has no positive cycles and no sources.} \medskip 
oindent Since $H$ is a subgraph of $G$ it has no positive cycles. If $j$ is a source of $H$, then $i$ is the unique in-neighbor of $j$ in $G$ and thus, by hypothesis, the arc from $i$ to $j$ is positive, which contradicts our choice of $i$. This proves (2).  igskip 
oindent (3) {\em $H$ is homogenous.} \medskip 
oindent Let $j$ be a vertex in $H$ and suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ has a strong component $F$ such that, for every vertex $\ell$ in $F$, $H$ has both a positive and negative forward path from $\ell$ to $j$. Since $G$ is $j$-homogenous, $S$ is not a strong component of $G$, so $G$ has an arc from $i$ to some vertex $\ell$ in $F$, and thus $H$ has a positive forward path $P^+$ from $\ell$ to $j$ and a negative forward path $P^-$ from $\ell$ to $j$. Since $i$ is in a terminal strong component of $G$ and $G$ has a path from $i$ to $j$, $G$ has also a path $P$ from $j$ to $i$. Since $P\setminus i$ is a path of $H$ starting from $j$ and $P^+,P^-$ are forward paths of $H$ ending in $j$, $P^+$ and $P^-$ intersect $P\setminus i$ in $j$ only. Thus $P^+\cup P$ and $P^-\cup P$ are paths of $G$ from $\ell$ to $i$ with opposite signs. Since $G$ has an arc from $i$ to $\ell$, we deduce that $G$ has a positive cycle, a contradiction. This proves (3).  igskip Let $K$ be the set of vertices of $H$ that belongs to an initial cycles of $H$. Since $i$ is not in an initial cycle of $G$, all the initial cycles of $G$ are initial cycles of $H$, so $I\subseteq K$. From the induction hypothesis, we get that two configurations that ``agree'' on $i$ and $K$ can be synchronized:  igskip 
oindent (4) {\em If $x,y$ are configurations on $V$ with $x_i=y_i=0$ and $x_K=y_K$, then there is a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$ and $|w|\leq g(n-1,|K|)$.} \medskip 
oindent Let $x,y$ be configurations on $V$ with $x_i=y_i=0$ and $x_K=y_K$. Let $h$ be the and-net on $H$. From (2), (3) and the induction hypothesis, there is a word $w$ on $V'=V\setminus i$ such that $h^w(x_{V'})=h^w(y_{V'})$ of length at most $g(n-1,|K|)$. Since $x_i=y_i=0$ and $i$ has only negative out-neighbors and $i
ot\in\{w\}$, we deduce that $f^w(x)_{V'}=h^w(x_{V'})$ and $f^w(y)_{V'}=h^w(y_{V'})$ and thus $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$. This proves (4).  igskip So, by (4), to prove the claim it is sufficient to prove that, for every configurations $x,y$ on $V$ with $x_I=y_I$, there is a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)_i=f^w(y)_i=0$ and $f^w(x)_K=f^w(x)_K$. This is done in several steps.  igskip 
oindent (5) {\em If $x,y$ are configurations $x,y$ on $V$ with $x_I=y_I$, then $f^w(x)_I=f^w(y)_I$ for any word $w$.} \medskip 
oindent Let $x,y$ be two configurations on $V$ with $x_I=y_I$. It is sufficient to prove that, for any $j\in V$, we have $f^j(x)_I=f^j(y)_I$. This is obvious if $j
ot\in I$. Otherwise, $j$ has a unique in-neighbor, say $k$, and since $k\in I$ we have $x_k=y_k$ and we deduce that $f_j(x)=f_j(y)$ and so $f^j(x)_I=f^j(y)_I$. This proves (5).  igskip 
oindent (6) {\em Each initial cycle of $H$ which is not an initial cycle of $G$ has a unique negative arc.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ has an initial cycle $C$, which is not an initial cycle of $G$, such that $C$ does not contain a unique negative arc. Since $C$ is negative, it has at least three negative arcs. Let $(j_k,i_k)$, $k=1,2,3$, be three negative arcs in $C$, and let $P_k$ be the path from $i_k$ to $i_{k+1}$ contained in $C$, where $i_4$ means $i_1$. Hence $C=P_1\cup P_2\cup P_3$. The three negative arcs can be chosen consecutively in $C$, that is, in such a way that $C=P_1\cup P_2\cup P_3$ and, for $k=1,2$, $P_k$ has a unique negative arc, which is $(j_{k+1},i_{k+1})$. Thus $P_1,P_2$ are negative, and so is $P_3$. Also, there is a negative arc from $i$ to each of $i_1,i_2,i_3$. Indeed, if there is no arc from $i$ to $i_k$ then $i_k$ is of in-degree one in $G$, so $(j_k,i_k)$ is positive by the hypothesis resulting from (1), a contradiction. Thus $(i,i_k)$ exists and is negative by the choice of $i$. Let $Q$ be a shortest path of $G$ from $C$ to $i$ (it exists since $i$ is in a terminal strong component of $G$) and let $j$ be its initial vertex. Then $j$ belongs to $P_k\setminus i_{k+1}$ for some $1\leq k\leq 3$. Let $P'_k$ be the path from $i_k$ to $j$ contained in $P_k$. Since $P_{k-1}$ is negative ($P_0$ means $P_3$), $P'_k$ and $P_{k-1}\cup P'_k$ have distinct signs. Since $G$ has a negative arc from $i$ to $i_k$ and $i_{k-1}$ ($i_0$ means $i_3$) we deduce that $G$ has a positive path $P^+$ from $i$ to $j$ and a negative path $P^-$ from $i$ to $j$ such that $P^+,P^-$ are internally vertex-disjoint from $Q$. Hence, $P^+\cup Q$ and $P^-\cup Q$ are cycles with distinct signs, and thus $G$ has a positive cycle, a contradiction. This proves (6).  igskip 
oindent (7) {\em Let $C$ be an initial cycle of $H$, which is not an initial cycle of $G$, and let $L$ its vertex~set. If $x,y$ are configurations on $V$ and $x_i=1$, then there is a word $w$ over $L$ such that $f^w(x)_L=f^w(y)_L={\mathbf{0}}$ and $|w|\leq 2|L|$.} \medskip 
oindent By (6), $C$ has a unique negative arc, say $(j_1,i_1)$. By the hypothesis resulting from (1), $i_1$ is of in-degree at least two, so $G$ has an arc from $i$ to $i_1$, which is negative by the choice of $i$. Let $u=i_1i_2\dots i_\ell$ be an enumeration of the vertices of $C$ in the order. \medskip Let $x$ be a configuration on $V$ with $x_i=1$. Since $G$ has a negative arc from $i$ to $i_1$, we have $f(x)_{i_1}=0$. Since there is a positive arc from $i_k$ to $i_{k+1}$ for all $1\leq k<\ell$, we deduce that $f^u(x)_L={\mathbf{0}}$. Furthermore, since $i
ot\in\{u\}$ we have $f^u(x)_i=x_i=1$ and the same argument shows that $f^{uu}(x)_L={\mathbf{0}}$ by $(a)$. Consequently, \[	ag{$a$} x_i=1\quad\Rightarrow\quad f^u(x)_L={\mathbf{0}}\quad	extrm{and}\quad f^{uu}(x)_L={\mathbf{0}}. \] \medskip Consider now a configuration $x$ on $V$ with $x_i=0$. Let $x(0)=x$ and $x(k)=f^{i_k}(x(k-1))$ for $1\leq k\leq \ell$, so that $x(\ell)=f^u(x)$. Note that $x(k)_i=0$ for $0\leq k\leq\ell$ since $i
ot\in\{u\}$. We will prove, by induction on $k$ from $1$ to $\ell$, that $x(k)_{i_k}=a$, where $a=x_{i_\ell}+1$. Since $i_1$ has exactly two in-neighbors, $i$ and $i_\ell$, both negative, and $x(0)_i=0$, we have $f(x(0))_{i_1}=(x(0)_i+1)\land (x(0)_{i_\ell}+1)=1\land a=a$, and thus $x(1)_{i_1}=a$. Let $1<k\leq\ell$. By induction, $x(k-1)_{i_{k-1}}=a$. Since there is a positive arc from $i_{k-1}$ to $i_k$, and since $i_k$ has at most one possible other in-neighbor, which is $i$ and then negative, we have either $f(x(k-1))_{i_k}=x(k-1)_{i_{k-1}}=a$ if there is no arc from $i$ to $i_k$ or $f(x(k-1))_{i_k}=x(k-1)_{i_{k-1}}\land (x(k-1)_i+1)=a\land 1=a$. Thus $x(k)_{i_k}=a$ in both cases. This completes the induction step. Consequently, if $x_{i_\ell}=1$ then $f^u(x)_L={\mathbf{0}}$, and if $x_{i_\ell}=0$ then $f^u(x)_L=\mathbf{1}$. So if $x_{i_\ell}=0$ then $f^u(x)_{i_\ell}=1$ and, since $f^{u}(x)_i=x(\ell)_i=0$, the same argument shows that $f^{uu}(x)_L={\mathbf{0}}$. Consequently, \[	ag{$b$} x_i=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad f^u(x)_L={\mathbf{0}}\quad	extrm{or}\quad f^{uu}(x)_L={\mathbf{0}}. \] \medskip Let $x,y$ be configurations on $V$ with $x_i=1$. By $(a)$ and $(b)$ we have $f^u(x)_L=f^u(y)_L={\mathbf{0}}$ or $f^{uu}(x)_L=f^{uu}(y)_L={\mathbf{0}}$. This proves (7).  igskip Let $J=K\setminus I$. So $J$ is the set of vertices if $H$ which belongs to an initial cycle of $H$ which is not an initial cycle of $G$.  igskip 
oindent (8) {\em If $x,y$ are configurations on $V$ and $x_i=1$, then there is a word $w$ over $J$ such that $f^w(x)_J=f^w(y)_J={\mathbf{0}}$ and $|w|\leq 2|J|$.} \medskip 
oindent If $J=\emptyset$ there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, $H$ has $p\geq 1$ initial cycles $C_1,\dots,C_p$ which are not initial cycles of $G$. For $1\leq k\leq p$, let $L_k$ be the vertex set of $C_k$, so that $J=L_1\cup\dots \cup L_p$. By (7), for each $1\leq k\leq p$, there is a word $u^k$ over $L_k$ with $f^{u^k}(x)_{L_k}=f^{u^k}(y)_{L_k}={\mathbf{0}}$ and $|u^k|\leq 2|L_k|$. Since, for every distinct $r,s\in [p]$, $L_r\cap L_s=\emptyset$ and $G$ has no arc between $L_r$ and $L_s$, we deduce that $f^w(x)_J=f^w(y)_J={\mathbf{0}}$ with $w=u^1,\dots,u^p$. This proves (8).  igskip We are now in position to prove that, for any pair of configurations $x,y$ on $V$ with $x_I=y_I$, there is a word $w$ such that $f^w(x)_i=f^w(y)_i=0$ and $f^w(x)_K=f^w(x)_K$. We consider two cases, giving (9) and (10) below. The first uses only Lemma~ef{lem:no_fixed_vertex_2} (giving a bound on $|w|$ of order $F(n+2)$), while the second uses Lemmas~ef{lem:no_fixed_vertex_2} and ef{lem:fixing_a_vertex} (giving a bound on $|w|$ of order $3F(n+2)$).  igskip
