But then, by Lemma~\ref{lem:acyclic_image}, we have $f^u(x')=f^u(y')$ and thus $x=y$, a contradiction. Hence $|X|\leq 2^{|I|}\leq 2^{n/2}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:2-synch}, there is a word $w$ such that $|f^w(X)|=1$ and $|w|\leq 5n(|X|-1)$. Thus $u,w$ is a synchronizing word for $f$ of length at most \[ n-|I|+5n(|X|-1)\leq n+5n(2^{n/2}-1)= 5n(\sqrt{2})^n-4n. \]
nodes.statement_short: Loop case by Lemma 13; otherwise remove an acyclic half (Millani-Steiner-Wiederrecht) so a topological sort maps all states into at most $2^{n/2}$, then merge them with Lemmas 13 and 10.

nodes.name: Loop case
nodes.statement: If $G$ has a loop then, by Lemma~\ref{lem:fast-3}, there is an and-or-net on $G$ with a synchronizing word of length at most $7n\leq 5n(\sqrt{2})^n$.
nodes.statement_short: With a loop, Lemma 13 gives length $7n\leq 5n(\sqrt2)^n$.

nodes.name: Small feedback set
nodes.statement: So suppose that $G$ has no loops. By Theorem~\ref{thm:chromatic}, there is a subset $I\subseteq V$ of size at most $n/2$ such that $G\setminus I$ is acyclic.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 7 gives $I$ with $|I|\leq n/2$ and $G\setminus I$ acyclic.

nodes.name: Fast pair merging
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:fast-3}, there is an and-or-net $f$ on $G$ such that, for every configurations $x,y$ on $V$, there is a word $v$ such that $f^v(x)=f^v(y)$ and $|v|\leq 5n$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 13 gives $f$ merging pairs within $5n$.

nodes.name: Image has at most 2^{n/2} states
nodes.statement: Let $u$ be a topological sort of $G\setminus I$, and let $X=f^u(\{0,1\}^V)$. If $|X|>2^{|I|}$ then there are $x,y\in X$ with $x\neq y$ and $x_I=y_I$. Since $x,y\in X$, there are configurations $x',y'$ on $V$ with $x=f^u(x')$ and $y=f^u(y')$. Since $I\cap\{u\}=\emptyset$, we have $x'_I=x_I=y_I=y'_I$. But then, by Lemma~\ref{lem:acyclic_image}, we have $f^u(x')=f^u(y')$ and thus $x=y$, a contradiction. Hence $|X|\leq 2^{|I|}\leq 2^{n/2}$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 14, $X=f^u(\{0,1\}^V)$ has at most $2^{|I|}\leq 2^{n/2}$ elements.

nodes.name: Merge the image
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:2-synch}, there is a word $w$ such that $|f^w(X)|=1$ and $|w|\leq 5n(|X|-1)$. Thus $u,w$ is a synchronizing word for $f$ of length at most \[ n-|I|+5n(|X|-1)\leq n+5n(2^{n/2}-1)= 5n(\sqrt{2})^n-4n. \]
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 10 merges $X$; total length $\leq 5n(\sqrt2)^n-4n$.

nodes.name: Polynomial-time detection of positive cycles
nodes.statement: Note that, since Robertson, Seymour and Thomas \cite{RST99} and McCuaig \cite{McC04} proved independently that we can decide in polynomial time if a signed digraph has a positive cycle, the conditions on the inputs of these two problems can be checked in polynomial time.
conclusions: we can decide in polynomial time if a signed digraph has a positive cycle

nodes.name: Strong-Synchronizing-Problem
nodes.statement: \begin{minipage}{13.5cm} {\sc Strong-Synchronizing-Problem} \begin{itemize} \item {\sc Input:} A simple signed digraph $G$, {\em strongly connected}, with maximum in-degree at most two, and containing a vertex meeting every cycle. \item {\sc Question:} Is every BN on $G$ synchronizing? \end{itemize} \end{minipage}
nodes.statement_short: Given a simple strong signed digraph of in-degree at most 2 with a vertex meeting all cycles, is every BN on it synchronizing?

nodes.name: Negative-Synchronizing-Problem
nodes.statement: \begin{minipage}{13.5cm} {\sc Negative-Synchronizing-Problem} \begin{itemize} \item {\sc Input:} A simple signed digraph $G$, {\em without positive cycles}, with maximum in-degree at most two, and containing a vertex meeting every cycle. \item {\sc Question:} Is every BN on $G$ synchronizing? \end{itemize} \end{minipage}
nodes.statement_short: Given a simple signed digraph without positive cycles, of in-degree at most 2, with a vertex meeting all cycles, is every BN on it synchronizing?

nodes.name: 3-CNF formula notation
nodes.statement: So consider a 3-CNF formula $\psi$ over a set of $n\geq 2$ variables $\boldsymbol{\lambda}=\{\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\}$ consisting of $m\geq 1$ clauses $\boldsymbol{\mu}=\{\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m\}$.

nodes.name: Positive and negative literals
nodes.statement: To each variable $\lambda_r$ is associated a positive literal $\lambda^+_r$ and a negative literal $\lambda^-_r$.

nodes.name: Literal sets
nodes.statement: The resulting sets of positive and negative literals are denoted $\boldsymbol{\lambda}^+$ and $\boldsymbol{\lambda}^-$.

nodes.name: Clause as a set of three literals
nodes.statement: Each clause $\mu_s$ is a subset of $\boldsymbol{\lambda}^+\cup\boldsymbol{\lambda}^-$ of size three, and we write $\mu_r=\{\mu_{r,1},\mu_{r,2},\mu_{r,3}\}$.

nodes.name: Assignment
nodes.statement: An \EM{assignment} for $\psi$ is regarded as a configuration $z$ on $[n]$.

nodes.name: Satisfied literal
nodes.statement: A positive literal $\lambda^+_r$ is satisfied by $z$ if $z_r=1$, and a negative literal $\lambda^-_r$ is satisfied by $z$ if $z_r=0$.

nodes.name: Satisfied clause
nodes.statement: A clause is satisfied by $z$ if at least one of its literals is satisfied by $z$.

nodes.name: Satisfying assignment
nodes.statement: The formula $\psi$ is \EM{satisfied} by $z$ (or $z$ is a \EM{satisfying assignment} for $\psi$) if every clause in $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ is satisfied by $z$.

nodes.name: Satisfiable formula
nodes.statement: We say that $\psi$ is \EM{satisfiable} if it has at least one satisfying assignment.

nodes.name: Signed digraph $H_\psi$
nodes.statement: Our reductions from 3-SAT are based on the simple signed digraph $H_\psi$ defined as follows; see Figure~\ref{fig:H_psi} for an illustration: \begin{itemize} \item The vertex set is $\boldsymbol{\lambda}^+\cup\boldsymbol{\lambda}^-\cup\boldsymbol{\ell}\cup \boldsymbol{\mu}'\cup\boldsymbol{\mu}\cup \boldsymbol{c}$, where $\boldsymbol{\ell}=\{\ell_0,\dots,\ell_n\}$, $\boldsymbol{\mu}'=\{\mu'_1,\dots,\mu'_m\}$ and $\boldsymbol{c}=\{c_1,\dots,c_m\}$; there are thus $3n+3m+1$ vertices. \item The arcs are, for all $r\in [n]$ and $s\in [m]$, \begin{itemize} \item $(\ell_{r-1},\lambda^+_r),(\ell_{r-1},\lambda^-_r)$, \item $(\lambda^+_r,\ell_r),(\lambda^-_r,\ell_r)$, \item $(c_1,\ell_0)$, \item $(\mu_{s,1},\mu'_s),(\mu_{s,2},\mu'_s)$,$(\mu_{s,3},\mu_s),(\mu'_s,\mu_s)$, \item $(\mu_s,c_s),(c_{s+1},c_s)$, where $c_{m+1}$ means $\ell_n$. \end{itemize} \item For all $s\in [m]$, the arc $(\mu_s,c_s)$ is negative, and all the other arcs are positive.
nodes.statement_short: A chain $\ell_0\to\lambda^\pm_r\to\ell_r$ through the literals, clause gadgets $\mu'_s,\mu_s$ and a return path $c_m\to\dots\to c_1\to\ell_0$ with negative arcs $\mu_s\to c_s$.

nodes.name: Satisfiability versus two fixed points on $H'_\psi$
nodes.statement: Actually, in that paper, the authors consider the signed digraph $H'_\psi$ obtained from $H_\psi$ by adding, for all $r\in [n]$, a new vertex $i_r$ with a positive arc $(i_r,\lambda^+_r)$ and a negative arc $(i_r,\lambda^-_r)$, and then prove the following: $\psi$ is satisfiable if and only if there is a BN on $H'_\psi$ with at least two fixed points.
conclusions: $\psi$ is satisfiable if and only if there is a BN on $H'_\psi$ with at least two fixed points
equivalent_conditions: there is a BN on $H'_\psi$ with at least two fixed points

nodes.name: Signed digraph $G_\psi$
nodes.statement: For the first, let $G_\psi$ be the signed digraph obtained from $H_\psi$ by adding: two new vertices, $q$ and $t$; a negative arc $(\ell_0,q)$; two positive arcs $(\ell_0,t),(q,t)$; and a positive arc $(t,i)$ for all $i\in\boldsymbol{\lambda}^+\cup\boldsymbol{\lambda}^-$.

nodes.name: $G_\psi$ is a valid instance of the Strong-Synchronizing-Problem
nodes.statement: Note that $G_\psi$ is strongly connected, simple and has maximum in-degree two (thus every BN on $G_\psi$ is an and-or-network). Also, $\ell_0$ meets every cycle. Thus $G_\psi$ is a valide instance of the {\sc Strong-Synchronizing-Problem}.
conclusions: $G_\psi$ is strongly connected, simple and has maximum in-degree two
$\ell_0$ meets every cycle
$G_\psi$ is a valide instance of the {\sc Strong-Synchronizing-Problem}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3 (strongly connected case)
nodes.statement: The following result shows that $G_\psi$ as the same property that $H'_\psi$: $\psi$ is satisfiable if and only if there is a BN on $H'_\psi$ with at least two fixed points. But it gives a stronger conclusion when $\psi$ is not satisfiable: every BN on $G$ is synchronizing. Thus $\psi$ is not satisfiable if and only if every BN on $G_\psi$ is synchronizing. Since the SAT problem is NP-complete and $G_\psi$ is a valid instance of the {\sc Strong-Synchronizing-Problem}, we deduce that this problem is coNP-hard.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce from 3-SAT: by Theorem 8, $\psi$ is unsatisfiable iff every BN on $G_\psi$ synchronizes, so the Strong-Synchronizing-Problem is coNP-hard.

nodes.name: Theorem 8 strengthens the fixed-point reduction
nodes.statement: The following result shows that $G_\psi$ as the same property that $H'_\psi$: $\psi$ is satisfiable if and only if there is a BN on $H'_\psi$ with at least two fixed points. But it gives a stronger conclusion when $\psi$ is not satisfiable: every BN on $G$ is synchronizing.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 8 gives the fixed-point equivalence plus synchronization when $\psi$ is unsatisfiable.

nodes.name: Reduction from SAT
nodes.statement: Thus $\psi$ is not satisfiable if and only if every BN on $G_\psi$ is synchronizing. Since the SAT problem is NP-complete and $G_\psi$ is a valid instance of the {\sc Strong-Synchronizing-Problem}, we deduce that this problem is coNP-hard.
nodes.statement_short: Unsatisfiability reduces to the Strong-Synchronizing-Problem, which is therefore coNP-hard.

nodes.name: Reduction theorem for $G_\psi$
nodes.statement: The following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $\psi$ is not satisfiable. \item Every BN on $G_\psi$ has at most one fixed point. \item There is a word of length $12n+12m+11$ which synchronizes every BN on~$G_\psi$. \item Every BN on $G_\psi$ is synchronizing. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: The following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $\psi$ is not satisfiable. \item Every BN on $G_\psi$ has at most one fixed point. \item There is a word of length $12n+12m+11$ which synchronizes every BN on~$G_\psi$. \item Every BN on $G_\psi$ is synchronizing. \end{enumerate}
equivalent_conditions: Every BN on $G_\psi$ has at most one fixed point.
There is a word of length $12n+12m+11$ which synchronizes every BN on~$G_\psi$.
nodes.statement_short: For $G_\psi$: $\psi$ unsatisfiable $\iff$ at most one fixed point $\iff$ a universal synchronizing word of length $12n+12m+11$ $\iff$ every BN synchronizes.
nodes.label: thm:fixed_point

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 8
nodes.statement:
\BF{($1\Rightarrow 2$)} Suppose that $\psi$ is not satisfiable and let $f$ be a BN on $G_\psi$. We will prove that $f$ has at most one fixed point. Suppose, for a contradiction, that $f$ has two distinct fixed points $x$ and $y$. As argued in \cite{A08}, $G_\psi$ has a positive cycle $C$ such that $x_i
eq y_i$ for every vertex $i$ in $C$. Since $x_q=f_q(x)=
eg x_{\ell_0}$ and $y_q=f_q(y)=
eg y_{\ell_0}$, we have $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=0$ if $f_t$ is a conjunction and $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=1$ if $f_t$ is a disjunction, and thus $x_t=y_t$. So $t$ is not in $C$. We deduce that  egin{itemize} \item $C$ is full-positive, \item $C$ contains all the vertices in $ oldsymbol{\ell}\cup oldsymbol{c}$, \item $C$ contains exactly one of $\lambda^+_r,\lambda^-_r$ for each $r\in [n]$. \end{itemize} Suppose, without loss of generality, that $x_{\ell_0}<y_{\ell_0}$. We prove, by induction on $s$ from $1$ to $m$ that $x_{c_s}<y_{c_s}$. Since $c_1$ is the unique in-neighbor of $\ell_0$ we have $x_{c_1}<y_{c_1}$. Let $1<s\leq m$. By induction, $x_{c_{s-1}}<y_{c_{s-1}}$. Suppose, for a contradiction, that $x_{c_s}>y_{c_s}$. If $f_{c_{s-1}}$ is a disjunction then, since $x_{c_s}=1$, we have $f_{c_{s-1}}(x)=1
eq x_{c_{s-1}}$, a contradiction, and if $f_{c_{s-1}}$ is a conjunction then, since $y_{c_s}=0$, we have $f_{c_{s-1}}(y)=0
eq y_{c_{s-1}}$, a contradiction. We deduce that $x_{c_s}\leq y_{c_s}$ and since the equality is not possible we obtain $x_{c_s}<y_{c_s}$. This completes the induction, and thus $x_{ oldsymbol{c}}={\mathbf{0}}$ and $y_{ oldsymbol{c}}=\mathbf{1}$. Since $x_{\ell_0}\leq y_{\ell_0}$ and $x_t=y_t$, we have $x_i\leq y_i$ for $i\in\{\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1\}$, and thus $x_{\ell_1}\leq y_{\ell_1}$. Repeating this argument we get $x_i\leq y_i$ for every $i\in  oldsymbol{\ell}\cup oldsymbol{\lambda}^+\cup oldsymbol{\lambda}^-$. Consequently, $x_i\leq y_i$ for all $i\in  oldsymbol{\mu}'$ and thus $x_i\leq y_i$ for all $i\in  oldsymbol{\mu}$. We deduce that $x_{\mu_s}=y_{\mu_s}$ for all $s\in [m]$. Indeed, otherwise $x_{\mu_s}<y_{\mu_s}$ so $f_{c_s}(x)=1
eq x_{c_s}$ if $f_i$ is a disjunction and $f_{c_s}(y)=0
eq y_{c_s}$ if $f_i$ is a conjunction. Thus $x_{\mu_s}=y_{\mu_s}$. Let us prove that $\mu_s$ contains a literal $i$ with $x_i=y_i$. Indeed, otherwise we have $x_i<y_i$ for the three literals $i$ contained in $\mu_s$, which implies $x_{\mu'_s}<y_{\mu'_s}$ and thus $x_{\mu_s}<y_{\mu_s}$, a contradiction. Thus each clause $\mu_s$ contains a literal which is not in $C$ (since $x_i
eq y_i$ for all vertex $i$ in $C$). Let $z\in\{0,1\}^n$ defined by $z_r=1$ if $\lambda^+_r$ is not in $C$ and $z_r=0$ if $\lambda^-_r$ is not in $C$; there is no ambiguity since exactly one of $\lambda^+_r,\lambda^-_r$ is in $C$. All the literals not in $C$ are satisfied by $z$, and thus each clause contains a literal satisfied by $z$. So $\psi$ is satisfiable, a contradiction. Thus $f$ has indeed at most one fixed point.  igskip 
oindent \BF{($2\Rightarrow 3$)} Suppose that every BN on $G_\psi$ has at most one fixed point. Let $u$ be a topological sort of $G_\psi\setminus\{\ell_0,q,t\}$; so $|u|=3n+3m$. The first two letters of $u$ are $\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1$ and we denote by $u'$ the suffix of $u$ obtained by removing these two letters; so $|u'|=3n+3m-2$. Let $V$ be the vertex set of $G_\psi$; so $|V|=3n+3m+3$. We will prove that the word ${\mathbf{w}}$ defined by \[ {\mathbf{w}}=v,\ell_0,v,w\quad	extrm{where}\quad v=q,t,u\quad	extrm{and}\quad w=\ell_0,u,t,\ell_0,\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1,t,u',\ell_0,q \] is a synchronizing word for every BN $f$ on $G_\psi$. Since $|v|=|V|-1$ and $|w|=2|V|$, we have $|{\mathbf{w}}|=4|V|-1=12n+12m+11$ as desired. \medskip Let $f$ be a BN on $G_\psi$. For $a=0,1$, let $f^a$ be the BN with component set $V$ such that $f^a_{\ell_0}$ is the $a$-constant function and $f^a_i=f_i$ for every $i
eq\ell_0$. Note that, for every word $w$ not containing $\ell_0$ and any configuration $x$ on $V$, we have $f^w(x)=(f^a)^w(x)$. Let $H$ be obtained from $G_\psi$ by deleting $(c_1,\ell_0)$. Then $H$ is the signed interaction digraph of $f^a$, and it is acyclic. Hence $f^a$ has a unique fixed point; let $x$ be the fixed point of $f^0$ and $y$ the fixed point of $f^1$. Obviously, $x_{\ell_0}<y_{\ell_0}$. It is clear that if $f(x)_{\ell_0}<f(y)_{\ell_0}$ then $x$ and $y$ are fixed points of $f$, a contradiction. Thus $f(x)_{\ell_0}\geq f(y)_{\ell_0}$.  igskip 
oindent (1) {\em We have $x_q>y_q$ and, for every configuration $z$ on $V$,  egin{itemize} \item $f^v(z)=x$ if $z_{\ell_0}=0$, \item $f^v(z)=y$ if $z_{\ell_0}=1$, \item $f^u(y+e_{\ell_0})=x+e_q$, \item $f^u(x+e_{\ell_0})=y+e_q$. \end{itemize}} \medskip 
oindent We have $x_q=f_q(x)=
eg x_{\ell_0}=1$ and $y_q=f_q(y)=
eg y_{\ell_0}=0$. We deduce that $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=1$ if $f_t$ is a disjunction and $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=0$ if $f_t$ is a conjunction. So $x_t=y_t$ in all cases. Let $z$ be a configuration on $V$. Since $\ell_0,v$ is a topological sort of $H$ and $x$ is a fixed point of $f^0$, we deduce from Lemma~ef{lem:acyclic_image} that $(f^0)^{\ell^0,v}(z)=x$. So if $z_{\ell_0}=0$ then $f^v(z)=(f^0)^v(z)=(f^0)^{\ell_0,v}(z)=x$. This proves the first item. Let $z=y+e_{\ell_0}$. Since $z_{\ell_0}=0$ we have $f^{q,t,u}(z)=f^v(z)=x$ by the first item and since $z_t=y_t=x_t$ we deduce that $f^{q,u}(z)=x$. Since $G_\psi$ has no arc from $q$ to a vertex in $\{u\}$ we have $f^u(z)_i=f^{q,u}(z)_i=x_i$ for all $i
eq q$. Since $f^u(z)_q=z_q=y_q
eq x_q$ we deduce that $f^u(z)=x+e_q$. This proves the third item. We prove similarly the second and fourth items, and (1) follows.  igskip 
oindent (2) {\em If $f^{\ell_0,v,w}(x)=f^{\ell_0,v,w}(y)$ then ${\mathbf{w}}$ is a synchronizing word for $f$.} \medskip 
oindent Let $z,z'$ be any configurations on $V$. If $z_{\ell_0}=z'_{\ell_0}$ then $f^v(z)=f^v(z')$ by the first two items of (1) and thus $f^{\mathbf{w}}(z)=f^{\mathbf{w}}(z')$. Suppose, without loss of generality, that $z_{\ell_0}< z'_{\ell_0}$. Then, by the first two items of (1) we have $f^v(z)=x$ and $f^v(z')=y$, and thus if $f^{\ell_0,v,w}(x)=f^{\ell_0,v,w}(y)$ we have $f^{\mathbf{w}}(z)=f^{\mathbf{w}}(z')$. This proves (2).  igskip 
oindent (3) {\em If $f(x)_{\ell_0}=f(y)_{\ell_0}$ then ${\mathbf{w}}$ is a synchronizing word for $f$.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose that $f(x)_{\ell_0}=f(y)_{\ell_0}$, that is, $f^{\ell_0}(x)_{\ell_0}=f^{\ell_0}(y)_{\ell_0}$. Then, by the first two items of (1) we have $f^{\ell_0,v}(x)=f^{\ell_0,v}(y)$, thus $f^{\ell_0,v,w}(x)=f^{\ell_0,v,w}(y)$ and by (2) ${\mathbf{w}}$ is a synchronizing word for $f$. This proves (3).  igskip By (3) we can suppose that $f(x)_{\ell_0}
eq f(y)_{\ell_0}$ and thus $f(x)_{\ell_0}> f(y)_{\ell_0}$. Consequently, by (1) we have $f^{\ell_0,v}(x)=y$ and $f^{\ell_0,v}(y)=x$. Thus, by (2), it is sufficient to prove that $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$. Since $f(x)_{\ell_0}> f(y)_{\ell_0}$ we have $f^{\ell_0}(x)=x+e_{\ell_0}$ and $f^{\ell_0}(y)=y+e_{\ell_0}$ and from the last two items of (1) we have $f^u(x+e_{\ell_0})=y+e_q$ and $f^u(y+e_{\ell_0})=x+e_q$. Since $(y+e_q)_{\ell_0}=(y+e_q)_q=1$ we have $f^t(y+e_q)_t=1$ and since $(x+e_q)_{\ell_0}=(x+e_q)_q=0$ we have $f^t(y+e_q)_t=0$. Since $G_\psi$ has no arc from $\{q,t\}$ to $\ell_0$ we have $f^{t,\ell_0}(y+e_q)_{\ell_0}=f(y)_{\ell_0}=0$ and $f^{t,\ell_0}(x+e_q)_{\ell_0}=f(x)_{\ell_0}=1$. Thus, summing up, we have  egin{itemize} \item $f^{\ell_0,u}(x)=y+e_q$ and $f^{t,\ell_0}(y+e_q)_{\ell_0}< f^{t,\ell_0}(y+e_q)_t$, \item $f^{\ell_0,u}(y)=x+e_q$ and $f^{t,\ell_0}(x+e_q)_{\ell_0}> f^{t,\ell_0}(x+e_q)_t$. \end{itemize} Setting $y'=f^{t,\ell_0,\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1}(y+e_q)$ and $x'=f^{t,\ell_0,\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1}(x+e_q)$ we deduce that  egin{itemize} \item $y'_{\lambda^+_1}=x'_{\lambda^+_1}=0$ if $f_{\lambda^+_1}$ is a conjunction, \item $y'_{\lambda^+_1}=x'_{\lambda^+_1}=1$ if $f_{\lambda^+_1}$ is a disjunction, \item $y'_{\lambda^-_1}=x'_{\lambda^-_1}=0$ if $f_{\lambda^-_1}$ is a conjunction, \item $y'_{\lambda^-_1}=x'_{\lambda^-_1}=1$ if $f_{\lambda^-_1}$ is a disjunction. \end{itemize} Furthermore, since  egin{itemize} \item $y'_{\ell_0}=f^{t,\ell_0}(y+e_q)_{\ell_0}=0$ and $y'_q=(y+e_q)_q=1$, \item $x'_{\ell_0}=f^{t,\ell_0}(x+e_q)_{\ell_0}=1$ and $x'_q=(x+e_q)_q=0$, \end{itemize} we have  egin{itemize} \item $f^t(y')_t=f^t(x')_t=0$ if $f_t$ is a conjunction, \item $f^t(y')_t=f^t(x')_t=1$ if $f_t$ is a disjunction. \end{itemize} Hence, setting $I=\{t,\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1\}$, we have $f^t(y')_I=f^t(x')_I$. Since $G_\psi\setminus I$ is acyclic and $u',\ell_0,q$ is a corresponding topological sort, by Lemma~ef{lem:acyclic_image} we have $f^{t,u',\ell_0,q}(y')=f^{t,u',\ell_0,q}(x')$, and thus $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$ as desired.  igskip 
oindent \BF{($3 \Rightarrow 4$)} This is obvious.  igskip 
oindent \BF{($4 \Rightarrow 1$)} Suppose that $z$ is a satisfying assignment of $\psi$, and let us prove that some BN on $G_\psi$ is not synchronizing. Let $ oldsymbol{\lambda}^1$ be the literals satisfied by $z$ and $ oldsymbol{\lambda}^0$ the literals not satisfied by $z$, hence $( oldsymbol{\lambda}^0, oldsymbol{\lambda}^1)$ is a balanced partition of $ oldsymbol{\lambda}^+\cup oldsymbol{\lambda}^-$. Let $f$ be the and-or-net on $G_\psi$ such that:  egin{itemize} \item for all $i\in  oldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup oldsymbol{\mu}\cup oldsymbol{\mu}'\cup oldsymbol{c}\cup\{t\}$, $f_i$ is a disjunction; \item for all $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup oldsymbol{\ell}$, $f_i$ is a conjunction. \end{itemize} \medskip Let $ oldsymbol{\mu}'^1$ be the vertices in $ oldsymbol{\mu}'$ with at least one in-neighbor in $ oldsymbol{\lambda}^1$ and $ oldsymbol{\mu}'^0= oldsymbol{\mu}'\setminus oldsymbol{\mu}'^1$. Let $I= oldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup oldsymbol{\mu}'^1\cup  oldsymbol{\mu}$ and $J= oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup oldsymbol{\ell}\cup oldsymbol{c}\cup oldsymbol{\mu}'^0$. Let us prove that the configurations $x,y$ on $V$ defined as follows are fixed points of $f$:  egin{itemize} \item $x_q=1$, $x_t=1$, $x_I=\mathbf{1}$, $x_J={\mathbf{0}}$, \item $y_q=0$, $y_t=1$, $y_I=\mathbf{1}$, $y_J=\mathbf{1}$. \end{itemize}  igskip 
oindent (4) {\em $f(x)_i=x_i$ and $f(y)_i=y_i$ for all $i\in \{q,t\}\cup I$.} \medskip 
oindent Since $x_q
eq x_{\ell_0}$ and $y_q
eq y_{\ell_0}$, we have $f(x)_q=
eg x_{\ell_0}=x_q$ and $f(y)_q=
eg y_{\ell_0}=y_q$, and since $f_t$ is a disjunction, we also deduce that $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=1=x_t=y_t$. We now prove that $f(x)_I=f(y)_I=\mathbf{1}$. If $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup oldsymbol{\mu}'^1$, then $f_i$ is a disjunction and $i$ has an in-neighbor $j\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup\{t\}$, so $x_j=y_j=1$ and we deduce that $f_i(x)=f_i(y)=1$. Next, consider a clause $\mu_s$ in $ oldsymbol{\mu}$. Then $f_{\mu_s}$ is a disjunction and, since $z$ is a satisfying assignment, $\mu_s$ contains a literal $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1$ and thus $x_i=y_i=1$. If $i$ is an in-neighbor of $\mu_s$ then $f_{\mu_s}(x)=f_{\mu_s}(y)=1$. Otherwise, $i$ is an in-neighbor of $\mu'_s$, so $\mu'_s\in oldsymbol{\mu}'^1$. Thus $x_{\mu'_s}=y_{\mu'_s}=1$ and we deduce that $f_{\mu_s}(x)=f_{\mu_s}(y)=1$. This proves~(4).  igskip 
oindent (5) {\em $f(x)_J={\mathbf{0}}$.} \medskip 
oindent If $i\in oldsymbol{\mu}'^0$ then for every in-neighbor $j$ of $i$ we have $j\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0$, thus $x_j=0$, and we deduce that $f_i(x)=0$. If $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup  oldsymbol{\ell}$, then $f_i$ is a conjunction and has an in-neighbor $j\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup oldsymbol{\ell}\cup oldsymbol{c}$. Thus $x_j=0$ we deduce that $f_i(x)=0$. Setting $c_{m+1}=\ell_n$, for all $s\in [m]$ we have $f_{c_s}(x)=
eg x_{\mu_s}\lor x_{c_{s+1}}=
eg 1\lor 0=0$. This proves (5).  igskip 
oindent (6) {\em $f(y)_J=\mathbf{1}$.} \medskip 
oindent If $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup  oldsymbol{\ell}\cup  oldsymbol{\mu}'^0$ then for every in-neighbor $j$ of $i$ we have $j
eq q$, thus $y_j=1$, and we deduce that $f_i(y)=1$. If $i\in  oldsymbol{c}$ then $i$ has a positive in-neighbor $j\in oldsymbol{c}\cup\{\ell_n\}$, thus $x_j=1$, and since $f_i$ is a disjunction, we have $f_i(x)=1$. This proves (6).  igskip By (4), (5) and (6), $x$ and $y$ are fixed points of $f$ and thus $f$ is not synchronizing.
nodes.statement_short: Cycle of implications. Two fixed points give a full-positive cycle encoding a satisfying assignment; with at most one fixed point an explicit word built from topological sorts synchronizes every BN; a satisfying assignment yields an and-or-net with two fixed points.

nodes.name: (1 ⇒ 2) Unsatisfiable implies at most one fixed point
nodes.statement:
\BF{($1\Rightarrow 2$)} Suppose that $\psi$ is not satisfiable and let $f$ be a BN on $G_\psi$. We will prove that $f$ has at most one fixed point. Suppose, for a contradiction, that $f$ has two distinct fixed points $x$ and $y$. As argued in \cite{A08}, $G_\psi$ has a positive cycle $C$ such that $x_i
eq y_i$ for every vertex $i$ in $C$. Since $x_q=f_q(x)=
eg x_{\ell_0}$ and $y_q=f_q(y)=
eg y_{\ell_0}$, we have $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=0$ if $f_t$ is a conjunction and $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=1$ if $f_t$ is a disjunction, and thus $x_t=y_t$. So $t$ is not in $C$. We deduce that  egin{itemize} \item $C$ is full-positive, \item $C$ contains all the vertices in $ oldsymbol{\ell}\cup oldsymbol{c}$, \item $C$ contains exactly one of $\lambda^+_r,\lambda^-_r$ for each $r\in [n]$. \end{itemize} Suppose, without loss of generality, that $x_{\ell_0}<y_{\ell_0}$. We prove, by induction on $s$ from $1$ to $m$ that $x_{c_s}<y_{c_s}$. Since $c_1$ is the unique in-neighbor of $\ell_0$ we have $x_{c_1}<y_{c_1}$. Let $1<s\leq m$. By induction, $x_{c_{s-1}}<y_{c_{s-1}}$. Suppose, for a contradiction, that $x_{c_s}>y_{c_s}$. If $f_{c_{s-1}}$ is a disjunction then, since $x_{c_s}=1$, we have $f_{c_{s-1}}(x)=1
eq x_{c_{s-1}}$, a contradiction, and if $f_{c_{s-1}}$ is a conjunction then, since $y_{c_s}=0$, we have $f_{c_{s-1}}(y)=0
eq y_{c_{s-1}}$, a contradiction. We deduce that $x_{c_s}\leq y_{c_s}$ and since the equality is not possible we obtain $x_{c_s}<y_{c_s}$. This completes the induction, and thus $x_{ oldsymbol{c}}={\mathbf{0}}$ and $y_{ oldsymbol{c}}=\mathbf{1}$. Since $x_{\ell_0}\leq y_{\ell_0}$ and $x_t=y_t$, we have $x_i\leq y_i$ for $i\in\{\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1\}$, and thus $x_{\ell_1}\leq y_{\ell_1}$. Repeating this argument we get $x_i\leq y_i$ for every $i\in  oldsymbol{\ell}\cup oldsymbol{\lambda}^+\cup oldsymbol{\lambda}^-$. Consequently, $x_i\leq y_i$ for all $i\in  oldsymbol{\mu}'$ and thus $x_i\leq y_i$ for all $i\in  oldsymbol{\mu}$. We deduce that $x_{\mu_s}=y_{\mu_s}$ for all $s\in [m]$. Indeed, otherwise $x_{\mu_s}<y_{\mu_s}$ so $f_{c_s}(x)=1
eq x_{c_s}$ if $f_i$ is a disjunction and $f_{c_s}(y)=0
eq y_{c_s}$ if $f_i$ is a conjunction. Thus $x_{\mu_s}=y_{\mu_s}$. Let us prove that $\mu_s$ contains a literal $i$ with $x_i=y_i$. Indeed, otherwise we have $x_i<y_i$ for the three literals $i$ contained in $\mu_s$, which implies $x_{\mu'_s}<y_{\mu'_s}$ and thus $x_{\mu_s}<y_{\mu_s}$, a contradiction. Thus each clause $\mu_s$ contains a literal which is not in $C$ (since $x_i
eq y_i$ for all vertex $i$ in $C$). Let $z\in\{0,1\}^n$ defined by $z_r=1$ if $\lambda^+_r$ is not in $C$ and $z_r=0$ if $\lambda^-_r$ is not in $C$; there is no ambiguity since exactly one of $\lambda^+_r,\lambda^-_r$ is in $C$. All the literals not in $C$ are satisfied by $z$, and thus each clause contains a literal satisfied by $z$. So $\psi$ is satisfiable, a contradiction. Thus $f$ has indeed at most one fixed point.
nodes.statement_short: Two fixed points would differ on a full-positive cycle avoiding $t$, whose missing literals satisfy $\psi$.

nodes.name: Assume unsatisfiable
nodes.statement: \BF{($1\Rightarrow 2$)} Suppose that $\psi$ is not satisfiable and let $f$ be a BN on $G_\psi$. We will prove that $f$ has at most one fixed point.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $\psi$ unsatisfiable and take a BN $f$ on $G_\psi$.

nodes.name: Positive cycle separating the fixed points
nodes.statement:
Suppose, for a contradiction, that $f$ has two distinct fixed points $x$ and $y$. As argued in \cite{A08}, $G_\psi$ has a positive cycle $C$ such that $x_i
eq y_i$ for every vertex $i$ in $C$. Since $x_q=f_q(x)=
eg x_{\ell_0}$ and $y_q=f_q(y)=
eg y_{\ell_0}$, we have $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=0$ if $f_t$ is a conjunction and $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=1$ if $f_t$ is a disjunction, and thus $x_t=y_t$. So $t$ is not in $C$. We deduce that  egin{itemize} \item $C$ is full-positive,
nodes.statement_short: By Aracena's argument a positive cycle $C$ separates two fixed points; $t\notin C$, and $C$ is full-positive,

nodes.name: C contains l and c
nodes.statement: \item $C$ contains all the vertices in $\boldsymbol{\ell}\cup\boldsymbol{c}$,
nodes.statement_short: $C$ contains all of $\boldsymbol\ell\cup\boldsymbol c$,

nodes.name: C picks one literal per variable
nodes.statement: \item $C$ contains exactly one of $\lambda^+_r,\lambda^-_r$ for each $r\in [n]$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: and exactly one of $\lambda^+_r,\lambda^-_r$.

nodes.name: Order along the c-vertices
nodes.statement: Suppose, without loss of generality, that $x_{\ell_0}<y_{\ell_0}$. We prove, by induction on $s$ from $1$ to $m$ that $x_{c_s}<y_{c_s}$. Since $c_1$ is the unique in-neighbor of $\ell_0$ we have $x_{c_1}<y_{c_1}$. Let $1<s\leq m$. By induction, $x_{c_{s-1}}<y_{c_{s-1}}$. Suppose, for a contradiction, that $x_{c_s}>y_{c_s}$. If $f_{c_{s-1}}$ is a disjunction then, since $x_{c_s}=1$, we have $f_{c_{s-1}}(x)=1\neq x_{c_{s-1}}$, a contradiction, and if $f_{c_{s-1}}$ is a conjunction then, since $y_{c_s}=0$, we have $f_{c_{s-1}}(y)=0\neq y_{c_{s-1}}$, a contradiction. We deduce that $x_{c_s}\leq y_{c_s}$ and since the equality is not possible we obtain $x_{c_s}<y_{c_s}$. This completes the induction, and thus $x_{\boldsymbol{c}}={\mathbf{0}}$ and $y_{\boldsymbol{c}}=\mathbf{1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $s$ shows $x_{c_s}<y_{c_s}$.

nodes.name: Clause vertices agree
nodes.statement: Since $x_{\ell_0}\leq y_{\ell_0}$ and $x_t=y_t$, we have $x_i\leq y_i$ for $i\in\{\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1\}$, and thus $x_{\ell_1}\leq y_{\ell_1}$. Repeating this argument we get $x_i\leq y_i$ for every $i\in \boldsymbol{\ell}\cup\boldsymbol{\lambda}^+\cup\boldsymbol{\lambda}^-$. Consequently, $x_i\leq y_i$ for all $i\in \boldsymbol{\mu}'$ and thus $x_i\leq y_i$ for all $i\in \boldsymbol{\mu}$. We deduce that $x_{\mu_s}=y_{\mu_s}$ for all $s\in [m]$. Indeed, otherwise $x_{\mu_s}<y_{\mu_s}$ so $f_{c_s}(x)=1\neq x_{c_s}$ if $f_i$ is a disjunction and $f_{c_s}(y)=0\neq y_{c_s}$ if $f_i$ is a conjunction. Thus $x_{\mu_s}=y_{\mu_s}$.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity propagates and forces $x_{\mu_s}=y_{\mu_s}$.

nodes.name: Each clause has a literal outside C
nodes.statement: Let us prove that $\mu_s$ contains a literal $i$ with $x_i=y_i$. Indeed, otherwise we have $x_i<y_i$ for the three literals $i$ contained in $\mu_s$, which implies $x_{\mu'_s}<y_{\mu'_s}$ and thus $x_{\mu_s}<y_{\mu_s}$, a contradiction. Thus each clause $\mu_s$ contains a literal which is not in $C$ (since $x_i\neq y_i$ for all vertex $i$ in $C$).
nodes.statement_short: Each clause contains a literal $i$ with $x_i=y_i$, hence not in $C$.

nodes.name: Contradiction otherwise
nodes.statement: Indeed, otherwise we have $x_i<y_i$ for the three literals $i$ contained in $\mu_s$, which implies $x_{\mu'_s}<y_{\mu'_s}$ and thus $x_{\mu_s}<y_{\mu_s}$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise $x_{\mu_s}<y_{\mu_s}$.

nodes.name: Literal outside C
nodes.statement: Thus each clause $\mu_s$ contains a literal which is not in $C$ (since $x_i\neq y_i$ for all vertex $i$ in $C$).
nodes.statement_short: So each clause has a literal outside $C$.

nodes.name: Satisfying assignment
nodes.statement: Let $z\in\{0,1\}^n$ defined by $z_r=1$ if $\lambda^+_r$ is not in $C$ and $z_r=0$ if $\lambda^-_r$ is not in $C$; there is no ambiguity since exactly one of $\lambda^+_r,\lambda^-_r$ is in $C$. All the literals not in $C$ are satisfied by $z$, and thus each clause contains a literal satisfied by $z$. So $\psi$ is satisfiable, a contradiction. Thus $f$ has indeed at most one fixed point.
nodes.statement_short: The literals outside $C$ define a satisfying assignment, a contradiction.

nodes.name: (2 ⇒ 3) Explicit synchronizing word; (3 ⇒ 4)
nodes.statement:
\BF{($2\Rightarrow 3$)} Suppose that every BN on $G_\psi$ has at most one fixed point. Let $u$ be a topological sort of $G_\psi\setminus\{\ell_0,q,t\}$; so $|u|=3n+3m$. The first two letters of $u$ are $\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1$ and we denote by $u'$ the suffix of $u$ obtained by removing these two letters; so $|u'|=3n+3m-2$. Let $V$ be the vertex set of $G_\psi$; so $|V|=3n+3m+3$. We will prove that the word ${\mathbf{w}}$ defined by \[ {\mathbf{w}}=v,\ell_0,v,w\quad	extrm{where}\quad v=q,t,u\quad	extrm{and}\quad w=\ell_0,u,t,\ell_0,\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1,t,u',\ell_0,q \] is a synchronizing word for every BN $f$ on $G_\psi$. Since $|v|=|V|-1$ and $|w|=2|V|$, we have $|{\mathbf{w}}|=4|V|-1=12n+12m+11$ as desired. \medskip Let $f$ be a BN on $G_\psi$. For $a=0,1$, let $f^a$ be the BN with component set $V$ such that $f^a_{\ell_0}$ is the $a$-constant function and $f^a_i=f_i$ for every $i
eq\ell_0$. Note that, for every word $w$ not containing $\ell_0$ and any configuration $x$ on $V$, we have $f^w(x)=(f^a)^w(x)$. Let $H$ be obtained from $G_\psi$ by deleting $(c_1,\ell_0)$. Then $H$ is the signed interaction digraph of $f^a$, and it is acyclic. Hence $f^a$ has a unique fixed point; let $x$ be the fixed point of $f^0$ and $y$ the fixed point of $f^1$. Obviously, $x_{\ell_0}<y_{\ell_0}$. It is clear that if $f(x)_{\ell_0}<f(y)_{\ell_0}$ then $x$ and $y$ are fixed points of $f$, a contradiction. Thus $f(x)_{\ell_0}\geq f(y)_{\ell_0}$.  igskip 
oindent (1) {\em We have $x_q>y_q$ and, for every configuration $z$ on $V$,  egin{itemize} \item $f^v(z)=x$ if $z_{\ell_0}=0$, \item $f^v(z)=y$ if $z_{\ell_0}=1$, \item $f^u(y+e_{\ell_0})=x+e_q$, \item $f^u(x+e_{\ell_0})=y+e_q$. \end{itemize}} \medskip 
oindent We have $x_q=f_q(x)=
eg x_{\ell_0}=1$ and $y_q=f_q(y)=
eg y_{\ell_0}=0$. We deduce that $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=1$ if $f_t$ is a disjunction and $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=0$ if $f_t$ is a conjunction. So $x_t=y_t$ in all cases. Let $z$ be a configuration on $V$. Since $\ell_0,v$ is a topological sort of $H$ and $x$ is a fixed point of $f^0$, we deduce from Lemma~ef{lem:acyclic_image} that $(f^0)^{\ell^0,v}(z)=x$. So if $z_{\ell_0}=0$ then $f^v(z)=(f^0)^v(z)=(f^0)^{\ell_0,v}(z)=x$. This proves the first item. Let $z=y+e_{\ell_0}$. Since $z_{\ell_0}=0$ we have $f^{q,t,u}(z)=f^v(z)=x$ by the first item and since $z_t=y_t=x_t$ we deduce that $f^{q,u}(z)=x$. Since $G_\psi$ has no arc from $q$ to a vertex in $\{u\}$ we have $f^u(z)_i=f^{q,u}(z)_i=x_i$ for all $i
eq q$. Since $f^u(z)_q=z_q=y_q
eq x_q$ we deduce that $f^u(z)=x+e_q$. This proves the third item. We prove similarly the second and fourth items, and (1) follows.  igskip 
oindent (2) {\em If $f^{\ell_0,v,w}(x)=f^{\ell_0,v,w}(y)$ then ${\mathbf{w}}$ is a synchronizing word for $f$.} \medskip 
oindent Let $z,z'$ be any configurations on $V$. If $z_{\ell_0}=z'_{\ell_0}$ then $f^v(z)=f^v(z')$ by the first two items of (1) and thus $f^{\mathbf{w}}(z)=f^{\mathbf{w}}(z')$. Suppose, without loss of generality, that $z_{\ell_0}< z'_{\ell_0}$. Then, by the first two items of (1) we have $f^v(z)=x$ and $f^v(z')=y$, and thus if $f^{\ell_0,v,w}(x)=f^{\ell_0,v,w}(y)$ we have $f^{\mathbf{w}}(z)=f^{\mathbf{w}}(z')$. This proves (2).  igskip 
oindent (3) {\em If $f(x)_{\ell_0}=f(y)_{\ell_0}$ then ${\mathbf{w}}$ is a synchronizing word for $f$.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose that $f(x)_{\ell_0}=f(y)_{\ell_0}$, that is, $f^{\ell_0}(x)_{\ell_0}=f^{\ell_0}(y)_{\ell_0}$. Then, by the first two items of (1) we have $f^{\ell_0,v}(x)=f^{\ell_0,v}(y)$, thus $f^{\ell_0,v,w}(x)=f^{\ell_0,v,w}(y)$ and by (2) ${\mathbf{w}}$ is a synchronizing word for $f$. This proves (3).  igskip By (3) we can suppose that $f(x)_{\ell_0}
eq f(y)_{\ell_0}$ and thus $f(x)_{\ell_0}> f(y)_{\ell_0}$. Consequently, by (1) we have $f^{\ell_0,v}(x)=y$ and $f^{\ell_0,v}(y)=x$. Thus, by (2), it is sufficient to prove that $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$. Since $f(x)_{\ell_0}> f(y)_{\ell_0}$ we have $f^{\ell_0}(x)=x+e_{\ell_0}$ and $f^{\ell_0}(y)=y+e_{\ell_0}$ and from the last two items of (1) we have $f^u(x+e_{\ell_0})=y+e_q$ and $f^u(y+e_{\ell_0})=x+e_q$. Since $(y+e_q)_{\ell_0}=(y+e_q)_q=1$ we have $f^t(y+e_q)_t=1$ and since $(x+e_q)_{\ell_0}=(x+e_q)_q=0$ we have $f^t(y+e_q)_t=0$. Since $G_\psi$ has no arc from $\{q,t\}$ to $\ell_0$ we have $f^{t,\ell_0}(y+e_q)_{\ell_0}=f(y)_{\ell_0}=0$ and $f^{t,\ell_0}(x+e_q)_{\ell_0}=f(x)_{\ell_0}=1$. Thus, summing up, we have  egin{itemize} \item $f^{\ell_0,u}(x)=y+e_q$ and $f^{t,\ell_0}(y+e_q)_{\ell_0}< f^{t,\ell_0}(y+e_q)_t$, \item $f^{\ell_0,u}(y)=x+e_q$ and $f^{t,\ell_0}(x+e_q)_{\ell_0}> f^{t,\ell_0}(x+e_q)_t$. \end{itemize} Setting $y'=f^{t,\ell_0,\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1}(y+e_q)$ and $x'=f^{t,\ell_0,\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1}(x+e_q)$ we deduce that  egin{itemize} \item $y'_{\lambda^+_1}=x'_{\lambda^+_1}=0$ if $f_{\lambda^+_1}$ is a conjunction, \item $y'_{\lambda^+_1}=x'_{\lambda^+_1}=1$ if $f_{\lambda^+_1}$ is a disjunction, \item $y'_{\lambda^-_1}=x'_{\lambda^-_1}=0$ if $f_{\lambda^-_1}$ is a conjunction, \item $y'_{\lambda^-_1}=x'_{\lambda^-_1}=1$ if $f_{\lambda^-_1}$ is a disjunction. \end{itemize} Furthermore, since  egin{itemize} \item $y'_{\ell_0}=f^{t,\ell_0}(y+e_q)_{\ell_0}=0$ and $y'_q=(y+e_q)_q=1$, \item $x'_{\ell_0}=f^{t,\ell_0}(x+e_q)_{\ell_0}=1$ and $x'_q=(x+e_q)_q=0$, \end{itemize} we have  egin{itemize} \item $f^t(y')_t=f^t(x')_t=0$ if $f_t$ is a conjunction, \item $f^t(y')_t=f^t(x')_t=1$ if $f_t$ is a disjunction. \end{itemize} Hence, setting $I=\{t,\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1\}$, we have $f^t(y')_I=f^t(x')_I$. Since $G_\psi\setminus I$ is acyclic and $u',\ell_0,q$ is a corresponding topological sort, by Lemma~ef{lem:acyclic_image} we have $f^{t,u',\ell_0,q}(y')=f^{t,u',\ell_0,q}(x')$, and thus $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$ as desired.  igskip 
oindent \BF{($3 \Rightarrow 4$)} This is obvious.
nodes.statement_short: With at most one fixed point, the explicit word $\mathbf w=v,\ell_0,v,w$ of length $12n+12m+11$ synchronizes every BN on $G_\psi$; (3⇒4) is immediate.

nodes.name: Define the word w
nodes.statement: \BF{($2\Rightarrow 3$)} Suppose that every BN on $G_\psi$ has at most one fixed point. Let $u$ be a topological sort of $G_\psi\setminus\{\ell_0,q,t\}$; so $|u|=3n+3m$. The first two letters of $u$ are $\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1$ and we denote by $u'$ the suffix of $u$ obtained by removing these two letters; so $|u'|=3n+3m-2$. Let $V$ be the vertex set of $G_\psi$; so $|V|=3n+3m+3$. We will prove that the word ${\mathbf{w}}$ defined by \[ {\mathbf{w}}=v,\ell_0,v,w\quad\textrm{where}\quad v=q,t,u\quad\textrm{and}\quad w=\ell_0,u,t,\ell_0,\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1,t,u',\ell_0,q \] is a synchronizing word for every BN $f$ on $G_\psi$. Since $|v|=|V|-1$ and $|w|=2|V|$, we have $|{\mathbf{w}}|=4|V|-1=12n+12m+11$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Build $\mathbf w$ from a topological sort $u$ of $G_\psi\setminus\{\ell_0,q,t\}$.

nodes.name: Fix l_0 to get acyclic networks
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a BN on $G_\psi$. For $a=0,1$, let $f^a$ be the BN with component set $V$ such that $f^a_{\ell_0}$ is the $a$-constant function and $f^a_i=f_i$ for every $i\neq\ell_0$. Note that, for every word $w$ not containing $\ell_0$ and any configuration $x$ on $V$, we have $f^w(x)=(f^a)^w(x)$. Let $H$ be obtained from $G_\psi$ by deleting $(c_1,\ell_0)$. Then $H$ is the signed interaction digraph of $f^a$, and it is acyclic. Hence $f^a$ has a unique fixed point; let $x$ be the fixed point of $f^0$ and $y$ the fixed point of $f^1$. Obviously, $x_{\ell_0}<y_{\ell_0}$. It is clear that if $f(x)_{\ell_0}<f(y)_{\ell_0}$ then $x$ and $y$ are fixed points of $f$, a contradiction. Thus $f(x)_{\ell_0}\geq f(y)_{\ell_0}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fixing $\ell_0$ to $a$ gives acyclic $f^a$ with unique fixed points $x$ ($a=0$), $y$ ($a=1$).

nodes.name: (1) Effect of v and u
nodes.statement:
(1) {\em We have $x_q>y_q$ and, for every configuration $z$ on $V$,  egin{itemize} \item $f^v(z)=x$ if $z_{\ell_0}=0$, \item $f^v(z)=y$ if $z_{\ell_0}=1$, \item $f^u(y+e_{\ell_0})=x+e_q$, \item $f^u(x+e_{\ell_0})=y+e_q$. \end{itemize}} \medskip 
oindent We have $x_q=f_q(x)=
eg x_{\ell_0}=1$ and $y_q=f_q(y)=
eg y_{\ell_0}=0$. We deduce that $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=1$ if $f_t$ is a disjunction and $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=0$ if $f_t$ is a conjunction. So $x_t=y_t$ in all cases. Let $z$ be a configuration on $V$. Since $\ell_0,v$ is a topological sort of $H$ and $x$ is a fixed point of $f^0$, we deduce from Lemma~ef{lem:acyclic_image} that $(f^0)^{\ell^0,v}(z)=x$. So if $z_{\ell_0}=0$ then $f^v(z)=(f^0)^v(z)=(f^0)^{\ell_0,v}(z)=x$. This proves the first item. Let $z=y+e_{\ell_0}$. Since $z_{\ell_0}=0$ we have $f^{q,t,u}(z)=f^v(z)=x$ by the first item and since $z_t=y_t=x_t$ we deduce that $f^{q,u}(z)=x$. Since $G_\psi$ has no arc from $q$ to a vertex in $\{u\}$ we have $f^u(z)_i=f^{q,u}(z)_i=x_i$ for all $i
eq q$. Since $f^u(z)_q=z_q=y_q
eq x_q$ we deduce that $f^u(z)=x+e_q$. This proves the third item. We prove similarly the second and fourth items, and (1) follows.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 14, $v$ sends every configuration to $x$ or $y$ according to $\ell_0$, and $u$ swaps $x+e_{\ell_0}$, $y+e_{\ell_0}$ up to $q$.

nodes.name: (2) Reduction to x and y
nodes.statement: (2) {\em If $f^{\ell_0,v,w}(x)=f^{\ell_0,v,w}(y)$ then ${\mathbf{w}}$ is a synchronizing word for $f$.} \medskip \noindent Let $z,z'$ be any configurations on $V$. If $z_{\ell_0}=z'_{\ell_0}$ then $f^v(z)=f^v(z')$ by the first two items of (1) and thus $f^{\mathbf{w}}(z)=f^{\mathbf{w}}(z')$. Suppose, without loss of generality, that $z_{\ell_0}< z'_{\ell_0}$. Then, by the first two items of (1) we have $f^v(z)=x$ and $f^v(z')=y$, and thus if $f^{\ell_0,v,w}(x)=f^{\ell_0,v,w}(y)$ we have $f^{\mathbf{w}}(z)=f^{\mathbf{w}}(z')$. This proves (2).
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to merge $x$ and $y$.

nodes.name: (3) Easy case
nodes.statement: (3) {\em If $f(x)_{\ell_0}=f(y)_{\ell_0}$ then ${\mathbf{w}}$ is a synchronizing word for $f$.} \medskip \noindent Suppose that $f(x)_{\ell_0}=f(y)_{\ell_0}$, that is, $f^{\ell_0}(x)_{\ell_0}=f^{\ell_0}(y)_{\ell_0}$. Then, by the first two items of (1) we have $f^{\ell_0,v}(x)=f^{\ell_0,v}(y)$, thus $f^{\ell_0,v,w}(x)=f^{\ell_0,v,w}(y)$ and by (2) ${\mathbf{w}}$ is a synchronizing word for $f$. This proves (3).
nodes.statement_short: If $f(x)_{\ell_0}=f(y)_{\ell_0}$ then $\mathbf w$ synchronizes $f$.

nodes.name: Remaining case
nodes.statement: By (3) we can suppose that $f(x)_{\ell_0}\neq f(y)_{\ell_0}$ and thus $f(x)_{\ell_0}> f(y)_{\ell_0}$. Consequently, by (1) we have $f^{\ell_0,v}(x)=y$ and $f^{\ell_0,v}(y)=x$. Thus, by (2), it is sufficient to prove that $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$. Since $f(x)_{\ell_0}> f(y)_{\ell_0}$ we have $f^{\ell_0}(x)=x+e_{\ell_0}$ and $f^{\ell_0}(y)=y+e_{\ell_0}$ and from the last two items of (1) we have $f^u(x+e_{\ell_0})=y+e_q$ and $f^u(y+e_{\ell_0})=x+e_q$. Since $(y+e_q)_{\ell_0}=(y+e_q)_q=1$ we have $f^t(y+e_q)_t=1$ and since $(x+e_q)_{\ell_0}=(x+e_q)_q=0$ we have $f^t(y+e_q)_t=0$. Since $G_\psi$ has no arc from $\{q,t\}$ to $\ell_0$ we have $f^{t,\ell_0}(y+e_q)_{\ell_0}=f(y)_{\ell_0}=0$ and $f^{t,\ell_0}(x+e_q)_{\ell_0}=f(x)_{\ell_0}=1$. Thus, summing up, we have \begin{itemize} \item $f^{\ell_0,u}(x)=y+e_q$ and $f^{t,\ell_0}(y+e_q)_{\ell_0}< f^{t,\ell_0}(y+e_q)_t$, \item $f^{\ell_0,u}(y)=x+e_q$ and $f^{t,\ell_0}(x+e_q)_{\ell_0}> f^{t,\ell_0}(x+e_q)_t$. \end{itemize} Setting $y'=f^{t,\ell_0,\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1}(y+e_q)$ and $x'=f^{t,\ell_0,\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1}(x+e_q)$ we deduce that \begin{itemize} \item $y'_{\lambda^+_1}=x'_{\lambda^+_1}=0$ if $f_{\lambda^+_1}$ is a conjunction, \item $y'_{\lambda^+_1}=x'_{\lambda^+_1}=1$ if $f_{\lambda^+_1}$ is a disjunction, \item $y'_{\lambda^-_1}=x'_{\lambda^-_1}=0$ if $f_{\lambda^-_1}$ is a conjunction, \item $y'_{\lambda^-_1}=x'_{\lambda^-_1}=1$ if $f_{\lambda^-_1}$ is a disjunction. \end{itemize} Furthermore, since \begin{itemize} \item $y'_{\ell_0}=f^{t,\ell_0}(y+e_q)_{\ell_0}=0$ and $y'_q=(y+e_q)_q=1$, \item $x'_{\ell_0}=f^{t,\ell_0}(x+e_q)_{\ell_0}=1$ and $x'_q=(x+e_q)_q=0$, \end{itemize} we have \begin{itemize} \item $f^t(y')_t=f^t(x')_t=0$ if $f_t$ is a conjunction, \item $f^t(y')_t=f^t(x')_t=1$ if $f_t$ is a disjunction. \end{itemize} Hence, setting $I=\{t,\lambda^+_1,\lambda^-_1\}$, we have $f^t(y')_I=f^t(x')_I$. Since $G_\psi\setminus I$ is acyclic and $u',\ell_0,q$ is a corresponding topological sort, by Lemma~\ref{lem:acyclic_image} we have $f^{t,u',\ell_0,q}(y')=f^{t,u',\ell_0,q}(x')$, and thus $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$ as desired. \bigskip \noindent \BF{($3 \Rightarrow 4$)} This is obvious.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise trace $w$ on $x$ and $y$ until they agree on $\{t,\lambda^\pm_1\}$, then apply Lemma 14.

nodes.name: (4 ⇒ 1) Satisfiable gives two fixed points
nodes.statement:
\BF{($4 \Rightarrow 1$)} Suppose that $z$ is a satisfying assignment of $\psi$, and let us prove that some BN on $G_\psi$ is not synchronizing. Let $ oldsymbol{\lambda}^1$ be the literals satisfied by $z$ and $ oldsymbol{\lambda}^0$ the literals not satisfied by $z$, hence $( oldsymbol{\lambda}^0, oldsymbol{\lambda}^1)$ is a balanced partition of $ oldsymbol{\lambda}^+\cup oldsymbol{\lambda}^-$. Let $f$ be the and-or-net on $G_\psi$ such that:  egin{itemize} \item for all $i\in  oldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup oldsymbol{\mu}\cup oldsymbol{\mu}'\cup oldsymbol{c}\cup\{t\}$, $f_i$ is a disjunction; \item for all $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup oldsymbol{\ell}$, $f_i$ is a conjunction. \end{itemize} \medskip Let $ oldsymbol{\mu}'^1$ be the vertices in $ oldsymbol{\mu}'$ with at least one in-neighbor in $ oldsymbol{\lambda}^1$ and $ oldsymbol{\mu}'^0= oldsymbol{\mu}'\setminus oldsymbol{\mu}'^1$. Let $I= oldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup oldsymbol{\mu}'^1\cup  oldsymbol{\mu}$ and $J= oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup oldsymbol{\ell}\cup oldsymbol{c}\cup oldsymbol{\mu}'^0$. Let us prove that the configurations $x,y$ on $V$ defined as follows are fixed points of $f$:  egin{itemize} \item $x_q=1$, $x_t=1$, $x_I=\mathbf{1}$, $x_J={\mathbf{0}}$, \item $y_q=0$, $y_t=1$, $y_I=\mathbf{1}$, $y_J=\mathbf{1}$. \end{itemize}  igskip 
oindent (4) {\em $f(x)_i=x_i$ and $f(y)_i=y_i$ for all $i\in \{q,t\}\cup I$.} \medskip 
oindent Since $x_q
eq x_{\ell_0}$ and $y_q
eq y_{\ell_0}$, we have $f(x)_q=
eg x_{\ell_0}=x_q$ and $f(y)_q=
eg y_{\ell_0}=y_q$, and since $f_t$ is a disjunction, we also deduce that $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=1=x_t=y_t$. We now prove that $f(x)_I=f(y)_I=\mathbf{1}$. If $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup oldsymbol{\mu}'^1$, then $f_i$ is a disjunction and $i$ has an in-neighbor $j\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup\{t\}$, so $x_j=y_j=1$ and we deduce that $f_i(x)=f_i(y)=1$. Next, consider a clause $\mu_s$ in $ oldsymbol{\mu}$. Then $f_{\mu_s}$ is a disjunction and, since $z$ is a satisfying assignment, $\mu_s$ contains a literal $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1$ and thus $x_i=y_i=1$. If $i$ is an in-neighbor of $\mu_s$ then $f_{\mu_s}(x)=f_{\mu_s}(y)=1$. Otherwise, $i$ is an in-neighbor of $\mu'_s$, so $\mu'_s\in oldsymbol{\mu}'^1$. Thus $x_{\mu'_s}=y_{\mu'_s}=1$ and we deduce that $f_{\mu_s}(x)=f_{\mu_s}(y)=1$. This proves~(4).  igskip 
oindent (5) {\em $f(x)_J={\mathbf{0}}$.} \medskip 
oindent If $i\in oldsymbol{\mu}'^0$ then for every in-neighbor $j$ of $i$ we have $j\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0$, thus $x_j=0$, and we deduce that $f_i(x)=0$. If $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup  oldsymbol{\ell}$, then $f_i$ is a conjunction and has an in-neighbor $j\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup oldsymbol{\ell}\cup oldsymbol{c}$. Thus $x_j=0$ we deduce that $f_i(x)=0$. Setting $c_{m+1}=\ell_n$, for all $s\in [m]$ we have $f_{c_s}(x)=
eg x_{\mu_s}\lor x_{c_{s+1}}=
eg 1\lor 0=0$. This proves (5).  igskip 
oindent (6) {\em $f(y)_J=\mathbf{1}$.} \medskip 
oindent If $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup  oldsymbol{\ell}\cup  oldsymbol{\mu}'^0$ then for every in-neighbor $j$ of $i$ we have $j
eq q$, thus $y_j=1$, and we deduce that $f_i(y)=1$. If $i\in  oldsymbol{c}$ then $i$ has a positive in-neighbor $j\in oldsymbol{c}\cup\{\ell_n\}$, thus $x_j=1$, and since $f_i$ is a disjunction, we have $f_i(x)=1$. This proves (6).  igskip By (4), (5) and (6), $x$ and $y$ are fixed points of $f$ and thus $f$ is not synchronizing.
nodes.statement_short: From a satisfying assignment build an and-or-net with two fixed points, hence not synchronizing.

nodes.name: Assume a satisfying assignment
nodes.statement: \BF{($4 \Rightarrow 1$)} Suppose that $z$ is a satisfying assignment of $\psi$, and let us prove that some BN on $G_\psi$ is not synchronizing. Let $\boldsymbol{\lambda}^1$ be the literals satisfied by $z$ and $\boldsymbol{\lambda}^0$ the literals not satisfied by $z$, hence $(\boldsymbol{\lambda}^0,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^1)$ is a balanced partition of $\boldsymbol{\lambda}^+\cup\boldsymbol{\lambda}^-$. Let $f$ be the and-or-net on $G_\psi$ such that: \begin{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Take a satisfying assignment $z$ and the and-or-net with disjunctions on satisfied literals:

nodes.name: Disjunctive components
nodes.statement: \item for all $i\in \boldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup\boldsymbol{\mu}\cup\boldsymbol{\mu}'\cup\boldsymbol{c}\cup\{t\}$, $f_i$ is a disjunction;
nodes.statement_short: disjunctions on $\boldsymbol\lambda^1$, clause vertices, $\boldsymbol c$ and $t$;

nodes.name: Conjunctive components
nodes.statement: \item for all $i\in\boldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup\boldsymbol{\ell}$, $f_i$ is a conjunction. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: conjunctions on $\boldsymbol\lambda^0\cup\boldsymbol\ell$.

nodes.name: Partition I, J
nodes.statement: Let $\boldsymbol{\mu}'^1$ be the vertices in $\boldsymbol{\mu}'$ with at least one in-neighbor in $\boldsymbol{\lambda}^1$ and $\boldsymbol{\mu}'^0=\boldsymbol{\mu}'\setminus\boldsymbol{\mu}'^1$. Let $I=\boldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup\boldsymbol{\mu}'^1\cup \boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $J=\boldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup\boldsymbol{\ell}\cup\boldsymbol{c}\cup\boldsymbol{\mu}'^0$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\boldsymbol\mu'^1$, $I$ and $J$.

nodes.name: Two fixed points
nodes.statement:
Let us prove that the configurations $x,y$ on $V$ defined as follows are fixed points of $f$:  egin{itemize} \item $x_q=1$, $x_t=1$, $x_I=\mathbf{1}$, $x_J={\mathbf{0}}$, \item $y_q=0$, $y_t=1$, $y_I=\mathbf{1}$, $y_J=\mathbf{1}$. \end{itemize}  igskip 
oindent (4) {\em $f(x)_i=x_i$ and $f(y)_i=y_i$ for all $i\in \{q,t\}\cup I$.} \medskip 
oindent Since $x_q
eq x_{\ell_0}$ and $y_q
eq y_{\ell_0}$, we have $f(x)_q=
eg x_{\ell_0}=x_q$ and $f(y)_q=
eg y_{\ell_0}=y_q$, and since $f_t$ is a disjunction, we also deduce that $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=1=x_t=y_t$. We now prove that $f(x)_I=f(y)_I=\mathbf{1}$. If $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup oldsymbol{\mu}'^1$, then $f_i$ is a disjunction and $i$ has an in-neighbor $j\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup\{t\}$, so $x_j=y_j=1$ and we deduce that $f_i(x)=f_i(y)=1$. Next, consider a clause $\mu_s$ in $ oldsymbol{\mu}$. Then $f_{\mu_s}$ is a disjunction and, since $z$ is a satisfying assignment, $\mu_s$ contains a literal $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1$ and thus $x_i=y_i=1$. If $i$ is an in-neighbor of $\mu_s$ then $f_{\mu_s}(x)=f_{\mu_s}(y)=1$. Otherwise, $i$ is an in-neighbor of $\mu'_s$, so $\mu'_s\in oldsymbol{\mu}'^1$. Thus $x_{\mu'_s}=y_{\mu'_s}=1$ and we deduce that $f_{\mu_s}(x)=f_{\mu_s}(y)=1$. This proves~(4).  igskip 
oindent (5) {\em $f(x)_J={\mathbf{0}}$.} \medskip 
oindent If $i\in oldsymbol{\mu}'^0$ then for every in-neighbor $j$ of $i$ we have $j\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0$, thus $x_j=0$, and we deduce that $f_i(x)=0$. If $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup  oldsymbol{\ell}$, then $f_i$ is a conjunction and has an in-neighbor $j\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup oldsymbol{\ell}\cup oldsymbol{c}$. Thus $x_j=0$ we deduce that $f_i(x)=0$. Setting $c_{m+1}=\ell_n$, for all $s\in [m]$ we have $f_{c_s}(x)=
eg x_{\mu_s}\lor x_{c_{s+1}}=
eg 1\lor 0=0$. This proves (5).  igskip 
oindent (6) {\em $f(y)_J=\mathbf{1}$.} \medskip 
oindent If $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup  oldsymbol{\ell}\cup  oldsymbol{\mu}'^0$ then for every in-neighbor $j$ of $i$ we have $j
eq q$, thus $y_j=1$, and we deduce that $f_i(y)=1$. If $i\in  oldsymbol{c}$ then $i$ has a positive in-neighbor $j\in oldsymbol{c}\cup\{\ell_n\}$, thus $x_j=1$, and since $f_i$ is a disjunction, we have $f_i(x)=1$. This proves (6).  igskip By (4), (5) and (6), $x$ and $y$ are fixed points of $f$ and thus $f$ is not synchronizing.
nodes.statement_short: The two explicit configurations $x,y$ are fixed points of $f$.

nodes.name: (4) Fixed on q, t and I
nodes.statement:
(4) {\em $f(x)_i=x_i$ and $f(y)_i=y_i$ for all $i\in \{q,t\}\cup I$.} \medskip 
oindent Since $x_q
eq x_{\ell_0}$ and $y_q
eq y_{\ell_0}$, we have $f(x)_q=
eg x_{\ell_0}=x_q$ and $f(y)_q=
eg y_{\ell_0}=y_q$, and since $f_t$ is a disjunction, we also deduce that $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=1=x_t=y_t$. We now prove that $f(x)_I=f(y)_I=\mathbf{1}$. If $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup oldsymbol{\mu}'^1$, then $f_i$ is a disjunction and $i$ has an in-neighbor $j\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup\{t\}$, so $x_j=y_j=1$ and we deduce that $f_i(x)=f_i(y)=1$. Next, consider a clause $\mu_s$ in $ oldsymbol{\mu}$. Then $f_{\mu_s}$ is a disjunction and, since $z$ is a satisfying assignment, $\mu_s$ contains a literal $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1$ and thus $x_i=y_i=1$. If $i$ is an in-neighbor of $\mu_s$ then $f_{\mu_s}(x)=f_{\mu_s}(y)=1$. Otherwise, $i$ is an in-neighbor of $\mu'_s$, so $\mu'_s\in oldsymbol{\mu}'^1$. Thus $x_{\mu'_s}=y_{\mu'_s}=1$ and we deduce that $f_{\mu_s}(x)=f_{\mu_s}(y)=1$. This proves~(4).
nodes.statement_short: Both are fixed on $\{q,t\}\cup I$.

nodes.name: q and t are fixed
nodes.statement:
(4) {\em $f(x)_i=x_i$ and $f(y)_i=y_i$ for all $i\in \{q,t\}\cup I$.} \medskip 
oindent Since $x_q
eq x_{\ell_0}$ and $y_q
eq y_{\ell_0}$, we have $f(x)_q=
eg x_{\ell_0}=x_q$ and $f(y)_q=
eg y_{\ell_0}=y_q$, and since $f_t$ is a disjunction, we also deduce that $f_t(x)=f_t(y)=1=x_t=y_t$.
nodes.statement_short: Components $q$ and $t$ are fixed.

nodes.name: I is fixed at 1
nodes.statement: We now prove that $f(x)_I=f(y)_I=\mathbf{1}$. If $i\in\boldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup\boldsymbol{\mu}'^1$, then $f_i$ is a disjunction and $i$ has an in-neighbor $j\in\boldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup\{t\}$, so $x_j=y_j=1$ and we deduce that $f_i(x)=f_i(y)=1$. Next, consider a clause $\mu_s$ in $\boldsymbol{\mu}$. Then $f_{\mu_s}$ is a disjunction and, since $z$ is a satisfying assignment, $\mu_s$ contains a literal $i\in\boldsymbol{\lambda}^1$ and thus $x_i=y_i=1$. If $i$ is an in-neighbor of $\mu_s$ then $f_{\mu_s}(x)=f_{\mu_s}(y)=1$. Otherwise, $i$ is an in-neighbor of $\mu'_s$, so $\mu'_s\in\boldsymbol{\mu}'^1$. Thus $x_{\mu'_s}=y_{\mu'_s}=1$ and we deduce that $f_{\mu_s}(x)=f_{\mu_s}(y)=1$. This proves~(4).
nodes.statement_short: Every vertex of $I$ evaluates to 1, using the satisfying assignment for clauses.

nodes.name: Literal and auxiliary clause vertices
nodes.statement: If $i\in\boldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup\boldsymbol{\mu}'^1$, then $f_i$ is a disjunction and $i$ has an in-neighbor $j\in\boldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup\{t\}$, so $x_j=y_j=1$ and we deduce that $f_i(x)=f_i(y)=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Disjunctions with an in-neighbor at 1.

nodes.name: Clause vertices
nodes.statement: Next, consider a clause $\mu_s$ in $\boldsymbol{\mu}$. Then $f_{\mu_s}$ is a disjunction and, since $z$ is a satisfying assignment, $\mu_s$ contains a literal $i\in\boldsymbol{\lambda}^1$ and thus $x_i=y_i=1$. If $i$ is an in-neighbor of $\mu_s$ then $f_{\mu_s}(x)=f_{\mu_s}(y)=1$. Otherwise, $i$ is an in-neighbor of $\mu'_s$, so $\mu'_s\in\boldsymbol{\mu}'^1$. Thus $x_{\mu'_s}=y_{\mu'_s}=1$ and we deduce that $f_{\mu_s}(x)=f_{\mu_s}(y)=1$. This proves~(4).
nodes.statement_short: Each clause contains a satisfied literal feeding $\mu_s$ or $\mu'_s$.

nodes.name: (5) x is fixed on J
nodes.statement:
(5) {\em $f(x)_J={\mathbf{0}}$.} \medskip 
oindent If $i\in oldsymbol{\mu}'^0$ then for every in-neighbor $j$ of $i$ we have $j\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0$, thus $x_j=0$, and we deduce that $f_i(x)=0$. If $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup  oldsymbol{\ell}$, then $f_i$ is a conjunction and has an in-neighbor $j\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup oldsymbol{\ell}\cup oldsymbol{c}$. Thus $x_j=0$ we deduce that $f_i(x)=0$. Setting $c_{m+1}=\ell_n$, for all $s\in [m]$ we have $f_{c_s}(x)=
eg x_{\mu_s}\lor x_{c_{s+1}}=
eg 1\lor 0=0$. This proves (5).
nodes.statement_short: $f(x)_J=\mathbf 0$.

nodes.name: (6) y is fixed on J
nodes.statement: (6) {\em $f(y)_J=\mathbf{1}$.} \medskip \noindent If $i\in\boldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup \boldsymbol{\ell}\cup \boldsymbol{\mu}'^0$ then for every in-neighbor $j$ of $i$ we have $j\neq q$, thus $y_j=1$, and we deduce that $f_i(y)=1$. If $i\in \boldsymbol{c}$ then $i$ has a positive in-neighbor $j\in\boldsymbol{c}\cup\{\ell_n\}$, thus $x_j=1$, and since $f_i$ is a disjunction, we have $f_i(x)=1$. This proves (6).
nodes.statement_short: $f(y)_J=\mathbf 1$.

nodes.name: Not synchronizing
nodes.statement: By (4), (5) and (6), $x$ and $y$ are fixed points of $f$ and thus $f$ is not synchronizing.
nodes.statement_short: Two fixed points prevent synchronization.

nodes.name: Signed digraph $F_\psi$
nodes.statement: Let $F_\psi$ be the signed digraph obtained from $H_\psi$~by: adding a new vertex $t$ and a positive arc $(t,i)$ for all $i\in\boldsymbol{\lambda}^+\cup\boldsymbol{\lambda}^-$; making negative the arc $(c_1,\ell_0)$; deleting the arc $(\mu_s,c_s)$ for $s\in [m]$ and adding, for all $s\in [m]$, two new vertices $q_s,q'_s$ and the positive arcs $(\mu_s,q'_s),(\mu_s,q_s),(q'_s,q_s)$ and $(q_s,c_s)$.

nodes.name: Properties of $F_\psi$
nodes.statement: Thus $F_\psi$ has a unique negative arc, $(c_1,\ell_0)$, and since all the cycles of $F_\psi$ contain this arc, all the cycles of $F_\psi$ are negative (and $\ell_0$ meets every cycle). Also $F_\psi$ is simple and has maximum in-degree two, thus every BN on $F_\psi$ is an and-or-net.
conclusions: all the cycles of $F_\psi$ are negative (and $\ell_0$ meets every cycle)
$F_\psi$ is simple and has maximum in-degree two

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3 (no positive cycles case)
nodes.statement: We prove below that $\psi$ is not satisfiable if and only if every BN on $F_\psi$ is synchronizing. Since the SAT problem is NP-complete and $F_\psi$ is a valid instance of the {\sc Negative-Synchronizing-Problem}, we deduce that this problem is coNP-hard, thus the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:complexity} is completed.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce from 3-SAT via Theorem 9 on $F_\psi$, a valid instance of the Negative-Synchronizing-Problem.

nodes.name: Reduction theorem for $F_\psi$
nodes.statement: The following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $\psi$ is not satisfiable. \item Every BN on $F_\psi$ is synchronizing. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: The following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $\psi$ is not satisfiable. \item Every BN on $F_\psi$ is synchronizing. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9
nodes.statement:
\BF{($1 \Rightarrow 2$)} Suppose that $\psi$ is not satisfiable and suppose, for a contradiction, that some BN $f$ on $F_\psi$ is not synchronizing. Since $t$ is a source, there is $a\in\{0,1\}$ such that $f_t$ is the $a$-constant function. Let $u$ be a longest canalizing word from $(t,a)$. Let $b$ be the configuration on $I=\{t\}\cup\{u\}$ such that $b_t=a$ and $b_{\{u\}}$ is the image of $u$. Hence for all configurations $x$ on $V$ we have $f^{t,u}(x)_I=b$. Let $V$ be the vertex set of $F_\psi$. If $I=V$ then $t,u$ is a synchronizing word for $f$, a contradiction. Thus $I$ is a strict subset of $V$. Let $J=V\setminus I$ and let $h$ be the BN with component set $J$ defined by $h(x_J)=f(x)_J$ for all configurations $x$ on $V$ with $x_I=b$. Let $H$ be the signed interaction digraph of $h$, which is a subgraph of $F_\psi[J]$.  igskip 
oindent (1) {\em $h$ is not synchronizing.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose that $h$ has a synchronizing word $v$ and let $w=t,u,v$. For all configurations $x,y$ on $V$ we have $f^{t,u}(x)_I=f^{t,u}(y)_I=b$, and since $v$ is a word over $J$ we deduce that $f^v(f^{t,u}(x))_J=h^v(f^{t,u}(x)_J)=h^v(f^{t,u}(y)_J)=f^v(f^{t,u}(y))_J$ and thus $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$. Hence $w$ is a synchronizing word for $f$, a contradiction. This proves (1).  igskip 
oindent (2) {\em $H$ has no sources.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ has a source $i$. Then there is $c$ such that $h(x_J)_i=c$ for all configurations $x$ on $V$. So if $x_I=b$ then $f(x)_J=h(y_J)$ and thus $f(x)_i=h(x_J)_i=c$. For all configurations $x$ on $V$ with $x_t=a$, we have $f^u(x)_I=b$ and we deduce that $f^{u,i}(x)_i=c$. Since $i
ot\in I$, $u,i$ is a canalizing word from $(t,a)$ longer than $u$, a contradiction. This proves (2).  igskip 
oindent (3) {\em $H$ has a unique initial strong component, say $S$, and is homogenous.} \medskip 
oindent Let $S$ be an initial strong component of $H$. Since $H$ has no source, $S$ contains a cycle, and since all the cycles of $F_\psi$ contains the arc $(c_1,\ell_0)$, this arc is in $S$ and $S$ is the unique initial strong component of $H$. Consequently, there is a path from $\ell_0$ to each vertex in $H$, and since all the paths of $F_\psi$ starting from $\ell_0$ are full-positive, we deduce that $H$ is homogenous. This proves (3).  igskip 
oindent (4) {\em $S$ is a cycle.} \medskip 
oindent If not then $H$, by (2) and (3), $H$ has no sources and no initial cycles, and since $H$ has only negative cycles, we deduce from Theorem~ef{thm:main2} that $h$ is synchronizing, and this contradicts (1). This proves (4).  igskip 
oindent (5) {\em If $F_\psi[J]$ has an arc from $j$ to $i$ and $F_\psi$ has no arc from $I$ to $i$, then $H$ has an arc from $j$~to~$i$.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose that $F_\psi[J]$ has an arc from $j$ to $i$ and $F_\psi$ has no arc from $I$ to $i$. There is a configuration $x$ on $V$ such that $f_i(x)
eq f_i(x+e_j)$, and since $F_\psi$ has no arc from $I$ to $i$ we can choose $x$ in such a way that $x_I=b$. Then $h_i(x_J)=f_i(x)$ and since $(x+e_j)_I=b$ we have $h_i(x_J+e_j)=h_i((x+e_j)_J)=f_i(x+e_j)$. Hence $h_i(x_J)
eq h_i(x_J+e_j)$ thus $H$ has an arc from $j$ to $i$. This proves (5).  igskip 
oindent (6) {\em For all $s\in [m]$, if $\mu_s,c_s\in J$ then $(\mu_s,q_s),(q'_s,q_s),(q_s,c_s)$ are arcs of $H$.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose that $\mu_s,c_s\in J$. We deduce that $q'_s\in J$. Indeed, the unique in-neighbor of $q'_s$ is $\mu_s$, which is in $J$, and so from Lemma~ef{lem:diffusion} we have $q'_s\in J$. So the two in-neighbors of $q_s$ are in $J$ and from the same lemma we deduce that $q_s\in J$. So $\mu_s,q'_s,q_s\in J$ hence $F_\psi$ has no arc from $I$ to $q_s$ and by (5) we deduce that $(\mu_s,q_s)$ and $(q'_s,q_s)$ are arcs of $H$. If $(q_s,c_s)$ is not in $H$, we deduce from (5) that $c_{s+1}\in I$, where $c_{m+1}$ means $\ell_n$, but then $c_s$ is a source of $H$ and this contradicts (2). Thus $(q_s,c_s)$ is in $H$. This proves (6).  igskip 
oindent (7) {\em $ oldsymbol{\mu}\subseteq I$.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose, for a contradiction, that some clause $\mu_s$ is in $H$, and let $s$ be minimal for that property. If $H$ has a cycle which does not contains $c_s$, then this cycle has necessarily a vertex in $\{\mu_1,\dots,\mu_{s-1}\}$, and this contradicts the choice of $s$. Thus every cycle of $H$ contains $c_s$. Thus $c_s$ is in $S$, and we deduce from (6) that $(\mu_s,q_s),(q'_s,q_s),(q_s,c_s)$ are arcs of $H$. Hence $q_s$ is in $S$ and has two in-neighbors in $S$. Thus $S$ is not a cycle, and this contradicts (4). This proves (7).  igskip By (4) and (7), $S$ is a cycle disjoint from $ oldsymbol{\mu}$. We deduce that $S$ contains each vertex in $ oldsymbol{\ell}\cup oldsymbol{c}$ and exactly one of $\lambda^+_r,\lambda^-_r$ for each $r\in [n]$. Let $z\in\{0,1\}^n$ defined by $z_r=1$ if $\lambda^+_r$ is not in $S$ and $z_r=0$ if $\lambda^-_r$ is not in $S$; there is no ambiguity since exactly one of $\lambda^+_r,\lambda^-_r$ is in $S$. By (7) and Lemma~ef{lem:diffusion}, for each $s\in [m]$, $G[I]$ has a path from $t$ to $\mu_s$, and thus each clause $\mu_s$ contains a literals in $I$. This literal is not in $C$, thus it is satisfied by $z$. So $\psi$ is satisfied by $z$, a contradiction. We deduce that if $\psi$ is not satisfiable, then every BN on $F_\psi$ is synchronizing.  igskip 
oindent \BF{($2 \Rightarrow 1$)} Suppose that $z$ is a satisfying assignment of $\psi$, and let us prove that some BN on $F_\psi$ is not synchronizing. Let $ oldsymbol{\lambda}^1$ be the literals satisfied by $z$ and $ oldsymbol{\lambda}^0$ the literals not satisfied by $z$, hence $( oldsymbol{\lambda}^0, oldsymbol{\lambda}^1)$ is a balanced partition of $ oldsymbol{\lambda}^+\cup oldsymbol{\lambda}^-$. Let $f$ be any and-or-net on $F_\psi$ such that:  egin{itemize} \item $f_t$ is the $1$-constant function, \item for all $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup oldsymbol{\mu}\cup oldsymbol{\mu}'$, $f_i$ is a disjunction, \item for all $i\in  oldsymbol{\ell}\cup oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup  oldsymbol{c}$, $f_i$ is a conjunction. \end{itemize} \medskip Let $ oldsymbol{\mu}'^1$ be the vertices in $ oldsymbol{\mu}'$ with at least one in-neighbors in $ oldsymbol{\lambda}^1$. Let ${ oldsymbol{q}}=\{q_1,\dots,q_m\}$ and ${ oldsymbol{q}}'=\{q'_1,\dots,q'_m\}$. Let $I=\{t\}\cup  oldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup oldsymbol{\mu}'^1\cup  oldsymbol{\mu}\cup{ oldsymbol{q}}\cup{ oldsymbol{q}}'$, and let $X$ be the set of configurations $x$ on the vertex set of $F_\psi$ with $x_I=\mathbf{1}$.  igskip 
oindent (1) {\em $f(X)\subseteq X$.} \medskip 
oindent Let $x\in X$. We have $f_t(x)=1$. For every $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1$, $f_i$ is a disjunction and since $x_t=1$ we have $f_i(x)=1$. For every $i\in oldsymbol{\mu}'^1$, $f_i$ is a disjunction and $i$ has an in-neighbor $j\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1$, and since $x_j=1$ we deduce that $f_i(x)=1$. Next, consider a clause $\mu_s$ in $ oldsymbol{\mu}$. Then $f_{\mu_s}$ is a disjunction and, since $z$ is a satisfying assignment, $\mu_s$ contains a literal $i\in oldsymbol{\lambda}^1$ and thus $x_i=1$. If $i$ is an in-neighbor of $\mu_s$ then $f_{\mu_s}(x)=1$. Otherwise, $i$ is an in-neighbor of $\mu'_s$, so $\mu'_s\in oldsymbol{\mu}'^1$. Thus $x_{\mu'_s}=1$ and we deduce that $f_{\mu_s}(x)=1$. Finally every $i\in{ oldsymbol{q}}\cup { oldsymbol{q}}'$ has only in-neighbors in ${ oldsymbol{q}}'\cup oldsymbol{\mu}\subseteq I$, and we deduce that $f_i(x)=1$. Thus $f(x)_I=\mathbf{1}$, that is, $f(x)\in X$. This proves (1).  igskip Let $J= oldsymbol{\ell}\cup oldsymbol{\lambda}^0\cup oldsymbol{c}$. So $(I,J)$ is a partition of the vertices of $F_\psi$. Note $F_\psi[J]$ is a negative cycle since exactly one of $\lambda^+_r,\lambda^-_r$ is in $ oldsymbol{\lambda}^0$ for each $r\in [n]$.  igskip 
oindent (2) {\em Let $i\in J$ and let $j$ its in-neighbor in $F_\psi[J]$. For all $x,y\in X$, if $x_j
eq y_j$ then $f_i(x)
eq f_i(y)$.} \medskip 
oindent Let $x,y\in X$ with $x_j
eq y_j$. If $i=\ell_0$ then $j=c_1$ and $f_i(x)=
eg x_j
eq 
eg y_j=f_i(y)$. Otherwise, $j$ is a positive in-neighbor of $i$. Furthermore, $i$ has exactly one in-neighbor $k
eq j$, which is positive and belongs to $\{t\}\cup oldsymbol{\lambda}^1\cup{ oldsymbol{q}}\subseteq I$. Hence $x_k=y_k=1$, and since $f_i$ is a conjunction, we obtain $f_i(x)=x_j\land x_k=x_j\land 1=x_j$ and $f_i(y)=y_j\land y_k=y_j\land 1=y_j$. Thus $f_i(x)
eq f_i(y)$. This proves~(2).  igskip Let $x$ and $y$ be $J$-opposite configurations in $X$, that is, $x,y\in X$ and $x_i
eq y_i$ for all $i\in J$. Let $i\in I$. By (1) we have $f(x),f(y)\in X$ and we deduce that $f^i(x)=x$ and $f^i(y)=y$, thus $f^i(x)$ and $f^i(y)$ are $J$-opposite configurations in $X$. Let $i\in J$. Obviously, $f^i(x),f^i(y)\in X$. Furthermore, by (2) we have $f_i(x)
eq f_i(y)$, thus $f^i(x)$ and $f^i(y)$ are $J$-opposite configurations in $X$. So for any vertex $i$ in $F_\psi$, $f^i(x)$ and $f^i(y)$ are $J$-opposite configurations in $X$. Satisfiable: an invariant set on which the residual negative cycle keeps $J$-opposite configurations apart.

nodes.statement_short: A non-synchronizing BN would leave, after canalizing from $t$, an initial cycle avoiding all clauses and encoding a satisfying assignment.

nodes.name: Canalize from the source t
nodes.statement: \BF{($1 \Rightarrow 2$)} Suppose that $\psi$ is not satisfiable and suppose, for a contradiction, that some BN $f$ on $F_\psi$ is not synchronizing. Since $t$ is a source, there is $a\in\{0,1\}$ such that $f_t$ is the $a$-constant function. Let $u$ be a longest canalizing word from $(t,a)$. Let $b$ be the configuration on $I=\{t\}\cup\{u\}$ such that $b_t=a$ and $b_{\{u\}}$ is the image of $u$. Hence for all configurations $x$ on $V$ we have $f^{t,u}(x)_I=b$. Let $V$ be the vertex set of $F_\psi$. If $I=V$ then $t,u$ is a synchronizing word for $f$, a contradiction. Thus $I$ is a strict subset of $V$. Let $J=V\setminus I$ and let $h$ be the BN with component set $J$ defined by $h(x_J)=f(x)_J$ for all configurations $x$ on $V$ with $x_I=b$. Let $H$ be the signed interaction digraph of $h$, which is a subgraph of $F_\psi[J]$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a longest canalizing word from $(t,a)$ and the subnetwork $h$ on the rest.

nodes.name: (1) h is not synchronizing
nodes.statement: (1) {\em $h$ is not synchronizing.} \medskip \noindent Suppose that $h$ has a synchronizing word $v$ and let $w=t,u,v$. For all configurations $x,y$ on $V$ we have $f^{t,u}(x)_I=f^{t,u}(y)_I=b$, and since $v$ is a word over $J$ we deduce that $f^v(f^{t,u}(x))_J=h^v(f^{t,u}(x)_J)=h^v(f^{t,u}(y)_J)=f^v(f^{t,u}(y))_J$ and thus $f^w(x)=f^w(y)$. Hence $w$ is a synchronizing word for $f$, a contradiction. This proves (1).
nodes.statement_short: A synchronizing word for $h$ would synchronize $f$.

nodes.name: (2) H has no sources
nodes.statement: (2) {\em $H$ has no sources.} \medskip \noindent Suppose, for a contradiction, that $H$ has a source $i$. Then there is $c$ such that $h(x_J)_i=c$ for all configurations $x$ on $V$. So if $x_I=b$ then $f(x)_J=h(y_J)$ and thus $f(x)_i=h(x_J)_i=c$. For all configurations $x$ on $V$ with $x_t=a$, we have $f^u(x)_I=b$ and we deduce that $f^{u,i}(x)_i=c$. Since $i\not\in I$, $u,i$ is a canalizing word from $(t,a)$ longer than $u$, a contradiction. This proves (2).
nodes.statement_short: A source would extend the canalizing word.

nodes.name: (3) Unique initial component; homogeneity
nodes.statement: (3) {\em $H$ has a unique initial strong component, say $S$, and is homogenous.} \medskip \noindent Let $S$ be an initial strong component of $H$. Since $H$ has no source, $S$ contains a cycle, and since all the cycles of $F_\psi$ contains the arc $(c_1,\ell_0)$, this arc is in $S$ and $S$ is the unique initial strong component of $H$. Consequently, there is a path from $\ell_0$ to each vertex in $H$, and since all the paths of $F_\psi$ starting from $\ell_0$ are full-positive, we deduce that $H$ is homogenous. This proves (3).
nodes.statement_short: All cycles use $(c_1,\ell_0)$ and paths from $\ell_0$ are full-positive.

nodes.name: (4) S is a cycle
nodes.statement: (4) {\em $S$ is a cycle.} \medskip \noindent If not then $H$, by (2) and (3), $H$ has no sources and no initial cycles, and since $H$ has only negative cycles, we deduce from Theorem~\ref{thm:main2} that $h$ is synchronizing, and this contradicts (1). This proves (4).
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise Theorem 4 would make $h$ synchronizing.

nodes.name: (5) Arcs survive in H
nodes.statement:
(5) {\em If $F_\psi[J]$ has an arc from $j$ to $i$ and $F_\psi$ has no arc from $I$ to $i$, then $H$ has an arc from $j$~to~$i$.} \medskip 
oindent Suppose that $F_\psi[J]$ has an arc from $j$ to $i$ and $F_\psi$ has no arc from $I$ to $i$. There is a configuration $x$ on $V$ such that $f_i(x)
eq f_i(x+e_j)$, and since $F_\psi$ has no arc from $I$ to $i$ we can choose $x$ in such a way that $x_I=b$. Then $h_i(x_J)=f_i(x)$ and since $(x+e_j)_I=b$ we have $h_i(x_J+e_j)=h_i((x+e_j)_J)=f_i(x+e_j)$. Hence $h_i(x_J)
eq h_i(x_J+e_j)$ thus $H$ has an arc from $j$ to $i$. This proves (5).

nodes.name: (6) Clause gadget arcs
nodes.statement: (6) {\em For all $s\in [m]$, if $\mu_s,c_s\in J$ then $(\mu_s,q_s),(q'_s,q_s),(q_s,c_s)$ are arcs of $H$.} \medskip \noindent Suppose that $\mu_s,c_s\in J$. We deduce that $q'_s\in J$. Indeed, the unique in-neighbor of $q'_s$ is $\mu_s$, which is in $J$, and so from Lemma~\ref{lem:diffusion} we have $q'_s\in J$. So the two in-neighbors of $q_s$ are in $J$ and from the same lemma we deduce that $q_s\in J$. So $\mu_s,q'_s,q_s\in J$ hence $F_\psi$ has no arc from $I$ to $q_s$ and by (5) we deduce that $(\mu_s,q_s)$ and $(q'_s,q_s)$ are arcs of $H$. If $(q_s,c_s)$ is not in $H$, we deduce from (5) that $c_{s+1}\in I$, where $c_{m+1}$ means $\ell_n$, but then $c_s$ is a source of $H$ and this contradicts (2). Thus $(q_s,c_s)$ is in $H$. This proves (6).
nodes.statement_short: If $\mu_s,c_s\in J$ the gadget arcs are in $H$ (Lemma 6).

nodes.name: (7) Clauses are canalized
nodes.statement: (7) {\em $\boldsymbol{\mu}\subseteq I$.} \medskip \noindent Suppose, for a contradiction, that some clause $\mu_s$ is in $H$, and let $s$ be minimal for that property. If $H$ has a cycle which does not contains $c_s$, then this cycle has necessarily a vertex in $\{\mu_1,\dots,\mu_{s-1}\}$, and this contradicts the choice of $s$. Thus every cycle of $H$ contains $c_s$. Thus $c_s$ is in $S$, and we deduce from (6) that $(\mu_s,q_s),(q'_s,q_s),(q_s,c_s)$ are arcs of $H$. Hence $q_s$ is in $S$ and has two in-neighbors in $S$. Thus $S$ is not a cycle, and this contradicts (4). This proves (7).
nodes.statement_short: A clause in $H$ would give a vertex of $S$ with two in-neighbors in $S$.

nodes.name: Satisfying assignment
nodes.statement: By (4) and (7), $S$ is a cycle disjoint from $\boldsymbol{\mu}$. We deduce that $S$ contains each vertex in $\boldsymbol{\ell}\cup\boldsymbol{c}$ and exactly one of $\lambda^+_r,\lambda^-_r$ for each $r\in [n]$. Let $z\in\{0,1\}^n$ defined by $z_r=1$ if $\lambda^+_r$ is not in $S$ and $z_r=0$ if $\lambda^-_r$ is not in $S$; there is no ambiguity since exactly one of $\lambda^+_r,\lambda^-_r$ is in $S$. By (7) and Lemma~\ref{lem:diffusion}, for each $s\in [m]$, $G[I]$ has a path from $t$ to $\mu_s$, and thus each clause $\mu_s$ contains a literals in $I$. This literal is not in $C$, thus it is satisfied by $z$. So $\psi$ is satisfied by $z$, a contradiction. We deduce that if $\psi$ is not satisfiable, then every BN on $F_\psi$ is synchronizing.
nodes.statement_short: The cycle $S$ selects literals whose complements satisfy $\psi$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7
nodes.statement: We proceed by induction on $|V|$. For $|V|=1$, since $f$ has a unique fixed point, $f$ is a constant function and the result is obvious. Suppose that $|V|\geq 2$. Since all the cycles of $G$ have the same sign and $f$ has a unique fixed point, we deduce from Theorem~\ref{thm:A08} that $G$ has a source, say $i$. Hence, $f_i$ is the $a$-constant function for some $a\in\{0,1\}$. Let $I=V\setminus\{i\}$, where $V$ is the vertex set of $G$. Let $h$ be the BN with component set $I$ defined by $h(x_I)=f(x)_I$ for all configurations $x$ on $V$ with $x_i=a$. Since $f$ has a unique fixed point, $h$ has a unique fixed point, and since $f_i$ is the $a$-constant function, for every configuration $x$ on $V$ and every word $v$ we have: \[\tag{1} x_i=a~\Rightarrow~ f^v(x)_I=h^v(x_I)\textrm{ and }f^v(x)_i=a. \] Let $H$ be the signed interaction digraph of $G$. Since $H$ is a subgraph of $G$, all the cycles of $H$ have the same sign. Hence, by induction hypothesis, there is a permutation $\sigma$ of $I$ such that any word containing $\sigma$ synchronizes $h$. Let $\pi=i,\sigma$, and let $w$ be a word containing $\pi$. Since $w$ contains $i$, there is $u,v$ such that $w=u,i,v$ where $u$ does not contains $i$. So $v$ contains $\sigma$, thus $v$ synchronizes $h$. Let $x,y$ be any two configurations on $V$, and let $x'=f^{u,i}(x)$ and $y'=f^{u,i}(y)$. Since $f_i$ is the $a$-constant function, we have $x'_i=y'_i=a$, and since $v$ synchronizes $h$ we deduce from (1) that $f^v(x')_I=h^v(x'_I)=h^v(y'_I)=f^v(y')_I$ and $f^v(x')_i=f^v(y')_i=a$. Thus $f^v(x')=f^v(y')$ and this proves that $w$ synchronizes $f$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Let $\pi=i,\sigma$, and let $w$ be a word containing $\pi$. Since $w$ contains $i$, there is $u,v$ such that $w=u,i,v$ where $u$ does not contains $i$. So $v$ contains $\sigma$, thus $v$ synchronizes $h$. Let $x,y$ be any two configurations on $V$, and let $x'=f^{u,i}(x)$ and $y'=f^{u,i}(y)$. Thus $f^v(x')=f^v(y')$ and this proves that $w$ synchronizes $f$.

nodes.statement: A word $w$ is \EM{$n$-complete} if it contains all the permutations of $[n]$.
nodes.section: A Synchronizing BNs with a unique fixed point
differentia: it contains all the permutations of $[n]$

nodes.name: Derivation of Theorem 10 from the fixing result of [AGRS20]
nodes.statement: Given a word $w$ and a BN $f$ with component set $V$, we say that $w$ \EM{fixes} $f$ if $f^w(x)$ is a fixed point of $f$ for all configurations $x$ on $V$. This notion was introduced in \cite{AGRS20}, where it is proved that a word fixes every BN in $\mathcal{A}(n)$ if and only if it is $n$-complete. It is clear that if $f$ has a unique fixed point, then $w$ fixes $f$ if and only if $w$ synchronizes $f$. Also, by Theorem~\ref{thm:A08}, every BN in $\mathcal{A}(n)$ has a unique fixed point. Consequently, we can restate the result of \cite{AGRS20} mentioned above as follows.
nodes.section: A Synchronizing BNs with a unique fixed point
nodes.statement_short: Fixing and synchronizing coincide for BNs with a unique fixed point, which all BNs in $\mathcal{A}(n)$ have by Aracena's theorem.

nodes.name: Recall fixing words
nodes.statement: Given a word $w$ and a BN $f$ with component set $V$, we say that $w$ \EM{fixes} $f$ if $f^w(x)$ is a fixed point of $f$ for all configurations $x$ on $V$. This notion was introduced in \cite{AGRS20}, where it is proved that a word fixes every BN in $\mathcal{A}(n)$ if and only if it is $n$-complete.
nodes.section: A Synchronizing BNs with a unique fixed point
nodes.statement_short: Recall fixing words and the AGRS20 characterization of words fixing $\mathcal{A}(n)$.

nodes.name: Fixing equals synchronizing here
nodes.statement: It is clear that if $f$ has a unique fixed point, then $w$ fixes $f$ if and only if $w$ synchronizes $f$. Also, by Theorem~\ref{thm:A08}, every BN in $\mathcal{A}(n)$ has a unique fixed point. Consequently, we can restate the result of \cite{AGRS20} mentioned above as follows.
nodes.section: A Synchronizing BNs with a unique fixed point
nodes.statement_short: With a unique fixed point (Theorem 6) fixing equals synchronizing, giving Theorem 10.

nodes.name: Words synchronizing all acyclic BNs are the n-complete words
nodes.statement: A word synchronizes $\mathcal{A}(n)$ if and only if it is $n$-complete.

conclusions: A word synchronizes $\mathcal{A}(n)$ if and only if it is $n$-complete

nodes.name: Family $\mathcal{F}(n)$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}(n)$ be the set of $f$ BN with component set $[n]$, with a unique fixed point, and such that all the cycles of the signed interaction digraph of $f$ have the same sign.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda(n)$ be the shortest length of an $n$-complete word, and let $\ell^+(n)$ the minimum length of a word that synchronizes $\mathcal{F}^+(n)$. By the previous proposition, $\ell^+(n)=\lambda(n)$, and it is proved in \cite{KK76} that $\lambda(n)=n^2-o(n^2)$. We thus obtain Proposition~\ref{pro:l+}.

nodes.statement_short: By Proposition 11, $\ell^+(n)$ equals the shortest length of an $n$-complete word, which is $n^2-o(n^2)$ by Kleitman-Kwiatkowski.
