nodes.name: Switch normal form for digraphs with a vertex meeting every cycle
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a strong signed digraph without positive cycles. Suppose that $G$ has a vertex $i$ that meets every cycle of $G$. Then $G$ is switch equivalent to a signed digraph $H$ in which all the in-coming arcs of $i$ are negative and all the other arcs are positive.
assumptions: $G$ be a strong signed digraph without positive cycles
$G$ has a vertex $i$ that meets every cycle of $G$
conclusions: $G$ is switch equivalent to a signed digraph $H$ in which all the in-coming arcs of $i$ are negative and all the other arcs are positive
nodes.label: lem:tau11

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 15
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be the vertex set of $G$. Let $G'$ be obtained by changing the sign of every in-coming arc of $i$. Then all the cycles of $G'$ are positive. By Proposition \ref{pro:harary}, the $I$-switch $H'$ of $G'$ is full positive for some $I\subseteq V$. Let $H$ by obtained from $H'$ by making negative the in-coming arcs of~$i$. One easily check that $H$ is the $I$-switch of $G$ and thus $H$ has the desired properties.
nodes.statement_short: Negate the in-arcs of $i$ to make all cycles positive, switch to full-positive by Harary's theorem, and negate the in-arcs of $i$ back.

nodes.name: Negate in-arcs of i
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be the vertex set of $G$. Let $G'$ be obtained by changing the sign of every in-coming arc of $i$. Then all the cycles of $G'$ are positive.
nodes.statement_short: Negating the in-arcs of $i$ makes every cycle positive.

nodes.name: Apply Harary
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{pro:harary}, the $I$-switch $H'$ of $G'$ is full positive for some $I\subseteq V$.
nodes.statement_short: Harary's theorem gives a full-positive switch $H'$ of $G'$.

nodes.name: Negate back
nodes.statement: Let $H$ by obtained from $H'$ by making negative the in-coming arcs of~$i$. One easily check that $H$ is the $I$-switch of $G$ and thus $H$ has the desired properties.
nodes.statement_short: Negating the in-arcs of $i$ in $H'$ gives the $I$-switch $H$ of $G$.

nodes.name: Universal synchronizing word of length 3n-1
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a $n$-vertex strong signed digraph, which is not a cycle. Suppose that $G$ has a vertex $i$ such that: $i$ meets every cycle; all the in-coming arcs of $G$ are negative and all the other arcs are positive; $i$ is of in-degree at least two. There is a word $w$ of length $3n-1$ which synchronizes every BN $f$ on $G$ such that $f_i$ is a conjunction or a disjunction.
assumptions: $G$ be a $n$-vertex strong signed digraph, which is not a cycle
$i$ meets every cycle
all the in-coming arcs of $G$ are negative and all the other arcs are positive
$i$ is of in-degree at least two
conclusions: There is a word $w$ of length $3n-1$ which synchronizes every BN $f$ on $G$ such that $f_i$ is a conjunction or a disjunction
nodes.label: lem:tau12

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 16
nodes.statement:
Let $V$ be the vertex set of $G$, and let $u$ be a topological sort of $G\setminus i$.  igskip 
oindent (1) {\em For every configuration $x$ on $V$ and prefix $v$ of $u$, we have $f^v(x)_j=x_i$ for all $j\in\{v\}\cup\{i\}$.} \medskip 
oindent We proceed by induction on $|v|$. This is obvious for $|v|=0$. Suppose that $|v|\geq 1$. Let $v'$ be the prefix of $u$ of length $|v|-1$, thus $v=v',k$ for some $k\in V$. Let $y=f^{v'}(x)$. For all $j\in\{v'\}\cup\{i\}$, we have $f^v(x)_j=y_j=x_i$, where the induction is used for the second equality. Since all the in-neighbors of $k$ are in $\{v'\}\cup\{i\}$ and positive, we deduce that $f_k(y)=x_i$, and since $f^v(x)_k=f_k(y)=x_i$ this completes the induction. This proves~(1).  igskip Let $v=\epsilon$ if $i$ has a loop, and let $v$ be the shortest prefix of $u$ containing an in-neighbor of $i$ otherwise. Note that $|v|\leq n-1$ since $|u|=n-1$. Let \[ w=u,i,v,i,u, \] of length $2n+|v|\leq 3n-1$. Let $f$ be a BN on $G$ such that $f_i$ is a conjunction or a disjunction. We will prove that $w$ synchronizes $f$. Let $x$ be any configuration on $V$. Let $y$ the configuration on $V$ such that $y_j=x_i$ for all $j\in V$. Let $I=\{v\}\cup\{i\}$, which contains an in-neighbor of $i$, and $z=y+e_I$. By (1) we have $f^u(x)=y$. Since $i$ has only negative in-neighbors, $f^i(y)=y+e_i$. We then deduce from (1) that $f^v(y+e_i)=y+e_I=z$. Let $j$ be an in-neighbor of $i$ in $I$. Since $i$ if of in-degree at least two, it has an in-neighbor $k
ot\in I$. Then $z_j=y_j+1=x_i+1$ and $z_k=y_k=x_i$. Thus $z_j
eq z_k$ and we deduce that $f(z)_i=0$ if $f_i$ is a conjunction, and $f(z)_i=1$ if $f_i$ is a disjunction. We deduce from (1) that $f^{i,u}(z)={\mathbf{0}}$ if $f_i$ is a conjunction, and $f^{i,u}(z)=\mathbf{1}$ if $f_i$ is a disjunction. Since $f^{u,i,v}(x)=z$ we have $f^w(x)=f^{i,u}(z)$. Hence $f^w(x)={\mathbf{0}}$ if $f_i$ is a conjunction and $f^w(x)=\mathbf{1}$ if $f_i$ is a disjunction. Thus $w$ synchronizes~$f$.
nodes.statement_short: A topological sort $u$ of $G\setminus i$ copies $x_i$ everywhere; the word $u,i,v,i,u$ creates disagreement among the in-neighbors of $i$, forcing $f_i$ to a constant and then propagating it.

nodes.name: (1) Prefixes of u copy x_i
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be the vertex set of $G$, and let $u$ be a topological sort of $G\setminus i$. \bigskip \noindent (1) {\em For every configuration $x$ on $V$ and prefix $v$ of $u$, we have $f^v(x)_j=x_i$ for all $j\in\{v\}\cup\{i\}$.} \medskip \noindent We proceed by induction on $|v|$. This is obvious for $|v|=0$. Suppose that $|v|\geq 1$. Let $v'$ be the prefix of $u$ of length $|v|-1$, thus $v=v',k$ for some $k\in V$. Let $y=f^{v'}(x)$. For all $j\in\{v'\}\cup\{i\}$, we have $f^v(x)_j=y_j=x_i$, where the induction is used for the second equality. Since all the in-neighbors of $k$ are in $\{v'\}\cup\{i\}$ and positive, we deduce that $f_k(y)=x_i$, and since $f^v(x)_k=f_k(y)=x_i$ this completes the induction. This proves~(1).
nodes.statement_short: With $u$ a topological sort of $G\setminus i$, every prefix of $u$ copies $x_i$ onto the updated vertices.

nodes.name: Define w = u,i,v,i,u
nodes.statement: Let $v=\epsilon$ if $i$ has a loop, and let $v$ be the shortest prefix of $u$ containing an in-neighbor of $i$ otherwise. Note that $|v|\leq n-1$ since $|u|=n-1$. Let \[ w=u,i,v,i,u, \] of length $2n+|v|\leq 3n-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $v$ and $w=u,i,v,i,u$ of length $\leq 3n-1$.

nodes.name: Trace w
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a BN on $G$ such that $f_i$ is a conjunction or a disjunction. We will prove that $w$ synchronizes $f$. Let $x$ be any configuration on $V$. Let $y$ the configuration on $V$ such that $y_j=x_i$ for all $j\in V$. Let $I=\{v\}\cup\{i\}$, which contains an in-neighbor of $i$, and $z=y+e_I$. By (1) we have $f^u(x)=y$. Since $i$ has only negative in-neighbors, $f^i(y)=y+e_i$. We then deduce from (1) that $f^v(y+e_i)=y+e_I=z$.
nodes.statement_short: Applying $u$, $i$, $v$ yields $z=y+e_I$.

nodes.name: In-neighbors of i disagree
nodes.statement: Let $j$ be an in-neighbor of $i$ in $I$. Since $i$ if of in-degree at least two, it has an in-neighbor $k\not\in I$. Then $z_j=y_j+1=x_i+1$ and $z_k=y_k=x_i$. Thus $z_j\neq z_k$ and we deduce that $f(z)_i=0$ if $f_i$ is a conjunction, and $f(z)_i=1$ if $f_i$ is a disjunction.
nodes.statement_short: Two in-neighbors of $i$ disagree in $z$, so $f_i(z)$ is 0 (conjunction) or 1 (disjunction).

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: We deduce from (1) that $f^{i,u}(z)={\mathbf{0}}$ if $f_i$ is a conjunction, and $f^{i,u}(z)=\mathbf{1}$ if $f_i$ is a disjunction. Since $f^{u,i,v}(x)=z$ we have $f^w(x)=f^{i,u}(z)$. Hence $f^w(x)={\mathbf{0}}$ if $f_i$ is a conjunction and $f^w(x)=\mathbf{1}$ if $f_i$ is a disjunction. Thus $w$ synchronizes~$f$.
nodes.statement_short: The final $i,u$ sends every configuration to $\mathbf 0$ or $\mathbf 1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5
nodes.statement: If $\tau(G)=0$, then, by Lemma \ref{lem:acyclic_image}, there is a word of length $n$ which synchronizes every BN on $G$ and we are done. Suppose that $\tau(G)=1$. Since $G$ is not a cycle, it has a vertex $i$ of in-degree at least two that meets every cycle of $G$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:tau11}, $G$ is switch equivalent to a signed digraph $H$ which satisfies the conditions of Lemma~\ref{lem:tau12}. By this lemma, there is a word $w$ of length at most $3n-1$ which synchronizes every and-or-net on $H$. We then deduce from Proposition~\ref{pro:BN_switch} that $w$ synchronizes every and-or-net on $G$.
nodes.statement_short: $\tau(G)=0$ by Lemma 14; $\tau(G)=1$ by switching to the normal form of Lemma 15 and applying Lemma 16.

nodes.name: Acyclic case
nodes.statement: If $\tau(G)=0$, then, by Lemma \ref{lem:acyclic_image}, there is a word of length $n$ which synchronizes every BN on $G$ and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: If $\tau(G)=0$, a topological sort synchronizes every BN (Lemma 14).

nodes.name: Case tau = 1
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\tau(G)=1$. Since $G$ is not a cycle, it has a vertex $i$ of in-degree at least two that meets every cycle of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick a vertex of in-degree $\geq2$ meeting every cycle.

nodes.name: Normal form and Lemma 16
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:tau11}, $G$ is switch equivalent to a signed digraph $H$ which satisfies the conditions of Lemma~\ref{lem:tau12}. By this lemma, there is a word $w$ of length at most $3n-1$ which synchronizes every and-or-net on $H$.
nodes.statement_short: Switch to the normal form (Lemma 15) and apply Lemma 16.

nodes.name: Switch back
nodes.statement: We then deduce from Proposition~\ref{pro:BN_switch} that $w$ synchronizes every and-or-net on $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 4 transfers the word back to $G$.

nodes.name: Sets containing all coordinate flips have at least n+1 elements
nodes.statement: Let $X\subseteq \{0,1\}^n$ such that, for all $i\in [n]$, there is $x,y\in X$ that only differ in component $i$. We have $|X|\geq n+1$.
nodes.section: C A result mentioned in Remark 1
assumptions: $X\subseteq \{0,1\}^n$ such that, for all $i\in [n]$, there is $x,y\in X$ that only differ in component $i$
conclusions: We have $|X|\geq n+1$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 12
nodes.statement: We proceed by induction on $n$. The case $n=1$ is obvious. Suppose that $n\geq 2$ and let $I=[n-1]$. For $a=0,1$, let $X^a=\{x_I\mid x\in X, x_n=a\}$. For every $i\in I$, there is $x,y\in X$ that only differ in $i$, so $x_I$ and $y_I$ only differ in $i$, and $x_I,y_I\in X^0\cup X^1$. Since $X^0\cup X^1\subseteq \{0,1\}^{n-1}$, by induction hypothesis, \[ n\leq |X^0\cup X^1|=|X^0|+|X^1|-|X^0\cap X^1|=|X|-|X^0\cap X^1|. \] Let $x,y\in X$ that only differ in $n$, say $x_n<y_n$. Then $x_I\in X^0$ and $y_I\in X^1$, and since $x_I=y_I$ we deduce that $|X^0\cap X^1|\geq 1$ and thus $|X|\geq n+1$.
nodes.section: C A result mentioned in Remark 1
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$: project $X$ along the last coordinate; the union of projections has at least $n$ elements and the two halves intersect.

nodes.name: Induction on n; base case
nodes.statement: We proceed by induction on $n$. The case $n=1$ is obvious.
nodes.section: C A result mentioned in Remark 1
nodes.statement_short: Induct on $n$; $n=1$ is trivial.

nodes.name: Project along coordinate n
nodes.statement: Suppose that $n\geq 2$ and let $I=[n-1]$. For $a=0,1$, let $X^a=\{x_I\mid x\in X, x_n=a\}$. For every $i\in I$, there is $x,y\in X$ that only differ in $i$, so $x_I$ and $y_I$ only differ in $i$, and $x_I,y_I\in X^0\cup X^1$. Since $X^0\cup X^1\subseteq \{0,1\}^{n-1}$, by induction hypothesis, \[ n\leq |X^0\cup X^1|=|X^0|+|X^1|-|X^0\cap X^1|=|X|-|X^0\cap X^1|. \]
nodes.section: C A result mentioned in Remark 1
nodes.statement_short: The projections $X^0\cup X^1$ satisfy the hypothesis in dimension $n-1$, so $n\leq |X|-|X^0\cap X^1|$.

nodes.name: Projections intersect
nodes.statement: Let $x,y\in X$ that only differ in $n$, say $x_n<y_n$. Then $x_I\in X^0$ and $y_I\in X^1$, and since $x_I=y_I$ we deduce that $|X^0\cap X^1|\geq 1$ and thus $|X|\geq n+1$.
nodes.section: C A result mentioned in Remark 1
nodes.statement_short: A pair differing only in $n$ gives $|X^0\cap X^1|\geq 1$.
